articles.title: 静止摩擦力と静止摩擦係数
articles.titleEn: Static friction and the coefficient of static friction
articles.latexEn:
Key points
  • Maximum static friction $F_s$: the largest static friction force acting just before the object starts to move.
  • Coefficient of static friction ${\mu_s}$: the dimensionless ratio of the maximum static friction to the normal force.
  • By definition, $\displaystyle \mu_s = \frac{F_s}{N}$.
Setup

(1) A string is attached to an object of mass ${m}$ on a table, and the pulling force is gradually increased until the object is about to move. The maximum force ${F_{s}}$ at that instant is measured. Find the coefficient of static friction ${\mu_s}$.

(2) Substitute the measured values ${m=651[g]}$ and ${F_{s}=2.5[N]}$ to find ${\mu_s}$.

Theory

By definition, the maximum static friction is the product of the normal force ${N}$ and the coefficient of static friction ${\mu_s}$: $F_{s} = \mu_s N$

On a horizontal surface the normal force equals the object's weight: $N = mg$

Therefore the maximum static friction is: $F_{s} = \mu_s mg$

Solving for the coefficient gives $\displaystyle \mu_s = \frac{F_{s}}{mg}$.

Substituting $m=651[g]=0.651[kg]$, $F_{s}=2.5[N]$ yields $\displaystyle \mu_{s}=\frac{2.5}{0.651 \cdot 9.8} \fallingdotseq 0.39$
Answer

The coefficient of static friction ${\mu_s}$ is $\displaystyle \mu_s = \frac{F_{s}}{mg}$. Every quantity on the right-hand side can be measured, so ${\mu_s}$ can be found experimentally. With $m=651[g]$ and $F_{s}=2.5[N]$, $\mu_s \fallingdotseq 0.39$.

articles.title: 動摩擦力と動摩擦係数
articles.titleEn: Kinetic friction and the coefficient of kinetic friction
articles.latexEn:
Key points
  • Kinetic friction $F_k$: the friction force while the object is moving, opposite to the direction of motion.
  • Coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k$: defined as the ratio of kinetic friction to the normal force.
  • By definition, $\displaystyle \mu_k = \frac{F_k}{N}$.
  • On a horizontal surface, $N = mg$, so $\displaystyle \mu_k = \frac{F_k}{mg}$.
  • At constant speed, tension $T$ balances kinetic friction $F_k$: $F_k = T$.
Setup

(1) A string is attached to an object of mass ${m}$ on a table and pulled slowly at constant speed so that the tension $T$ can be measured. Find the coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k$.

(2) Substitute the measured values ${m=151[g]}$ and ${T=0.3[N]}$ to find ${\mu_k}$.

Theory

When the object moves at constant speed, the acceleration $a$ is $0$, so the net force from $ma = F$ is $F = 0$.

Thus tension $T$ and kinetic friction $F_k$ are in balance: $F_k = T$

Kinetic friction is the product of the normal force $N$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k$: $F_k = \mu_k N$

On a horizontal surface, $N = mg$, so $F_k = \mu_k mg$

Therefore $\displaystyle \mu_k = \frac{F_k}{mg} = \frac{T}{mg}$:

Substituting $m = 151[g] = 0.151[kg]$, $T = 0.3[N]$ gives $\displaystyle \mu_k =\frac{0.3}{0.151 \cdot 9.8} \fallingdotseq 0.20$

Answer

The coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k$ is $\displaystyle \mu_k = \frac{T}{mg}$. Every quantity on the right-hand side can be measured, so $\mu_k$ can be found experimentally.

With $m=151[g]$ and $T=0.3[N]$, $\mu_k \fallingdotseq 0.20$.

articles.title: 水平面上の動摩擦力
articles.titleEn: Kinetic friction on a horizontal surface
articles.latexEn:
Key points

On a horizontal surface the only horizontal force is kinetic friction. The normal force is $N=mg$, so the magnitude of kinetic friction is $\mu mg$. Taking rightward as positive, the acceleration is

$$a=-\mu g$$

Mass cancels and does not appear in the acceleration. After a slide with initial speed $v_0$ to the right, until the speed reaches 0,

$$x=v_0 t-\frac{1}{2}\mu g t^{2},\quad v=v_0-\mu g t$$

The stopping time and distance are

$$t=\frac{v_0}{\mu g},\quad x=\frac{v_0^{2}}{2\mu g}$$

After stopping, both velocity and friction are 0. The block does not reverse and come back. If $\mu=0$, then $a=0$ and the motion remains uniform rectilinear.

articles.title: 斜面上の動摩擦力
articles.latexEn:
Key points

This is an incline of angle $\theta$. Take the downhill direction as positive. The normal force is $N=mg\cos\theta$.

When at rest, the downhill component of weight is $mg\sin\theta$. With coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$, if $\displaystyle \mu_s\ge\tan\theta$ static friction cancels this component and the block does not start sliding. If $\displaystyle \mu_s<\tan\theta$, static friction cannot hold it and it starts to slide.

While sliding, the magnitude of kinetic friction is $\mu mg\cos\theta$ uphill. The acceleration is

$$a=g(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)$$

While moving,

$$s=v_0 t+\frac{1}{2}at^{2},\quad v=v_0+at$$

If $\mu>\tan\theta$, the block decelerates and stops. The stopping time and distance are

$$t=\frac{v_0}{g(\mu\cos\theta-\sin\theta)},\quad s=\frac{v_0^{2}}{2g(\mu\cos\theta-\sin\theta)}$$

After stopping, the velocity stays 0; it does not reverse. Here $\displaystyle \mu_s\ge\mu+0.15$, so if $\mu>\tan\theta$ it also will not start sliding again after stopping. If $\mu<\tan\theta$ it keeps accelerating; if $\mu=\tan\theta$ the speed is constant. When $\theta=0$ the result reduces to the horizontal case $a=-\mu g$.

articles.title: 浮力と作用反作用
articles.latexEn:
Key points 1

Archimedes' principle: "An object in a fluid experiences a buoyancy equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces."

The magnitude of the buoyancy is $ F = \rho V g $:

Here, $F$ is the buoyancy [N], $\rho$ is the fluid density [kg/m³], $V$ is the object's volume [m³], and $g$ is the gravitational acceleration [m/s²].

Key points 2

Action–reaction law: $\overrightarrow{F}_{1 \leftarrow 2} + \overrightarrow{F}_{2 \leftarrow 1} = \overrightarrow{0}$

Setup

A container of water sits on a scale. If a weight hung from a string is submerged in the water, how does the scale reading change?

Theory
Buoyancy is the upward force that water exerts on the object, so by the action–reaction law the water receives an equal downward force.

The buoyancy on the weight is $F = \rho V g $

Therefore the water receives a downward force $\rho V g $ from the object.

The scale supports this, so the normal force $N$ that the scale exerts on the water and container is the sum of the weight $Mg$ of the water and container and the reaction to the buoyancy $\rho V g$. The weight of the hanging mass itself is supported by the string and does not rest on the scale.

$$\displaystyle N = Mg + \rho V g$$

Answer

Compared with before the weight was submerged, the scale reading increases by the buoyancy $\rho V g$.

articles.title: 浮力(食塩水・普通の水・油での比較)
articles.titleEn: Buoyancy (salt water, fresh water, and oil)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Archimedes' principle: "An object in a fluid experiences a buoyancy equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces."

The magnitude of the buoyancy is$\ F = \rho V g $

Here, $F$ is the buoyancy [N], $\rho$ is the fluid density [kg/m³], $V$ is the object's volume [m³], and $g$ is the gravitational acceleration [m/s²].

Setup

A wooden rod of radius $r=0.5\,\mathrm{cm}$, length $L=20\,\mathrm{cm}$, and mass $m=8\,\mathrm{g}$ has volume $\displaystyle V=\pi r^{2}L=5\pi\,[\mathrm{cm^3}]$.

When it floats in fluids of density

  • saturated salt water: $\rho_{salt}=1.20\,[\mathrm{g/cm^3}]$
  • fresh water: $\rho_{water}=0.998\,[\mathrm{g/cm^3}]$
  • oil: $\rho_{oil}=0.90\,[\mathrm{g/cm^3}]$

what is the submerged length in each case?

Theory

From force balance and Archimedes' principle,

$$\begin{aligned} m g &= \rho_{fluid}\,\pi r^2\,l_{fluid}\,g \\ \ \\ \Leftrightarrow \ l_{fluid} &= L\frac{\rho}{\rho_{fluid}} \end{aligned}$$

Here the wood density is $\displaystyle \rho = \frac{m}{\pi r^2 L}=0.509\,[\mathrm{g/cm^3}]$.

Therefore,

$$ l_{salt} = 20 \times \frac{0.509}{1.20} \fallingdotseq 8.48\,[\mathrm{cm}] $$

$$ l_{water} = 20 \times \frac{0.509}{0.998} \fallingdotseq 10.20\,[\mathrm{cm}] $$

$$ l_{oil} = 20 \times \frac{0.509}{0.90} \fallingdotseq 11.31\,[\mathrm{cm}] $$

articles.title: バネの伸びと弾性力の関係
articles.titleEn: Spring extension and elastic force (Hooke's law)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

$\displaystyle F=-kx$（$F$: elastic force, $k$: spring constant, $x$: displacement）

The spring constant $k$ measures how stiff the spring is.

Explanation

The results of this experiment are shown below.

Fitting a least-squares regression line in Python gives $y=3.95x+0.09$, which matches the data well.

Note

A real spring needs a certain force before it begins to stretch.

The value at zero extension (0.09 in this case) is called the initial tension.

The coefficient of $x$ (3.95 here) is the spring constant.

articles.title: 水平バネ
articles.latexEn:
Key points

On a smooth horizontal surface, the only force is the spring force. With displacement $x$ from equilibrium (natural length),

$$\displaystyle m\ddot x=-kx,\quad \omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$

Released from initial position $x_0$ and initial velocity $v_0$ relative to equilibrium, taking rightward as positive,

$$\displaystyle x=x_0\cos\omega t+\frac{v_0}{\omega}\sin\omega t$$

The period does not depend on the initial position or initial velocity.

$$\displaystyle T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$

articles.title: 水平バネ(粗い床)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

On a rough horizontal surface, the normal force is $N=mg$. While moving, taking rightward as positive,

$$\displaystyle m\ddot x=-kx-\mu' mg\,\mathrm{sgn}(v)$$

Kinetic friction opposes the velocity and has magnitude $\mu' mg$. The motion is simple harmonic motion about an equilibrium shifted by $\displaystyle \delta'=\frac{\mu' mg}{k}$. Each half-period, the amplitude decreases by $2\delta'$.

When the velocity becomes 0, if the spring force magnitude $|kx|$ is at most the static friction $\mu mg$, the mass stops there.

$$\displaystyle |x|\le \frac{\mu mg}{k}$$

Static friction acts only when the velocity is 0 and does no work. The lost mechanical energy becomes heat.

articles.title: 鉛直バネ
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A vertically hanging spring equilibrates a distance $\displaystyle \delta=\frac{mg}{k}$ below its natural length. With displacement $x$ from equilibrium,

$$\displaystyle m\ddot x=-kx,\quad \omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$

Gravity only shifts the equilibrium position; it does not enter the period.

$$\displaystyle T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$

From a distance $y_0$ below the ceiling with initial velocity $v_0$, taking downward positive from equilibrium $\displaystyle y_{\mathrm{eq}}=\ell+\delta$,

$$\displaystyle y=y_{\mathrm{eq}}+(y_0-y_{\mathrm{eq}})\cos\omega t+\frac{v_0}{\omega}\sin\omega t$$

Released gently from the natural length $y_0=\ell$, the amplitude is exactly $\delta$.

articles.title: 鉛直バネ
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The period of a vertical spring oscillator depends only on the mass and the spring constant, regardless of gravity.

$$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$

Here, $T$: period [s], $m$: mass [kg], $k$: spring constant [N/m]

Setup

A mass $m = 0.1\,\mathrm{kg}$ is attached to a spring of spring constant $k = 4.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and hung vertically. Find the period $T$ when it undergoes simple harmonic motion along the vertical direction.

Theory

The period of simple harmonic motion is

$$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$

Substituting the given values,

$$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{0.1}{4.0}} = 2\pi \sqrt{0.025} \fallingdotseq 0.99\,\mathrm{s}$$

Answer
$$\boxed{T \fallingdotseq 0.99\,\mathrm{s}}$$

articles.title: 浮力による単振動
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Consider an object of constant horizontal cross section. Let the object density be $\rho_0$, height $H$, cross-sectional area $S$, and liquid density $\rho$. The mass is $m=\rho_0 S H$.

Take downward as positive, the water surface as $0$, and the depth of the object's bottom as $y$. When only partly submerged, the submerged length is $y$, so the buoyancy is $\rho S y g$.

$$my''=mg-\rho Syg$$

The bottom depth at which weight and buoyancy balance (the draft) is $\displaystyle h=\frac{\rho_0}{\rho}H$. With displacement $x=y-h$ from there, while the object neither leaves the water nor fully submerges,

$$\displaystyle x''=-\frac{\rho g}{\rho_0 H}x,\quad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\rho_0 H}{\rho g}}$$

The area $S$ cancels. The liquid density $\rho$ remains in the period. Increasing $\rho$ makes $h$ shallower, and the same period can be written $\displaystyle T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}$.

When fully submerged, the buoyancy is the constant $\rho SHg$, and the acceleration is $\displaystyle a=g\left(1-\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}\right)$. In air, only gravity acts.

articles.title: ばね上の台とおもり
articles.titleEn: Platform and mass on a spring
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A flat platform of mass $M$ sits on a vertical spring fixed to the floor, with a mass $m$ on the platform. Let the spring constant be $k$, take downward as positive, and set the natural length at $y=0$. While the mass stays on the platform they move as one:

$$\displaystyle (M+m)\ddot y=(M+m)g-ky$$

With displacement $x=y-\delta$ from equilibrium $\displaystyle \delta=\frac{(M+m)g}{k}$,

$$\displaystyle \ddot x=-\omega^{2}x,\quad \omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{M+m}},\quad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{M+m}{k}}$$

From the mass equation $\displaystyle mg-N=ma$, the normal force is

$$\displaystyle N=m(g-a)=\frac{mky}{M+m}$$

At the natural length $y=0$, $N=0$. Released gently from compression, the opposite turning point is $2\delta-y_0$, so if $y_0\ge 2\delta$ the mass leaves the platform along the way. After separation the mass is in free fall and the platform undergoes simple harmonic motion with mass $M$ alone.

Let $e$ be the coefficient of restitution on recontact ($e=0$ sticks as one body, $e=1$ is perfectly elastic). Momentum conservation and

$$\displaystyle v_m'-v_M'=-e(v_m-v_M)$$

determine the post-collision velocities; if $e>0$ they bounce and separate again.

articles.title: 自由落下
articles.latexEn:
Key points

$\displaystyle x(t)=\frac12 gt^2$（$x$: displacement, $g$: gravitational acceleration, $t$: time）

$\displaystyle t=\sqrt{\frac{2x}{g}}$（$t$: time, $x$: displacement, $g$: gravitational acceleration）

Setup

An object is released from rest at height $h$. Ignoring air resistance, find the time to reach the ground and the velocity on impact for $h = 0.60$ m and $h = 1.00$ m.

Theory

In free fall with initial velocity $v_0 = 0$, $\displaystyle t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$,   $v = \sqrt{2gh}$

Take $g = 9.8 \, [m/s^2]$.

(1) Height $h = 0.60$ m:

Time to reach the ground: $\displaystyle t = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 0.60}{9.8}} \fallingdotseq 0.350$ s

Impact velocity: $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 0.60} \fallingdotseq 3.43$ m/s

(2) Height $h = 1.00$ m:

Time to reach the ground: $\displaystyle t = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.00}{9.8}} \fallingdotseq 0.452$ s

Impact velocity: $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 1.00} \fallingdotseq 4.43$ m/s

Answer

・For height 0.60 m: $t \fallingdotseq 0.350$ s, $v \fallingdotseq 3.43$ m/s

・For height 1.00 m: $t \fallingdotseq 0.452$ s, $v \fallingdotseq 4.43$ m/s

articles.title: 自由落下
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Ignoring air resistance, the only force is gravity. The acceleration is always downward $g$ and does not depend on mass.

Taking upward as positive and releasing gently from height $h$,

$$\displaystyle y=h-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2},\quad v=-gt$$

The time and speed to reach the ground are

$$\displaystyle t=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}},\quad |v|=\sqrt{2gh}$$

articles.title: 鉛直投げ上げ・投げ下げ
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Ignoring air resistance, the only force is gravity. The acceleration is always downward $g$ and does not depend on the throw direction.

Take upward as positive. Vertical throw upward (initial speed $v_0$ from the ground):

$$\displaystyle y=v_0 t-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2},\quad v=v_0-gt$$

At the highest point $v=0$, but the force remains $mg$ downward.

$$\displaystyle H=\frac{v_0^{2}}{2g}$$

Vertical throw downward (downward initial speed $v_0$ from height $h$):

$$\displaystyle y=h-v_0 t-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2},\quad v=-(v_0+gt)$$

articles.title: 速度比例の空気抵抗
articles.latexEn:
Key points

When drag is proportional to velocity and upward is taken as positive, the equation of motion is

$$ma=-mg-bv$$

Writing $\displaystyle k=\frac{b}{m}$,

$$a=-g-kv$$

As the speed increases, so does the drag, and the downward acceleration becomes smaller. The speed at which the acceleration is zero is the terminal speed,

$$v_t=\frac{g}{k}=\frac{mg}{b}$$

For initial height $y_0$ and initial velocity $v_0$ (upward positive),

$$v(t)=-v_t+(v_0+v_t)e^{-kt}$$

$$y(t)=y_0-v_t t+\frac{v_0+v_t}{k}\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)$$

Released from rest ($v_0=0$), the speed approaches the terminal speed but never reaches it in finite time. Thrown downward faster than the terminal speed, the drag exceeds gravity and the speed decreases toward the terminal value. After a throw upward, the return speed is smaller than the launch speed.

articles.title: 斜方投射
articles.latexEn:
Key points

From a platform of height $h$, launch with speed $v_0$ at angle $\theta$ from the horizontal. Upward $\theta$ is positive and downward is negative. Neglecting air resistance, the horizontal motion is uniform and the vertical motion is under gravity alone.

$$\displaystyle x=(v_0\cos\theta)\,t$$

$$\displaystyle y=h+(v_0\sin\theta)\,t-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$$

$$\displaystyle v_x=v_0\cos\theta,\quad v_y=v_0\sin\theta-gt$$

The time to reach the ground $y=0$ is

$$\displaystyle T=\frac{v_0\sin\theta+\sqrt{(v_0\sin\theta)^{2}+2gh}}{g}$$

For an upward launch ($\theta>0$), the apex is $\displaystyle H=h+\frac{(v_0\sin\theta)^{2}}{2g}$. For a downward launch ($\theta\le 0$), the launch point is the highest point and the height remains $h$.

articles.title: 定滑車(アトウッドの器械)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Assume the fixed pulley is light, with no axle friction or inertia. The string is inextensible and massless. Let the left mass be $m_1$ and the right mass $m_2$.

Because the string does not stretch, if the left mass descends by $s$, the right mass rises by $s$. The magnitude of the acceleration is the same on both sides. Taking downward on the left as positive,

$$a=\frac{(m_1-m_2)g}{m_1+m_2}$$

The tension is the same on both sides:

$$T=\frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1+m_2}$$

Released from rest, until one mass hits the floor,

$$s=\frac{1}{2}at^{2},\quad v=at$$

If $m_1>m_2$, the left side descends; if $m_1

The time and speed until the descending side travels distance $h$ to the floor are

$$t=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{|a|}},\quad |v|=\sqrt{2|a|h}$$

articles.title: 動滑車
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A string over a fixed pulley has mass $M$ on one end and a movable pulley on the other. The movable pulley together with the object hanging from it is treated as mass $m$. The pulleys have no inertia or friction, and the string does not stretch.

Two segments of string support the movable pulley, so if mass $M$ descends by $x$, the movable pulley rises by $\displaystyle \frac{x}{2}$. With upward acceleration $\alpha$ of the movable pulley and downward acceleration $\beta$ of mass $M$, one has $\beta=2\alpha$.

$$m\alpha=2T-mg,\quad M\beta=Mg-T$$

$$ \alpha=\frac{(2M-m)g}{m+4M},\quad \beta=\frac{2(2M-m)g}{m+4M},\quad T=\frac{3mMg}{m+4M} $$

If $2M>m$, the movable pulley rises and mass $M$ descends. If $m>2M$, the movable pulley descends. If $2M=m$, then $\alpha=0$ and the tension is $\displaystyle T=\frac{1}{2}mg$.

Released from rest, when the movable pulley has moved a distance $\displaystyle \frac{h}{2}$ ($h$ is the magnitude of the displacement of mass $M$), the speed of mass $M$ is

$$v=2\sqrt{\frac{|2M-m|gh}{m+4M}}$$

articles.title: 動く斜面と慣性力
articles.latexEn:
Key points

On a smooth horizontal surface sits a cart of mass $M$ with incline angle $\theta$. The incline is also smooth and has length $l$. Place a small block of mass $m$ gently at the top; the cart does not rotate and accelerates to the right with acceleration $A$.

In the lab frame, the only horizontal force on the block is a component of the normal force. The cart feels the reaction.

$$m\ddot x=-N\sin\theta,\quad MA=N\sin\theta$$

Together with the condition that the block stays on the incline,

$$A=\frac{mg\sin\theta\cos\theta}{M+m\sin^{2}\theta}$$

The relative acceleration along the incline is $a=g\sin\theta+A\cos\theta$, and the time to slide off is

$$t=\sqrt{\frac{2l}{a}}$$

In the frame moving with the cart, add a leftward inertial force $mA$ to analyze the block. The list of forces differs, but $A$, $t$, and the cart displacement $L$ are the same. With no external horizontal force the center of mass does not move horizontally, and

$$L=\frac{ml\cos\theta}{M+m}$$

articles.title: エレベータの上昇・下降
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Hang an object from the elevator ceiling by a string. The object is at rest relative to the elevator, so in the lab frame it has the same acceleration $a$ as the elevator. Taking upward as positive,

$$T-mg=ma,\quad T=m(g+a)$$

When accelerating while ascending, $a=+A$ and the tension exceeds the weight. When accelerating while descending, $a=-A$ and the tension is

$$T=m(g-A)$$

To an observer moving with the elevator, the object is at rest. Adding an inertial force $ma$ opposite to the acceleration, tension, gravity, and the inertial force balance. The resulting $T$ matches the lab-frame value.

articles.title: 加速する電車の振り子
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A train moves to the right with constant acceleration $A$. A mass $m$ hangs from the ceiling on a string of length $l$. The angle $\theta$ is measured from the downward vertical, positive in the direction of the acceleration.

When the mass is at rest relative to the train, in the lab frame it also has acceleration $A$. Only gravity and tension act, and the string tilts by an angle $a$ opposite to the acceleration.

$$T\sin a=mA,\quad T\cos a=mg,\quad \tan a=\frac{A}{g},\quad T=m\sqrt{g^{2}+A^{2}}$$

Inside the train the mass is at rest. Adding an inertial force $mA$ opposite to the acceleration gives the same $a$ and $T$ in equilibrium.

While swinging, the angular equation is the same in the lab frame and in the train.

$$l\ddot{\theta}=-g\sin\theta-A\cos\theta$$

The period of small oscillations about equilibrium is that of an ordinary pendulum with $g$ replaced by $\displaystyle g_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sqrt{g^{2}+A^{2}}$.

$$T_{\mathrm{period}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{\sqrt{g^{2}+A^{2}}}}$$

Taking the support position as $\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}At^{2}$, the lab-frame trajectory is

$$x=\frac{1}{2}At^{2}+l\sin\theta,\quad y=-l\cos\theta$$

In the train, the trajectory is a circular arc about the support:

$$x=l\sin\theta,\quad y=-l\cos\theta$$

When at rest, $\theta$ is constant, so the lab path is a horizontal straight line and the train path is a single point.

articles.title: 遠心力
articles.latexEn:
Key points

On a horizontal table, a ball on an inextensible string tied to a pin moves in uniform circular motion without friction. On a wide screen the views are side by side; on a narrow screen they are stacked. Top or left is the lab frame; bottom or right is the frame of a person rotating with the ball about the center.

In the lab frame the only force is tension,

$$T=m\frac{v^{2}}{R}=m\omega^{2}R$$

The person's angular velocity matches the ball's. Relative to the person the ball is at rest, so the velocity in this frame is $0$. The outward centrifugal force $\displaystyle m\omega^{2}R$ balances the tension. Floor markings are fixed in the lab, so in the rotating frame they appear to turn the opposite way.

articles.title: 遠心力とコリオリ力(等速直線運動)
articles.titleEn: Centrifugal and Coriolis forces (uniform straight-line motion)

articles.title: オイラー力
articles.latexEn:
Key points

On a horizontal platform, an object at distance $R$ from the center is fixed to the platform. Starting from rest, the platform begins to rotate with constant angular acceleration $\alpha$. On a wide screen the views are side by side; on a narrow screen they are stacked. Top or left is the lab frame; bottom or right is the platform frame.

$$ \omega=\alpha t,\quad \theta=\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^{2} $$

The object rests on the platform, so the force acting is static friction. In the lab frame the object moves on a circle with increasing speed. Static friction splits into a centripetal part $\displaystyle m\omega^{2}R$ and a tangential part $\displaystyle m\alpha R$ in the sense of speeding up.

Relative to a person rotating with the platform, the object is at rest. The velocity in this frame is $0$, so there is no Coriolis force. The outward centrifugal force $\displaystyle m\omega^{2}R$ balances the inward friction, and the Euler force $\displaystyle m\alpha R$ opposite to the tangential direction balances the tangential friction. At $t=0$ the centrifugal force is still $0$, so the only inertial force is the Euler force.

articles.title: 回転する円環上のビーズ
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A vertical ring rotates at constant angular speed $\omega$ about its vertical diameter. The ring is smooth, so the bead can move only along the ring. On a wide screen the views are side by side; on a narrow screen they stack. Top or left is the ground (inertial frame); bottom or right is the frame rotating with the ring.

With angle $\theta$ measured from the bottom, the equation of motion is

$$\ddot{\theta}=\sin\theta\left(\omega^{2}\cos\theta-\frac{g}{R}\right)$$

The true forces are gravity and the constraint force from the ring. In the frame rotating with the ring, the ring appears fixed, and centrifugal force and (if the bead moves) Coriolis force appear as well. Only gravity and the centrifugal force have tangential components; the Coriolis force is normal to the surface, so the constraint force balances it and it does not enter the $\theta$ equation. The animation draws all forces in both frames. The gravity vector itself is constant.

When $\omega^{2}>g/R$, the position $\displaystyle\cos\theta=\frac{g}{\omega^{2}R}$ is a stable equilibrium. For small $\omega$, the bottom $\theta=0$ is stable.

articles.title: 地上に立つ人と遠心力
articles.titleEn: Person standing on Earth and centrifugal force
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Compare a person standing on a spherically symmetric Earth in space (inertial frame) and in the frame rotating with Earth. On a wide screen the views are side by side; on a narrow screen they stack. The person already rotates with Earth’s angular speed $\omega$. $\omega$ is exaggerated for visibility, and force arrows are emphasized further.

With latitude $\lambda$ and radius $R$, the distance from the rotation axis is $\displaystyle\rho=R\cos\lambda$. In the inertial frame the person moves in uniform circular motion about the axis, with acceleration toward the axis $\displaystyle\vec{a}=-\omega^{2}\vec{\rho}$. Speed is constant, but direction changes, so there is acceleration.

The true forces are gravity $\vec{F}_g$ (toward Earth’s center) and the contact force $\vec{R}$ from Earth. In the inertial frame their resultant provides the centripetal acceleration. On the left (or top) panel, this resultant $\vec{R}+\vec{F}_g=m\vec{a}$ is shown as an axis-directed arrow.

$$\vec{R}+\vec{F}_g=m\vec{a}$$

At mid-latitudes the needed $\vec{a}$ is not toward Earth’s center, so $\vec{R}$ is not parallel to gravity. In the spherical model, that tangential component is called static friction. At the equator and poles the tangential component is $0$. The animation also draws the plane of the circular motion (radius $\rho$) perpendicular to the axis.

In the frame rotating with Earth the person appears at rest and there is no Coriolis force. Adding the outward centrifugal force $\displaystyle m\omega^{2}\rho$ gives equilibrium; the resultant is $0$ (the right/bottom panel draws the centrifugal force and omits a resultant arrow).

$$\vec{R}+\vec{F}_g+\vec{F}_{\mathrm{cf}}=\vec{0}$$

At the equator, $\displaystyle N=mg-m\omega^{2}R$. A real Earth is an oblate spheroid, so local vertical nearly aligns with effective gravity and little tangential force is needed; here we keep a consistent sphere-plus-friction model.

articles.title: 単振り子の近似と厳密
円錐振り子
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A bob on a string of length $l$ moves horizontally about a vertical axis at constant angular velocity $\omega$. The string keeps a fixed angle $\theta$ from the vertical and sweeps out a cone. On a wide screen the views are side by side; on a narrow screen they are stacked. Top or left is the lab (inertial) frame; bottom or right is the frame rotating with the pendulum.

With the support as the origin and upward as positive $z$, the horizontal radius and the vertical distance from the support to the orbit plane are

$$r=l\sin\theta,\qquad h=l\cos\theta$$

The true forces are gravity and the string tension $\vec{S}$. In the inertial frame the bob moves in uniform horizontal circular motion with acceleration toward the axis $\displaystyle\vec{a}=-\omega^{2}\vec{r}$. Vertically the forces balance; horizontally a component of tension supplies the centripetal force.

$$S\cos\theta=mg,\qquad S\sin\theta=m\omega^{2}r$$

When $\theta$ is not zero, the angular velocity and tension are fixed by the following. The period is independent of mass and depends only on the vertical distance $h$.

$$\omega^{2}=\frac{g}{l\cos\theta},\qquad S=\frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$$

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l\cos\theta}{g}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}$$

In the frame rotating with the pendulum the bob appears at rest. Adding an outward centrifugal force $\displaystyle m\omega^{2}r$ from the axis, the net of gravity, tension, and centrifugal force is $0$. Because the bob is at rest there is no Coriolis force. The magnitude ratios of the three forces match the right triangle in a cross section of the cone.

$$\vec{S}+\vec{F}_{g}+\vec{F}_{\mathrm{cen}}=\vec{0}$$

$$S:mg:m\omega^{2}r=l:h:r$$

The animation draws forces in both frames. Centrifugal force is dashed. Orbit points are equally spaced in time. $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$.

articles.title: 単振り子の周期
articles.latexEn:
Key points

When the angle $\theta(t)$ is sufficiently small, $\sin \theta(t)$ can be approximated by $\theta(t)$.

Under this condition, Newton's equation of motion gives the period $T$ of a simple pendulum as

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$

Here $T$: period [s], $L$: string length [m], $g$: gravitational acceleration ($9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)

Setup

Find the period of a simple pendulum for string lengths $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $60\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Theory

・For $L = 30\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}$:

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.30}{9.8}} \fallingdotseq 1.10\,\mathrm{s}$$

・For $L = 60\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}$:

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.60}{9.8}} \fallingdotseq 1.55\,\mathrm{s}$$

Answer

The periods are $\displaystyle \begin{cases} L = 30\,\mathrm{cm}: & T \fallingdotseq 1.10\,\mathrm{s} \\ L = 60\,\mathrm{cm}: & T \fallingdotseq 1.55\,\mathrm{s} \end{cases}$

The time for 30 oscillations is $\begin{cases} L = 30\,\mathrm{cm}: & 30T \fallingdotseq 33.0\,\mathrm{s} \\ L = 60\,\mathrm{cm}: & 30T \fallingdotseq 46.6\,\mathrm{s} \end{cases}$

articles.title: 1次元の衝突
articles.latexEn:
Key points

This is a one-dimensional collision. A mass $M$ sits at rest at the origin, and a mass $m$ approaches from the left with speed $v$. There is no friction, so before and after the collision both move in uniform straight-line motion. Rightward is positive. The axis stays fixed.

Momentum is conserved.

$$mv=mv_{m}'+Mv_{M}'$$

The coefficient of restitution $e$ means the relative speed of separation is $e$ times the relative speed of approach.

$$e=\frac{v_{M}'-v_{m}'}{v}$$

From these two relations, the velocities after the collision are

$$v_{m}'=\frac{m-eM}{m+M}v,\quad v_{M}'=\frac{(1+e)m}{m+M}v$$

If $e=1$ and $m=M$, the incoming mass stops and the one that was at rest moves on with speed $v$. If $e=0$, both continue with the same velocity $\displaystyle \frac{m}{m+M}v$. When $e<1$, part of the mechanical energy becomes heat.

articles.title: 弾性衝突(1次元)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Conservation of momentum: $\displaystyle m_1v_1 + m_2v_2 = m_1v_1' + m_2v_2'$

Conservation of mechanical energy: $\displaystyle \frac12 m_1 v_1^2 + \frac12 m_2 v_2^2 = \frac12 m_1 v_1'^2 + \frac12 m_2 v_2'^2$

($m_1$, $m_2$: masses; $v_1$, $v_2$: velocities before collision; $v_1'$, $v_2'$: velocities after collision)

Setup

Two objects A and B of equal mass $m$ collide head-on on a smooth horizontal surface.
Before the collision, A has velocity $v_1$ and B has velocity $v_2$. The collision is perfectly elastic (coefficient of restitution $e=1$).
Find the post-collision velocities $v_1'$ and $v_2'$ in general form.

Theory

The definition of the coefficient of restitution is

$$ e = \frac{v_2' - v_1'}{v_1 - v_2}. $$

Substituting $e=1$ gives

$$ v_1 - v_2 = v_2' - v_1'. \quad (1) $$

From conservation of momentum,

$$\begin{aligned} &m v_1 + m v_2 = m v_1' + m v_2' \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &v_1 + v_2 = v_1' + v_2'. \quad (2) \end{aligned}$$

Solving (1) and (2) together,

$$\begin{aligned} &\begin{cases} v_1 - v_2 = v_2' - v_1' \\ v_1 + v_2 = v_1' + v_2' \end{cases} \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow &\begin{cases} v_1' = v_2 \\ v_2' = v_1 \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$
Answer

The post-collision velocities are $v_1' = v_2$, $v_2' = v_1$: the two objects exchange velocities.

In this experiment, with $v_2=0$, one has $v_1' = 0$, $v_2' = v_1$.

articles.title: 弾性衝突(2次元)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

・Conservation of momentum: $\displaystyle m_1\overrightarrow{v_1} + m_2\overrightarrow{v_2} = m_1\overrightarrow{v_1'} + m_2\overrightarrow{v_2'}$

・Conservation of mechanical energy: $\displaystyle \frac12 m_1 |\overrightarrow{v_1}|^2 + \frac12 m_2 |\overrightarrow{v_2}|^2 = \frac12 m_1 |\overrightarrow{v_1'}|^2 + \frac12 m_2 |\overrightarrow{v_2'}|^2$

$m_1$, $m_2$: masses; $\overrightarrow{v_1}$, $\overrightarrow{v_2}$: velocities before collision; $\overrightarrow{v_1'}$, $\overrightarrow{v_2'}$: velocities after collision

Setup

An object of mass $m$ at rest is struck elastically by another object of the same mass $m$ with velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$. Find the angle between the two post-collision velocity vectors $\overrightarrow{v_1}$ and $\overrightarrow{v_2}$.

Theory

Conservation of momentum in 2D (vector form) reads

$$\begin{aligned} m \overrightarrow{v} &= m \overrightarrow{v_1} + m \overrightarrow{v_2} \\ \Longleftrightarrow \overrightarrow{v} &= \overrightarrow{v_1} + \overrightarrow{v_2}. \end{aligned}$$

For an elastic collision, mechanical energy is also conserved:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} m |\overrightarrow{v}|^2 &= \frac{1}{2} m |\overrightarrow{v_1}|^2 + \frac{1}{2} m |\overrightarrow{v_2}|^2 \\ \Longleftrightarrow |\overrightarrow{v}|^2 &= |\overrightarrow{v_1}|^2 + |\overrightarrow{v_2}|^2. \end{aligned}$$

When both conditions hold and neither post-collision velocity is zero, the two velocities are at right angles (90°). In a head-on collision, the initially resting object takes $\overrightarrow{v}$ and the striking object stops.

articles.title: 跳ね返り1次元
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Let the velocity just before hitting the ground be $v$, and just after be $v'$. With coefficient of restitution $e$ ($0\le e\le 1$),

$$\displaystyle v'=-ev$$

In free fall from height $H$, the next peak height is

$$\displaystyle H'=e^{2}H$$

While falling, the acceleration remains downward $g$, whether thrown upward or downward.

articles.title: 跳ね返り2次元
articles.latexEn:
Key points

On a smooth horizontal ground, the horizontal velocity does not change on landing. Only the vertical component reverses with coefficient of restitution $e$.

$$\displaystyle v_x'=v_x,\quad v_y'=-ev_y$$

Launch from a platform of height $h$ at angle $\theta$ and speed $v_0$. $\theta$ is positive upward and negative downward. If the vertical speed just before impact is $v_y$, the peak height after the bounce is $\displaystyle H=\frac{(ev_y)^{2}}{2g}$. For $\theta\ge 0$, this is $e^{2}$ times the previous peak. For a downward launch ($\theta<0$), the speed just before impact is larger, so even with $e=1$ the next peak can exceed the launch height.

articles.title: 等速円運動
articles.latexEn:
Key points

On a horizontal table, a ball on an inextensible string tied to a pin moves in uniform circular motion with no friction. The only force acting is tension.

$$\displaystyle x=R\cos\omega t,\quad y=R\sin\omega t$$

$$\displaystyle \omega=\frac{v}{R},\quad T=\frac{2\pi R}{v}$$

The magnitudes of the centripetal acceleration and tension are

$$\displaystyle a=\frac{v^{2}}{R},\quad F=m\frac{v^{2}}{R}$$

Acceleration points toward the center; velocity is always tangential. Speed stays constant; only the direction changes.

articles.title: ジェットコースター
articles.latexEn:
Key points

From height $h$ at point A, enter a smooth vertical circle of radius $R$. Angle $\theta$ is measured from the bottom.

$$\displaystyle \frac{N}{m}=\frac{v^{2}}{R}+g\cos\theta$$

Leaving the track occurs only in the upper half, at the angle

$$\displaystyle \cos\theta=\frac{2(R-h)}{3R}$$

If $\displaystyle h\le R$, it returns. If $\displaystyle R<h<\frac{5}{2}R$, it lands after projectile motion. If $\displaystyle h\ge\frac{5}{2}R$, it completes a loop and continues to the right.

Landing is perfectly inelastic; the velocity becomes zero momentarily.

articles.title: 向心力が突如消えた時の物体運動
articles.titleEn: Motion when the centripetal force suddenly vanishes
articles.latexEn:
Key points

An object of mass $m$ in circular motion with radius $r$ and speed $v$ experiences a centripetal force toward the center, $\displaystyle F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$. If this force suddenly disappears and friction is neglected, Newton's first law implies that the object continues in uniform rectilinear motion along the tangent to the circle.

Note: even if friction acts, it only reduces the magnitude of the velocity (the speed) and does not change its direction by itself.

Therefore the object leaves the circular path and flies off along the tangential direction.

articles.title: ケプラーの3法則
articles.latexEn:
Key points

When the central star is heavy enough, a bound orbit about a mass fixed at the origin is an ellipse. Starting at periapsis with velocity perpendicular to the radius, semi-major axis $a$ and eccentricity $e$ are in one-to-one correspondence with periapsis $r,v$.

For an ellipse ($e<1$), periapsis distance and periapsis speed are

$$r_{\min}=a(1-e),\quad v_{\mathrm{peri}}=\sqrt{\frac{GM(1+e)}{a(1-e)}}$$

Orbit shape (first law)

$$r=\frac{a(1-e^{2})}{1+e\cos\theta}$$

Closed orbits follow this. Time is closed by the change of variable to eccentric anomaly $u$, $\displaystyle r=a(1-e\cos u)$, yielding Kepler’s equation.

$$nt=u-e\sin u,\quad n=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{a^{3}}}$$

Position is $\displaystyle x=a(\cos u-e),\; y=a\sqrt{1-e^{2}}\sin u$.

$e=1$ is a parabola. The slider’s $a$ is the periapsis distance, with

$$r_{\min}=a,\quad r=\frac{2a}{1+\cos\theta},\quad v_{\mathrm{peri}}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{a}}$$

$e>1$ is a hyperbola. There is no period, and

$$r_{\min}=a(e-1),\quad r=\frac{a(e^{2}-1)}{1+e\cos\theta}$$

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a^{3}}{GM}}$$

hence the third law

$$\frac{T^{2}}{a^{3}}=\frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM}$$

Areal velocity is constant at $\displaystyle \frac{h}{2}$ (second law). For a central force this holds for ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas.

$a=1$ is one astronomical unit, with $\displaystyle T=365.25$ days. Changing $a$ gives $\displaystyle T\propto a^{3/2}$; doubling the semi-major axis multiplies the period by $\displaystyle 2\sqrt{2}$.

The energy gauge does not plot the true mechanical energy $\displaystyle E=K-\frac{GMm}{r}$ (negative for ellipses); it uses a relative potential with zero at periapsis. The green band is $\displaystyle U'=GMm\left(\frac{1}{r_{\min}}-\frac{1}{r}\right)$, equal to the work an external agent does carrying the mass from periapsis to the present position. The frame length is the kinetic energy at periapsis; along the orbit $K+U'$ is constant.

articles.title: 太陽系惑星の天文データとケプラー第3法則
articles.titleEn: Solar-system planet data and Kepler's third law
articles.latexEn:
Astronomical data
Key points

Let the Sun's mass be $M$ and the gravitational constant be $G$. Under the approximation that the central star is much heavier than each planet, every planet's orbital period $T$ and semi-major axis $a$ satisfy $\displaystyle \frac{T^2}{a^3} = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}$ (Kepler's third law).

Theory vs astronomical data

Using the Sun's mass $M = 1.98 \times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3/(kg\cdot s^2)}$:

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} &= \frac{4 \times 3.14^2}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.98 \times 10^{30}} \\ &= \frac{4 \times 3.14^2}{6.67 \times 1.98} \times 10^{-19} \\[5pt] &\fallingdotseq 2.99 \times 10^{-19} \ \ [\mathrm{s^2\cdot m^{-3}}] \end{aligned}$$

This agrees well with the values of $\displaystyle \frac{T^2}{a^3}$ shown at the right of the table, so Kepler's law is a good approximation for the planets of the solar system.

articles.title: 月までの距離とケプラー第3法則
articles.titleEn: Distance to the Moon and Kepler's third law
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Let Earth's mass be $M$ and the gravitational constant be $G$. Under the approximation that Earth is much heavier than the Moon, the Moon's orbital period $T$ and semi-major axis $a$ satisfy $\displaystyle \frac{T^2}{a^3} = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}$ (Kepler's third law).

Finding $GM$ from Earth's basic data

Earth's circumference is about $4 \times 10^7$ m. With Earth's radius $R$, the circumference is $2\pi R$, so

$$2\pi R = 4 \times 10^7 \Rightarrow R = \frac{4 \times 10^7}{2\pi} \fallingdotseq 6.37 \times 10^6 \ [\mathrm{m}]$$

Surface gravity is $g = 9.8$ [m/s²], so

$$\displaystyle g = \frac{GM}{R^2} \Rightarrow GM = gR^2$$

$$GM = 9.8 \times (6.37 \times 10^6)^2 \fallingdotseq 3.97 \times 10^{14}$$

(1) Period taken as 30 days

$$T = 30 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 = 2.592 \times 10^6 \ [\mathrm{s}]$$

\begin{align}a^3 & \fallingdotseq \frac{GM T^2}{4\pi^2} \\ &= \frac{3.97 \times 10^{14} \times (2.592 \times 10^6)^2}{4\pi^2} \\ &\fallingdotseq \frac{3.97 \times 6.72}{39.5} \times 10^{26} \fallingdotseq 6.76 \times 10^{25}\end{align}

$$\Rightarrow a \fallingdotseq \sqrt[3]{6.76 \times 10^{25}} \fallingdotseq 4.08 \times 10^8 \ [\mathrm{m}]$$

(2) Period taken as 27.3 days

$$T = 27.3 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 = 2.36 \times 10^6 \ [\mathrm{s}]$$

$$\displaystyle a^3 = \frac{GM T^2}{4\pi^2} = \frac{3.97 \times 10^{14} \times (2.36 \times 10^6)^2}{4\pi^2}$$

$$\Rightarrow a^3 \fallingdotseq \frac{3.97 \times 5.57}{39.5} \times 10^{26} \fallingdotseq 5.60 \times 10^{25}$$

$$\Rightarrow a \fallingdotseq \sqrt[3]{5.60 \times 10^{25}} \fallingdotseq 3.84 \times 10^8 \ [\mathrm{m}]$$

Answer

・With a 30-day period, $\displaystyle a \fallingdotseq 4.08 \times 10^8$ [m]

・With the more realistic 27.3-day period, $\displaystyle a \fallingdotseq 3.84 \times 10^8$ [m]

This agrees well with the Moon's actual mean distance (about 384,000 km).

articles.title: 木星のガリレオ衛星とケプラー第3法則
articles.titleEn: Jupiter's Galilean moons and Kepler's third law
articles.latexEn:
Data
Key points

Let Jupiter's mass be $M$ and the gravitational constant be $G$. Under the approximation that Jupiter is much heavier than its moons, every moon's orbital period $T$ and semi-major axis $a$ satisfy $\displaystyle \frac{T^2}{a^3} = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}$ (Kepler's third law).

Theory vs data

With Jupiter's mass $M = 1.90 \times 10^{27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3/(kg\cdot s^2)}$:

$$GM = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.90 \times 10^{27} = 1.27 \times 10^{17}$$

The constant in Kepler's third law:

$$\displaystyle \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} = \frac{4 \times \pi^2}{1.27 \times 10^{17}} \fallingdotseq 3.11 \times 10^{-16} \ \mathrm{[s^2\cdot m^{-3}]}$$

This agrees well with the values of $\displaystyle \frac{T^{2}}{a^{3}}$ computed in the table.

articles.title: 2体問題(ばね・1次元)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Two masses linked by a spring with no external force: the center of mass moves at constant velocity, and the relative motion is simple harmonic motion of the reduced mass.

$$\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1+m_2}$$

$$\mu\,\ddot R = -k(R-\ell)$$

$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}$$

The exact solution for the relative coordinate $R=x_2-x_1$ is

$$\begin{aligned} R(t)&=\ell+(R(0)-\ell)\cos\omega t\\ &\quad+\frac{\dot R(0)}{\omega}\sin\omega t \end{aligned}$$

Each mass position follows from the center of mass $R_G(t)=R_G(0)+V_G t$:

$$x_1(t)=R_G(t)-\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}R(t)$$

$$x_2(t)=R_G(t)+\frac{m_1}{m_1+m_2}R(t)$$

The masses do not cross when the amplitude $A=\sqrt{(R(0)-\ell)^2+\Biggl(\frac{\dot R(0)}{\omega}\Biggr)^2}$ satisfies $A<\ell$ (that is, $R_{\min}=\ell-A>0$).

articles.title: 2体問題(重力・連星)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Two masses with no external force orbit a common center of mass. With the origin at the CM, the relative vector $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1$ is a fixed-center Kepler problem of mass $M=m_1+m_2$; if bound, the orbit is an ellipse. Each star’s orbit is similar, with semi-major axes $a_1,a_2$ fixed by the lever rule.

$$\displaystyle a=a_1+a_2,\quad \frac{m_1}{m_2}=\frac{a_2}{a_1}$$

$$\displaystyle \mathbf{r}_1=-\frac{a_1}{a}\mathbf{r},\quad \mathbf{r}_2=\frac{a_2}{a}\mathbf{r}$$

If velocity at periapsis is perpendicular to the radius, $(a_i,e)$ and $(r_i,v_i)$ are in one-to-one correspondence. Kepler’s third law for the relative semi-major axis is

$$\displaystyle \frac{T^{2}}{a^{3}}=\frac{4\pi^{2}}{G(m_1+m_2)}$$

When the mass ratio is near one, the CM lies outside the primary. For Earth–Moon and Sun–Earth, the CM lies inside the primary.

The energy gauge uses the reduced mass of the relative motion and takes periapsis as the zero of potential energy (it does not show the true $E<0$). The green band corresponds to the work $\displaystyle U'=G\mu M\left(\frac{1}{r_{\min}}-\frac{1}{r}\right)$ to carry the mass from periapsis to the current distance.

articles.title: 立て掛けた棒（壁滑らか）
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Lean a uniform rod of length $L$ and mass $m$ against a wall at angle $\theta$ with the wall. The wall is smooth; the floor has static friction coefficient $\mu_s$ and kinetic friction coefficient $\mu_k$.

At rest

Friction at the wall is zero, so

$$N_f=mg,\qquad f_f=N_w=\frac{1}{2}mg\tan\theta$$

The rest condition is $\displaystyle\mu_s\ge\frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$.

Sliding while both ends stay in contact

When the condition fails, the foot slides outward. Kinetic friction $f=\mu_k N_f$ (toward the wall) acts at the floor. The only degree of freedom is the angle. When the wall normal $N_w$ reaches 0, the rod leaves the wall. For $\mu_k=0$, detachment occurs at

$$\cos\theta=\frac{2}{3}\cos\theta_0$$

($\theta_0$ is the initial angle with the wall).

After leaving the wall

It falls with two degrees of freedom: foot position $x_A$ and angle.

articles.title: 直方体を押す（滑りと転倒）
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Place a rectangular block of width $w$, height $H$, and mass $m$ on a rough floor, and apply a constant horizontal force $F$ at height $h$ above the floor. The floor has static friction coefficient $\mu_s$ and kinetic friction coefficient $\mu_k$.

At rest

No sliding requires $F\le\mu_s mg$. No tipping, about the lower-right edge, requires

$$\displaystyle F\le mg\cdot\frac{w}{2h}$$

If both hold, it stays at rest. Raising $F$ slowly, tipping comes first if $\displaystyle h>\frac{w}{2\mu_s}$; if $h$ is smaller, sliding comes first.

Sliding

After sliding starts, the acceleration is $\displaystyle a=\frac{F-\mu_k mg}{m}$.

Tipping

It rotates about the lower-right edge. Hand height stays fixed at $h$; when the left face clears $y=h$, the hand loses contact and $F=0$ (roughly $\displaystyle\theta=\arcsin\frac{h}{w}$). Then it falls onto its side.

While the lower-right edge stays put, the floor’s horizontal force and normal force follow from the CM acceleration. While the hand is in contact,

$$\displaystyle I_P\ddot\theta=-mg\Bigl(\frac{w}{2}\cos\theta-\frac{H}{2}\sin\theta\Bigr)+Fh$$

After the hand leaves, the $Fh$ term vanishes.

articles.title: 片側持ち上げ
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Let all forces on the object be $\vec{F_1}, \vec{F_2}, \cdots$

and all moments about a chosen point be $\tau_1, \tau_2, \cdots$. Then

Force and moment balance

$\displaystyle \vec{F_1} + \vec{F_2} + \cdots = \vec{0}$（force balance）

$\displaystyle \tau_1 + \tau_2 + \cdots = 0$（moment balance）

Setup

Treat a wooden block of mass $m = 273\,\mathrm{g}$ as a rigid body. When one side is lifted, what reading does the scale show in grams?

Theory

Use force and moment balance to find the force needed to lift one side.

The center of mass is at the midpoint, so lifting one end requires supporting half the total weight.

Thus the required force equals the weight of $136.5\mathrm{g}$.

Answer

The spring scale reads $136.5 \mathrm{g}$.

articles.title: 積み木
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Let all forces on the object be $\vec{F_1}, \vec{F_2}, \cdots$

and all moments about a chosen point be $\tau_1, \tau_2, \cdots$. Then

Force and moment balance

$\displaystyle \vec{F_1} + \vec{F_2} + \cdots = \vec{0}$（force balance）

$\displaystyle \tau_1 + \tau_2 + \cdots = 0$（moment balance）

Stability condition for stacked blocks

For the object to remain stable without tipping, the balance conditions above must hold.

articles.title: コンデンサーとはどういうものか？
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The capacitance of a capacitor is the amount of charge stored per unit voltage, and is defined by:

$$\displaystyle Q = CV$$

  • $Q$: charge [C]
  • $C$: capacitance [F]
  • $V$: voltage [V]

articles.title: 平行板コンデンサの電気容量の測定
articles.titleEn: Measuring the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The capacitance $C$ of a parallel-plate capacitor is given by the permittivity $\varepsilon$, the area $S$, and the plate separation $d$ as:

$$C = \varepsilon \frac{S}{d}$$

Here $\varepsilon$ is $\varepsilon_0$ (the vacuum permittivity) in air; with a dielectric inserted, $\varepsilon = \kappa \varepsilon_0$, where $\kappa$ is the relative permittivity (dielectric constant) of the dielectric.

Setup

Consider a parallel-plate capacitor in air. Find the capacitance $C$ under the following conditions.

  • Permittivity of air (nearly the same as vacuum): $$\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \ \mathrm{F \cdot m^{-1}}$$
  • Area of the plates: $$S = 10^2 \ \mathrm{cm^2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2} \ \mathrm{m^2}$$
  • Separation between the plates: $$d = 0.7 \ \mathrm{mm} = 7 \times 10^{-4} \ \mathrm{m}$$
Theoretical calculation

The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is:

$$C = \varepsilon_0 \cdot \frac{S}{d}$$

Substituting the values:

$$\begin{aligned} C &= 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-2}}{7 \times 10^{-4}} \\ &= \frac{8.854 \times 10^{-14}}{7 \times 10^{-4}} \\ &\fallingdotseq 126.5 \times 10^{-12} \ \mathrm{F} = 126.5 \ \mathrm{pF} \end{aligned}$$

Answer

The capacitance of this parallel-plate capacitor is

$$\boxed{C \fallingdotseq 126.5 \ \mathrm{pF}}$$

articles.title: コンデンサの合成容量(直列)
articles.titleEn: Equivalent capacitance of capacitors in series
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The equivalent capacitance $C$ of capacitors connected in series is given by $$\displaystyle \frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{C_n}$$.

Here,

  • $C$: equivalent capacitance [F]
  • $C_1, C_2, \dots, C_n$: capacitance of each capacitor [F]
Setup

Find the equivalent capacitance $C$ when two $3300\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors are connected in series.

Theory

For a series connection, the equivalent capacitance $C$ follows:

$$\displaystyle \frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}$$

With $C_1 = C_2 = 3300\ \mu\mathrm{F}$,

$$\displaystyle \frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{3300} + \frac{1}{3300} = \frac{2}{3300}$$

Therefore,

$$C = \frac{3300}{2} = 1650\ \mu\mathrm{F}$$

Answer

Equivalent capacitance:

$$\boxed{1650\ \mu\mathrm{F}}$$

articles.title: コンデンサの合成容量(並列)
articles.titleEn: Equivalent capacitance of capacitors in parallel
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The equivalent capacitance $C$ of capacitors connected in parallel is $$\displaystyle C = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots + C_n$$.

Here,

  • $C$: equivalent capacitance [F]
  • $C_1, C_2, \dots, C_n$: capacitance of each capacitor [F]
Setup

Find the equivalent capacitance $C$ when two $3300\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors are connected in parallel.

Theory

For a parallel connection, the equivalent capacitance $C$ is

$$\displaystyle C = C_1 + C_2$$

With $C_1 = C_2 = 3300\ \mu\mathrm{F}$,

$$C = 3300 + 3300 = 6600\ \mu\mathrm{F}$$

Answer

Equivalent capacitance:

$$\boxed{6600\ \mu\mathrm{F}}$$

articles.title: コンデンサに蓄えられる電気量
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The charge $Q$ stored in a capacitor is proportional to the applied voltage $V$.

This relation is written as:

$$\displaystyle Q = CV$$

  • $Q$: stored charge [C]
  • $C$: capacitance [F]
  • $V$: voltage [V]
Setup

Find the charge $Q$ stored when a voltage of $1.5\,\mathrm{V}$ is applied to a capacitor of capacitance $5\,\mathrm{F}$. A value of $5\,\mathrm{F}$ is much larger than ordinary $\mu\mathrm{F}$-class capacitors and is typical of electric double-layer capacitors.

Theory

The charge stored in a capacitor is the product of the capacitance $C$ and the applied voltage $V$:

$$\displaystyle Q = CV$$

Substituting the values:

$$Q = 5 \times 1.5 = 7.5\ [\mathrm{C}]$$

Answer

The stored charge $Q$ is:

$$\boxed{7.5\ \mathrm{C}}$$

articles.title: 抵抗の測定
articles.latexEn:
Key points

When a voltage $V$ is applied to a resistor and a current $I$ flows, Ohm's law gives the resistance as

$$\displaystyle R=\frac{V}{I}$$

A digital multimeter on the resistance range drives a small current from its internal supply and displays $R$ using this relation.

articles.title: 抵抗の長さと抵抗値
articles.titleEn: Resistance versus length of a conductor
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The resistance $R$ of a conductor is given by:

$$ R = \rho \frac{L}{A} $$

  • $R$: resistance ($\Omega$)
  • $\rho$: resistivity ($\Omega \cdot m$)
  • $L$: length of the conductor ($m$)
  • $A$: cross-sectional area ($m^2$)
Setup

Find the resistance of a nichrome wire under the following conditions.

  • Resistivity $\rho = 1.10 \times 10^{-6}\,\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$
  • Diameter $d = 0.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ or $0.35\,\mathrm{mm}$
  • Length $L = 0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ or $1.0\,\mathrm{m}$
Theoretical calculation

The cross-sectional area $A$ from the diameter $d$ is:

$$ A = \pi \left( \frac{d}{2} \right)^2 $$

The resistance is:

$$ R = \rho \frac{L}{A} $$

Answer

The calculated results are as follows.

Diameter $d$ (mm) Length $L$ (m) Area $A$ ($m^2$) Resistance $R$ ($\Omega$)
0.5 0.5 $$1.96 \times 10^{-7}$$ 2.80
0.5 1.0 $$1.96 \times 10^{-7}$$ 5.60
0.35 0.5 $$9.62 \times 10^{-8}$$ 5.72
0.35 1.0 $$9.62 \times 10^{-8}$$ 11.43

articles.title: 抵抗の直列接続
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The equivalent resistance of a series connection is the sum of all resistances, $R_{\mathrm{series}} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n$.

Setup

Find the equivalent resistance when two $200\,\Omega$ resistors are connected in series.

Theoretical calculation

$$R_{\mathrm{series}} = 200 + 200 = 400 \, \Omega$$

Answer

The equivalent resistance in series is $$\boxed{400 \Omega}$$

articles.title: 抵抗の並列接続
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The equivalent resistance of resistors in parallel is given by $\displaystyle \frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{parallel}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{R_n}$.

If all resistors have the same resistance $R$,

$$R_{\mathrm{parallel}} = \frac{R}{n}$$

Setup

Find the equivalent resistance when two $200\,\Omega$ resistors are connected in parallel.

Theoretical calculation

$$R_{\mathrm{parallel}} = \frac{200}{2} = 100 \, \Omega$$

Answer

The equivalent resistance for the parallel connection is

$$\boxed{100 \Omega}$$

articles.title: 温度による銅線の抵抗変化
articles.titleEn: Temperature dependence of copper wire resistance
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Resistance changes with temperature. For a metal, the resistance $R_T$ is given by

$$R_T = R_0 (1 + \alpha T)$$

The basic formula for resistance is

$$R = \rho \frac{ L}{A}$$

where $\rho$: resistivity, $L$: length, $A$: cross-sectional area.

Setup

Find the resistance of a copper wire with diameter $d = 0.16 \mathrm{mm}$ and length $L = 15 \mathrm{m}$ at $10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and at $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

Given:

  • Resistivity of copper (at $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$): $\rho_0 = 1.55 \times 10^{-8} \, \Omega\cdot m$
  • Temperature coefficient: $\alpha = 0.00393\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}$ (referenced to $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$)
Theoretical calculation

Cross-sectional area: $\displaystyle A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi \times (0.00016)^2}{4} \fallingdotseq 2.0106 \times 10^{-8} \, m^2$

(1) At temperature $10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$:

$$R_{10} = \frac{\rho_0 (1 + \alpha \times 10) L}{A}$$

$$R_{10} = \frac{1.55 \times 10^{-8} \times (1 + 0.00393 \times 10) \times 15}{2.0106 \times 10^{-8}} \fallingdotseq 12.02 \, \Omega$$

(2) At temperature $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$:

$$R_{100} = \frac{\rho_0 (1 + \alpha \times 100) L}{A}$$

$$R_{100} = \frac{1.55 \times 10^{-8} \times (1 + 0.00393 \times 100) \times 15}{2.0106 \times 10^{-8}} \fallingdotseq 16.11 \, \Omega$$

Answer

$$\boxed{\begin{aligned} 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}&:\ R \fallingdotseq 12.02 \, \Omega \\ 100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}&:\ R \fallingdotseq 16.11 \, \Omega \end{aligned}}$$

articles.title: レモン電池の電圧
articles.latexEn:
Key points

When a copper plate and a zinc plate are inserted into a lemon, a voltage appears.

This happens because a difference in how strongly each metal tends to release electrons and form cations (ionization tendency) produces a flow of electrons.

Zinc has a greater ionization tendency than copper, so the following reaction occurs:

$$ \text{Zn} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+} + 2e^- $$

The electrons travel through the external circuit to the copper plate and react with hydrogen ions in the lemon:

$$ 2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2 $$

In this way a flow of electrons is produced, and a voltage of about 1 V was obtained.

The magnitude of the voltage depends on the combination of metals used and on the acidic properties of the lemon electrolyte.

articles.title: オームの法則
articles.latexEn:
Key points

Using Ohm's law $V = IR$, you can find the current and potential differences in a series circuit.

Here, 100 Ω and 200 Ω resistors were connected in series to a 4.5 V battery.

The total resistance of the circuit is:

$$ R_{\text{total}} = 100\,\Omega + 200\,\Omega = 300\,\Omega $$

The current $I$ is:

$$ \begin{aligned} I &= \frac{V}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{4.5}{300} = 0.015\,\text{A} \\ &= 15\,\text{mA} \end{aligned} $$

The potential difference across the 100 Ω resistor, $V_{100}$, and across the 200 Ω resistor, $V_{200}$, are:

$$ \begin{aligned} V_{100} &= IR = 0.015 \times 100 = 1.5\,\text{V} \\ V_{200} &= IR = 0.015 \times 200 = 3.0\,\text{V} \end{aligned} $$

Their sum is $1.5+3.0=4.5\,\text{V}$, which matches the battery voltage.

  • In a series circuit, the same current flows through every resistor
  • Potential difference is divided in proportion to resistance
  • Battery voltage = sum of the potential differences across the resistors

articles.title: RC回路
articles.latexEn:
Symbols
・$t$: time
・$I(t)$: current in the circuit at time $t$
・$Q(t)$: charge stored on the capacitor at time $t$
・$RI(t)$: voltage drop across the resistor
Key points
  • In an RC circuit, the time dependence of the capacitor charge and the current can be expressed with differential equations.
  • By Kirchhoff's second law (loop rule), the source voltage equals the sum of the voltage drops across the resistor and the capacitor:
    $$V = RI(t) + \frac{Q(t)}{C}$$
  • Also, the current $I(t)$ is the time derivative of the charge:
    $$I(t) = \frac{dQ(t)}{dt}$$
Setup
(1) For a series RC circuit with resistance $R$, capacitance $C$, and source voltage $V$, find the time dependence of the charge $Q(t)$ and the current $I(t)$ when the switch is closed at $t=0$.

(2) For $V=3\ [\mathrm{V}]$, $R=2000\ [\Omega]$, and capacitance $C=3300\ [\mu\mathrm{F}]=3.3\times 10^{-3}\ [\mathrm{F}]$, find explicit expressions for $Q(t)$, $I(t)$, and $RI(t)$.

Theoretical calculation More details

From Kirchhoff's laws, set up the following differential equations:

$$ \begin{cases} \displaystyle V = RI(t) + \frac{Q(t)}{C} \\ \displaystyle I(t) = \frac{dQ}{dt}(t) \end{cases} $$

With the initial condition $Q(0) = 0$, substituting the integration constant $A = -CV$ gives:

$$\begin{aligned} Q(t) &= CV \left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}} \right) \\ &\quad \text{(charge on the capacitor)} \\ I(t) &= \frac{V}{R} e^{-\frac{t}{RC}} \\ &\quad \text{(current in the circuit)} \\ RI(t) &= V e^{-\frac{t}{RC}} \\ &\quad \text{(voltage drop across the resistor)} \end{aligned}$$

Times at which the voltage drop is $\displaystyle \frac{V}{2}$ and $\displaystyle \frac{V}{4}$:

$$\begin{aligned} t &= RC\ln 2 \fallingdotseq 0.693 RC \\ t &= 2RC\ln 2 \fallingdotseq 1.386 RC \end{aligned}$$

Answer

Substituting the given values:

  • $$RC = 6.6\ [\mathrm{s}]$$

The expressions for charge and current are:

$$\begin{aligned} Q(t) &= 9.9 \times 10^{-3} \left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{6.6}}\right) \\ &\quad \text{(charge on the capacitor)} \\ I(t) &= \frac{3}{2000} e^{-\frac{t}{6.6}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} e^{-\frac{t}{6.6}} \\ &\quad \text{(current in the circuit)} \\ RI(t) &= 3 e^{-\frac{t}{6.6}} \\ &\quad \text{(voltage drop across the resistor)} \end{aligned}$$

The times when the voltage drop is $\displaystyle \frac{3}{2}\ [\mathrm{V}]$ and $\displaystyle \frac{3}{4}\ [\mathrm{V}]$ are:

$$\begin{aligned} t &= 6.6 \times 0.693 \fallingdotseq 4.6\ [\mathrm{s}] \\ t &= 6.6 \times 1.386 \fallingdotseq 9.1\ [\mathrm{s}] \end{aligned}$$

articles.title: ダイオードとはどういうものか
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A diode is a device that allows current to flow in only one direction; this property is called rectification.

It is made of a PN junction. When a voltage is applied from the P side (anode) to the N side (cathode), the diode is forward-biased and current flows.

Conversely, when a voltage is applied from the N side to the P side, the diode is reverse-biased and almost no current flows.

articles.title: ネオジム磁石の磁場の測定
articles.titleEn: Measuring the magnetic field of a neodymium magnet
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The strength of a magnetic field is expressed in tesla (T); 1 tesla corresponds to a magnetic flux density of 1 weber per square meter.

As an everyday example, the magnetic field of a neodymium magnet was measured in the video at about 180 mT (millitesla).

Earth's magnetic field is about 50 μT (microtesla).

articles.title: アンペールの法則と直線電流の磁場
articles.titleEn: Ampère's law and the magnetic field of a straight current
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The magnetic field strength $B$ around an infinitely long straight current $I$ at distance $r$ is given by (magnitude of the field produced by a straight current):

$$ B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r} $$

※ Symbol definitions:

  • $B$: magnitude of the magnetic field vector (T)
  • $\mu_0$: permeability of free space (about $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
  • $I$: magnitude of the straight current (A)
  • $r$: distance from the straight current (m)
  • Ampère's law relates the circulation of the magnetic field to current
  • The magnetic field of a straight current falls off inversely with distance
  • The direction of the magnetic field is determined by the current direction and the right-hand rule

articles.title: 直線電流と地磁気の重ね合わせ：方位磁石の向き（arctan回避・矢ベクトル）
articles.titleEn: Superposition of a straight current and geomagnetism: compass direction (no arctan; vector arrows)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A compass points along the resultant magnetic field in the horizontal plane, \(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}\). The magnetic field of a long straight current is \[ B_{\text{wire}}=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \] and its direction follows the right-hand rule (tangential).

Setup

Current \(I=1\,\mathrm{A}\). Distance \(r=1\,\mathrm{cm}=0.01\,\mathrm{m}\). Take the horizontal component of geomagnetism to be \(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{E}}=(0,\ 3.0\times10^{-5})\ \mathrm{T}\) (north \(+\hat{y}\)). The wire lies along the \(z\) axis, and the compass is placed north of the wire.

Theoretical calculation

Magnitude of the wire's magnetic field: \[ B_{\text{wire}}=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times 1}{2\pi\times 0.01} \] \[ B_{\text{wire}}=2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}\ (=20\ \mu\mathrm{T}) \] At this location the direction is west (\(-\hat{x}\)). Hence \(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{wire}}=(-2.0\times10^{-5},\,0)\ \mathrm{T}\).

Components of the resultant magnetic field: \[ \overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}=\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{E}}+\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{wire}} \] \[ \overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}=\big(-2.0\times10^{-5},\ 3.0\times10^{-5}\big)\ \mathrm{T} \] Magnitude: \[ |\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}|=\sqrt{(2.0\times10^{-5})^2+(3.0\times10^{-5})^2} \] \[ |\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}|=3.606\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}\ (=36.06\ \mu\mathrm{T}) \]

Deflection angle (angle \(\theta\) from north toward west). Without using arctan, find it from cosine and sine:

\[ \cos\theta=\frac{(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}})_y}{|\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}|} \] \[ \cos\theta=\frac{3.0\times10^{-5}}{3.606\times10^{-5}}\fallingdotseq 0.8321 \] Likewise check: \[ \sin\theta=\frac{|(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}})_x|}{|\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}|} \] \[ \sin\theta=\frac{2.0\times10^{-5}}{3.606\times10^{-5}}\fallingdotseq 0.5547 \] Therefore \[ \theta\fallingdotseq \cos^{-1}(0.8321)\fallingdotseq 33.7^\circ \] The direction is “\(33.7^\circ\) west of north.”

Answer

\(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}=\big(-20,\ 30\big)\ \mu\mathrm{T}\), \(|\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}|\fallingdotseq 36.1\ \mu\mathrm{T}\).
The compass points \(33.7^\circ\) west of north (azimuth \(\fallingdotseq 326.3^\circ\)).

When the position changes: if placed on the east side, \(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{wire}}\) points north and reinforces (about \(50\ \mu\mathrm{T}\)). On the west side it points south and reduces the field (about \(10\ \mu\mathrm{T}\)). Always evaluate \(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{E}}+\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{wire}}\), and find the angle from \(\displaystyle \cos\theta=\frac{(\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}})_y}{|\overrightarrow{B}_{\text{tot}}|}\).

articles.title: 円形電流の中心における磁場の大きさ
articles.titleEn: Magnitude of the magnetic field at the center of a circular current
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The magnetic field strength $B$ at the center of a circular current of radius $a$ is given by:

$$ B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 a} $$

※ Definition of symbols:

  • $B$: magnitude of the magnetic field (T)
  • $\mu_0$: permeability of free space (about $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
  • $I$: magnitude of the current (A)
  • $a$: radius of the circular loop (m)
  • The magnitude of the magnetic field is proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the loop radius
  • The magnetic field direction is perpendicular to the plane of the loop and is given by the right-hand rule
  • The expression $B =\displaystyle \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 a}$ can be derived from the Biot–Savart law

articles.title: ソレノイドコイルの作る磁場
articles.titleEn: Magnetic field produced by a solenoid coil
articles.latexEn:
Key points

For a uniform solenoid of length $L = 39\,\text{cm} = 0.39\,\text{m}$ and $N = 210$ turns carrying current $I = 1.05\,\text{A}$, the magnetic field strength $B$ inside can be approximated by:

$$ B = \mu_0 n I = \mu_0 \frac{N}{L} I $$

※ Definition of symbols:

  • $B$: magnitude of the magnetic field inside the solenoid (T)
  • $\mu_0$: permeability of free space ($4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{T·m/A}$)
  • $N$: number of turns
  • $L$: length of the coil (m)
  • $n$: turn density ($m^{-1} $)
  • $I$: current (A)

Substituting these values:

$$ \begin{aligned} B &= 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \cdot \frac{210}{0.39} \cdot 1.05 \\ &\fallingdotseq 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \cdot 538.46 \cdot 1.05 \\ &\fallingdotseq 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \cdot 565.38 \\ &\fallingdotseq 7.1 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{T} \\ &= 0.71\,\text{mT} \end{aligned} $$

  • The magnetic field inside a solenoid is nearly uniform
  • The turn density (number of turns divided by length) determines the field strength
  • The magnetic field direction is set by the current direction and the right-hand rule

articles.title: ローレンツ力
articles.latexEn:
Key points
  • The magnitude of the force on a moving charge is $F = qvB\sin\theta$
  • This force acts perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field (right-hand rule)
  • The magnitude of the force exerted by a magnetic field on a current $I$ is $F = IlB\sin\theta$
  • When the magnetic field and the wire are perpendicular ($\theta = 90^\circ$), the force is maximum and $F = IlB$
  • The Lorentz force changes the direction of motion but does not change the kinetic energy

Definition of symbols:

  • $F$: magnitude of the force (N)
  • $q$: charge (C)
  • $v$: speed of the charge (m/s)
  • $B$: magnetic field strength (T)
  • $\theta$: angle between the velocity (or current) and the magnetic field
  • $I$: current (A)
  • $l$: length of the wire (m)

articles.title: 平行電流間に働く力
articles.latexEn:
Key points

When currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ flow in two parallel wires, the magnetic force $F$ between them is given by:

$$ F = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 l}{2 \pi r} $$

  • Currents in the same direction attract each other.
  • Currents in opposite directions repel each other.

※ Definition of symbols:

  • $F$: magnitude of the force (N)
  • $\mu_0$: permeability of free space (about $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A)
  • $I_1$, $I_2$: magnitudes of the currents in each wire (A)
  • $l$: length of wire over which the force acts (m)
  • $r$: distance between the two wires (m)

※ This formula is an approximation when the wire length $l$ is much larger than the separation $r$ ($l \gg r$).
If the wires are short, end effects cannot be neglected and the actual force differs from this formula.

articles.title: 回転磁石（x軸回り）と30巻コイルの交流起電力：数値代入（r_m=1.5 cm, B̂=0.200 T）
articles.titleEn: AC emf from a rotating magnet (about the x-axis) and a 30-turn coil: numerical substitution (r_m=1.5 cm, B̂=0.200 T)
articles.latexEn:
Key points

The coil plane is fixed in the \(xy\) plane, and the magnet rotates about the \(x\) axis at angular speed \(2\pi f\). Because of axial magnetization, the component normal to the coil is \[ B_z(t)=\hat B\cos\theta(t),\quad \theta(t)=2\pi f t+\theta_0. \] From Faraday's law and \(\Phi(t)\fallingdotseq A\,B_z(t)\), \[ \mathcal{E}(t)=N\,A\,\hat B\,(2\pi f)\,\sin(2\pi f t+\theta_0). \]

Numerical substitution

Magnet radius \(r_m=1.5\ \mathrm{cm}=0.015\ \mathrm{m}\). As an upper-bound estimate, approximate the effective area by the magnet's circular area: \[ \begin{aligned} A &= \pi r_m^2 = \pi (0.015)^2 \\ &= \pi \times 2.25\times 10^{-4} \\ &= 7.0685834706\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}. \end{aligned} \] Substituting \(N=30\) turns and magnetic flux density amplitude \(\hat B=0.200\ \mathrm{T}\) gives \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{E}_{\rm peak} &= N\,A\,\hat B\,(2\pi f) \\ &= 30 \times (7.06858\times 10^{-4}) \times 0.200 \times (2\pi f) \\ &= 2.664793188\times 10^{-2}\ f\ \ \mathrm{[V]}. \end{aligned} \] Hence the time waveform is \[ \boxed{ \ \mathcal{E}(t)=\big(2.664793\times 10^{-2}\ f\big)\, \sin\!\big(2\pi f t+\theta_0\big)\ \ \mathrm{[V]}\ }. \] The rms value is \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{E}_{\rm rms} &= \frac{\mathcal{E}_{\rm peak}}{\sqrt{2}} = 1.88429333\times 10^{-2}\ f\ \ \mathrm{[V]}. \end{aligned} \]

Note
  • Here we take \(A\fallingdotseq \pi r_m^2\) as an upper-bound estimate (in a real setup, leakage flux and misalignment typically make the effective \(A\hat B\) smaller).
  • The coefficient has units \([\mathrm{V/Hz}]\). Example: for \(f=100\ \mathrm{Hz}\), \(\mathcal{E}_{\rm peak}\fallingdotseq 2.6648\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(\mathcal{E}_{\rm rms}\fallingdotseq 1.8843\ \mathrm{V}\).

articles.title: コンデンサのリアクタンス
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A capacitor passes alternating current, but current flows less readily at lower frequencies. The quantity that expresses this property is called reactance.

The capacitor reactance $X_C$ is given by

$$\displaystyle X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}$$

where

  • $X_C$: capacitive reactance [Ω]
  • $f$: frequency [Hz]
  • $C$: capacitance [F]
Setup

When an AC voltage of rms value $V = 2.0\ \mathrm{V}$ is applied to a capacitor of capacitance $C = 1.5\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ at frequency $f = 100\ \mathrm{Hz}$, what is the rms current $I$?

Theoretical calculation

First, the reactance is

$$ \begin{aligned} X_C &= \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi \times 100 \times 1.5\times10^{-6}} \\ &= 1.06\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{Ω} \end{aligned} $$

From Ohm's law for AC ($\displaystyle I = \frac{V}{X_C}$), the rms current $I$ is

$$ \begin{aligned} I &= \frac{V}{X_C} = \frac{2.0}{1.06\times10^{3}} \\ &= 1.9\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A} \end{aligned} $$

Answer

rms current:

$$\boxed{I \fallingdotseq 1.9\ \mathrm{mA}}$$

articles.title: コイルのリアクタンス
articles.latexEn:
Key points

A coil impedes alternating current. The quantity that expresses this property is inductive reactance,

$$\displaystyle X_L = 2\pi f L$$

  • $X_L$: inductive reactance [Ω]
  • $f$: frequency [Hz]
  • $L$: inductance [H]

(Note) In a coil, the current lags the voltage by 90°.

Setup

When an AC voltage of rms value $V = 2.0\ \mathrm{V}$ is applied to a coil of inductance $L = 300\ \mu\mathrm{H}$ at frequency $f = 70{,}000\ \mathrm{Hz}$, what is the rms current $I$?

Theoretical calculation

First, the inductive reactance is

$$ \begin{aligned} X_L &= 2\pi f L \\ &= 2\pi \times 70{,}000 \times 300\times10^{-6} \\ &= 2\pi \times 21 \\ &= 42\pi \\ &\fallingdotseq 131.95\ \mathrm{Ω} \end{aligned} $$

From Ohm's law for AC, $\displaystyle I = \frac{V}{X_L}$,

$$ \begin{aligned} I_{\mathrm{rms}} &= \frac{2.0}{131.95} \\ &\fallingdotseq 1.52\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{A} \end{aligned} $$

Answer

rms current:

$$\boxed{I_{\mathrm{rms}} \fallingdotseq 15.2\ \mathrm{mA}}$$

articles.title: 交流におけるオームの法則
articles.latexEn:
Key points

For an ideal resistor, as in DC, voltage and current are in phase (phase difference 0°) under AC, and the impedance is only the real resistance $R$. Therefore it does not depend on the frequency $f$.

Ohm's law for AC:

$$\displaystyle I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{rms}}}{R}$$

  • $R$: resistance [Ω]
  • $V_{\mathrm{rms}}$: RMS voltage [V]
  • $I_{\mathrm{rms}}$: RMS current [A]
Setup

When an AC voltage with RMS value $V = 2.0\ \mathrm{V}$ at frequency $f = 100\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is applied to a resistor $R = 3.3\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$, what is the RMS current $I$?

Theoretical calculation

From Ohm's law for AC,

$$ \begin{aligned} I_{\mathrm{rms}} &= \frac{V}{R} = \frac{2.0}{3300} \\ &= 6.06\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{A} \end{aligned} $$

Answer

RMS current:

$$\boxed{I_{\mathrm{rms}} \fallingdotseq 0.606\ \mathrm{mA}\ (\fallingdotseq 0.61\ \mathrm{mA})}$$

(Note) For an ideal resistor the value is independent of $f$. In practice, parasitic inductance and capacitance in the wiring can introduce a slight frequency dependence at high frequencies.

articles.title: RLC回路（直列・放電）観測量：コンデンサ電圧 v_C(t)／代表値：周期T（L=5 mH, R=10 Ω, C=22 μF）
articles.titleEn: RLC circuit (series discharge): observe capacitor voltage v_C(t) / representative value: period T (L=5 mH, R=10 Ω, C=22 μF)
articles.latexEn:
Observed quantity and representative value

The observed physical quantity is the voltage across the capacitor plates \(v_C(t)\). As a representative value, we compare the period \(T\).

Conditions

\(R=10\ \Omega,\quad L=5.0\ \mathrm{mH},\quad C=22\ \mu\mathrm{F},\quad V_0=4.5\ \mathrm{V}\) (initial voltage), no applied voltage (free discharge).

Ideal LC (neglecting resistance)
\[ \begin{aligned} T_{LC} &= 2\pi\sqrt{LC}\\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{(5.0\,\mathrm{mH})(22\,\mu\mathrm{F})}\\ &\fallingdotseq 2.0839\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s} \\ &\fallingdotseq \boxed{2.084\ \mathrm{ms}} \end{aligned} \]
Actual RLC (underdamped: oscillating while decaying)

Underdamped condition: \(\displaystyle R<2\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\). Numerically \(\displaystyle 2\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\fallingdotseq 30.15\ \Omega > 10\ \Omega\), so the circuit is underdamped.

The oscillation period \(T\) is then

\[ \begin{aligned} T &= \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{LC}-\left(\frac{R}{2L}\right)^2}}\\ &= \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{(5.0\,\mathrm{mH})(22\,\mu\mathrm{F})}-\left(\frac{10}{2\cdot 5.0\,\mathrm{mH}}\right)^2}}\\ &\fallingdotseq \boxed{2.209\ \mathrm{ms}} \end{aligned} \]
Period comparison
\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{T - T_{LC}}{T_{LC}}\times 100\% &\fallingdotseq \frac{2.209 - 2.084}{2.084}\times 100\%\\ &\fallingdotseq \boxed{+6.00\%}\quad(\text{actual RLC is longer}) \end{aligned} \]
Time response (observed quantity \(v_C(t)\))

Applying the general solution to the initial conditions \(q(0)=Q_0=C V_0,\ i(0)=0\), write \(v_C(t)=q(t)/C\) without introducing extra symbols:

\[ \begin{aligned} v_C(t) &= V_0\,\exp\!\Big(-\frac{R}{2L}t\Big)\, \Bigg[ \cos\!\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{1}{LC}-\Big(\frac{R}{2L}\Big)^2}\Big) + \frac{\frac{R}{2L}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{LC}-\Big(\frac{R}{2L}\Big)^2}}\, \sin\!\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{1}{LC}-\Big(\frac{R}{2L}\Big)^2}\Big) \Bigg] \end{aligned} \]

Numerical substitution (\(V_0=4.5\ \mathrm{V}\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} v_C(t) &= 4.5\,\exp(-1000\,t)\, \Big[\cos(2844.452\,t)+0.35156\,\sin(2844.452\,t)\Big]\ \mathrm{V} \end{aligned} \]
Note
  • The period is about 6% longer than the ideal value. Larger resistance makes it longer, and eventually oscillation ceases.
  • With an oscilloscope you can read the period from the decaying oscillation of \(v_C(t)\). With a multimeter, visual timing of peak intervals is also possible.

articles.title: コイル
articles.latexEn:
Key points

・When a current flows through a coil, a magnetic field is produced, and changes in that magnetic field in turn induce an emf (induced emf) in the coil. This phenomenon is called self-inductance (self-induction).

・A coil exhibits self-inductance in response to changes in current and tends to oppose those changes.

articles.title: 自己誘導：スイッチ開閉によるコイルの高電圧発生（E=3V, R1=47Ω, R2=100Ω, L=5mH）
articles.titleEn: Self-inductance: high voltage from a coil when switching (E=3V, R1=47Ω, R2=100Ω, L=5mH)
articles.latexEn:
Symbols (all defined at the start)
\[ \begin{aligned} E & = \text{supply voltage} \\[2pt] & = 3\,\mathrm{V} \\[6pt] R_1 & = \text{series resistance (common path ON/OFF)} \\[2pt] & = 47\,\Omega \\[6pt] R_2 & = \text{resistance in series on the OFF path} \\[2pt] & = 100\,\Omega \\[6pt] L & = \text{inductance} \\[2pt] & = 5.0\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{H} \\[6pt] i_1(t) & = \text{coil current while ON} \\[6pt] i(t) & = \text{coil current after OFF} \\[6pt] \tau_1 & = \frac{L}{R_1} \\[6pt] \tau_2 & = \frac{L}{R_1+R_2} \\[6pt] I_0 & = \frac{E}{R_1} \end{aligned} \]
Setup / geometry (observed quantities and wiring)

Connect DC supply \(E\), resistor \(R_1\), and coil \(L\) in series, and switch ON/OFF with a push button. For OFF, provide a path that adds \(R_2\) in series as a current escape route. The main observed quantities are \(i_1(t),\, i(t),\, v_{R_2}(0^+),\, v_L(0^+)\).

Kirchhoff's laws (KCL/KVL formulation)

KCL: In a series circuit the branch current is the same in each element (no branching).

\[ \begin{aligned} i_{\mathrm{src}}(t) & = i_{R_1}(t) \\[2pt] & = i_L(t) \end{aligned} \]

KVL (while ON): Around the supply, resistor, and coil, the sum of voltages is zero.

\[ \begin{aligned} E - R_1\,i_1(t) - L\,\frac{di_1}{dt} & = 0 \end{aligned} \]

KVL (from immediately after OFF): The supply is disconnected; go around resistors \(R_1+R_2\) and the coil.

\[ \begin{aligned} - R_1\,i(t) - R_2\,i(t) - L\,\frac{di}{dt} & = 0 \end{aligned} \]
Differential equation form (rearranged KVL)
\[ \begin{aligned} L\,\frac{di_1}{dt} + R_1\,i_1(t) & = E \\[6pt] L\,\frac{di}{dt} + (R_1+R_2)\,i(t) & = 0 \end{aligned} \]
Initial conditions and continuity (coil current cannot jump)
