articles.title: 剛体のつり合いに関する諸命題
articles.titleEn: Propositions on equilibrium of a rigid body
articles.latexEn:
Proposition (force balance): If a rigid body is at rest, the total external force on it is $\overrightarrow 0$.

Proof
Regard the rigid body as a system of particles. When the body is at rest, in particular its center of mass is at rest, so the center-of-mass acceleration is $\overrightarrow 0$. From the particle-system proposition “total mass × center-of-mass acceleration equals the total external force,” the total external force is $\overrightarrow 0$. 　Q.E.D

Proposition 1: If the resultant of the external forces on a rigid body is $\overrightarrow 0$, then the total moment of the external forces is independent of the choice of reference point.

Proof
Regard the rigid body as a system of particles. Taking a point $O$ as origin, let $\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)$ be the position of the $i$-th particle and $\overrightarrow{f_i}(t)$ the external force on it. The total moment about $O$ is $\overrightarrow{M_O} (t) = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \overrightarrow {r_i}(t) \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t)$. Taking another point $P$ as origin, the total moment is $\overrightarrow{M_P} (t) = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Bigr(\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow {r_i}(t)\Bigr) \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t)$. Rewriting, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle &\qquad \overrightarrow{M_P} (t) \\[6pt]&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Bigr(\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow {r_i}(t)\Bigr) \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t)\\[6pt] &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Bigr(\overrightarrow{OP}+ \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t) + \overrightarrow {r_i}(t) \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t)\Bigr) \\[6pt] &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \overrightarrow{OP} \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t) + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \overrightarrow {r_i}(t) \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t) \\[6pt] &= \overrightarrow{OP} \times \Bigr( \sum_{i=1}^{n} \overrightarrow {F_i}(t)\Bigr) + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Bigr( \overrightarrow {r_i}(t) \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t) \Bigr) \\[6pt] &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Bigr( \overrightarrow {r_i}(t) \times \overrightarrow {F_i}(t) \Bigr)\\[6pt] &= \overrightarrow{M_O} (t) \end{aligned}$$ 　Q.E.D

Proposition 2: If a rigid body remains at rest, then about any point the total moment of the external forces is $\overrightarrow 0$.

Proof
Regard the rigid body as a system of particles. When the body is at rest, its angular momentum remains $\overrightarrow{0}$, so the time derivative of the angular momentum $\overrightarrow{L}(t)$ is also $\overrightarrow{0}$.
From the particle-system proposition, the total external moment equals the time derivative of the angular momentum, hence the total external moment is $\ 0$. 　Q.E.D

articles.title: 等加速度直線運動
articles.latexEn:
Proposition 1 (1D equation of motion): A constant force $F$ acts along a straight line on a particle of mass $m$. Then the equation of motion is $ F = m a $.
Proof

Taking a 1D axis in the vector equation $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ and comparing components yields $F = ma$. $\square$

Proposition 2 (uniform acceleration): If a constant force $F$ acts on a particle of mass $m$, then the acceleration of the particle is constant.
Proof

From Proposition 1, $\displaystyle a= \frac{F}{m} $. If $m$ and $F$ are constant, then $a$ is constant.

(Note) This constant $a$ depends on the orientation of the axis.
(Note) If the initial velocity is along the force, the motion is uniformly accelerated linear motion.

Proposition 3 (velocity formula): When the acceleration of a particle of mass $m$ is a constant $a$, the velocity is $ v(t) = v_0 + a t $.
Proof
$$\begin{aligned} v' &= a \quad \quad \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \int_{0}^{t} v' \, dt &= \int_{0}^{t} a \, dt \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow v(t) - v_0 &= a t \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow v(t) &= v_0 + at \end{aligned}$$ $\square$
Proposition 4 (position formula): When a particle of mass $m$ starts at position $x_0$ with initial velocity $v_0$ and has constant acceleration $a$, its position is $ \displaystyle x(t) = x_0 + v_0 t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2$.
Proof
$$\begin{aligned} x' &= v \quad \quad \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \int_{0}^{t} x' \, dt &= \int_{0}^{t} (v_0 + a t) \, dt \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow x(t) - x_0 &= v_0 t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow x(t) &= x_0 + v_0 t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2 \end{aligned}$$ $\square$
Proposition 5 (relation between velocity and displacement): Velocity and displacement satisfy $$ v^2 - v_0^2 = 2 a (x - x_0) $$
Proof
From Propositions 3 and 4, $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} & v = v_0 + a t& \quad \\[6pt] &x - x_0 = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2 & \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Rewriting the first as $\displaystyle t = \frac{v - v_0}{a}$ and substituting into the second, $$\begin{aligned} x - x_0 &= v_0\frac{v-v_0}{a} + \frac{1}{2}a \left(\frac{v-v_0}{a}\right)^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow x - x_0 &= \frac{v_0(v-v_0)}{a} + \frac{1}{2a}(v-v_0)^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow a(x-x_0) &= v_0(v-v_0) +\frac{1}{2}(v-v_0)^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow v^2 &= v_0^2 + 2a(x-x_0)\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow v^2 - v_0^2 &= 2a(x-x_0)\\[6pt] \end{aligned}$$ $\square$
Proposition 6 (work and energy): When a constant force $F$ acts on a particle, the change in kinetic energy equals the work done by the force: $$ \frac12 m v^2 - \frac12 m v_0^2 = F (x - x_0) $$
Proof
Multiplying the equation of Proposition 5 by $\displaystyle \frac {m} {2} $ gives $$ \frac{1}{2} m (v^2 - v_0^2) = m a (x - x_0) $$ . Using $F=ma$, $$ \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 = F(x-x_0) $$ . The left-hand side is the change in kinetic energy; the right-hand side is the work done by the force.

articles.title: 質点における運動量と力積
articles.titleEn: Momentum and impulse for a particle
articles.latexEn:
Definition of momentum

When a particle of mass $m$ moves with velocity $\vec{v}$, $\, m \vec{v}\,$ is called the momentum of the particle.

Definition of impulse

When a force $\vec{F}(t)$ acts on a particle from time $t_0$ to $t_1$, the vector $\displaystyle \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{F}(t)\, dt$ is called the impulse received by the particle.

Definition of average force

When a force $\vec{F}(t)$ acts on a particle from time $t_0$ to $t_1$, $\displaystyle \vec{F}_{\mathrm{ave}} = \frac{1}{t_1 - t_0} \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{F}(t)\, dt$ is called the average force on the body in that interval.

Proposition: Over a time interval, the change in a particle's momentum equals the impulse received in that interval.
Proof

When a force $\vec{F}(t)$ acts on a particle of mass $m$ from $t_0$ to $t_1$, we show that $$ m \vec{v}(t_1) - m \vec{v}(t_0) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{F}(t)\, dt $$ holds.

Integrating the equation of motion $m \vec{a}(t) = \vec{F}(t)$ from $t_0$ to $t_1$ gives $$ \int_{t_0}^{t_1} m \vec{a}(t)\, dt = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{F}(t)\, dt $$

Substituting $\vec{a}(t) = \vec{v}'(t)$ yields $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ &\int_{t_0}^{t_1} m \vec{v}'(t)\, dt = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{F}(t)\, dt\\[7pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &\Bigl[ m \vec{v}(t) \Bigr]_{t_0}^{t_1} = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{F}(t)\, dt\\[7pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &m \vec{v}(t_1) - m \vec{v}(t_0) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{F}(t)\, dt \qquad \text{Q.E.D.} \end{aligned}$$

articles.title: 定義および命題
articles.latexEn:
Definition of work for a constant force and straight-line motion
When a body moves in a straight line by $\Delta \vec x$ under a constant force $ \vec F $, the work $W$ done by the force on the particle is defined by $$ W = |\vec F| | \Delta \vec x| \cos\theta = \vec F \cdot \vec x $$ ※ Here $ \theta $ is the angle between the force and the direction of motion.
Definition of work in general (line integral)
In general, when a body moves along a curve under a force that may change in direction and magnitude, the work $W$ done by the force is defined by $$\begin{aligned} \quad \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r &:= \lim_{| P | \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} (\vec F_i\cdot\vec\tau_i)\,\Delta s_i \\[4pt] &\;\Bigl(= \lim_{| P | \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} |\vec F_i|\cos\theta_i\,\Delta s_i\Bigr) \end{aligned}$$
Notation

  • $ P = \{t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_N \}$ : a partition
  • $N(P)$ : number of subintervals
  • $ | P| := \displaystyle \max_i |t_i-t_{i-1}| $ : mesh (largest subinterval width)
  • $\Delta s_i$ : arc length of the $i$-th subinterval
  • $\vec F_i$ : the vector field $ \vec F $ at a representative point of the $i$-th arc
  • $\vec\tau_i$ : unit tangent at a representative point of the $i$-th arc
  • $\theta_i$ : angle between $ \vec F_i $ and $ \vec\tau_i $
  • $\vec F_i\cdot\vec\tau_i\,\Delta s_i,\ |\vec F_i|\cos\theta_i\,\Delta s_i$: approximate work by $\vec F$ on the $i$-th arc
Proposition: If $|\vec F|$ is a constant $F$ along a curve $C$ and the angle with the tangent is a constant $ \theta $ along the curve, then with curve length $L$, $$ \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = F\cos\theta\cdot L $$

Proof
By definition $$ \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \lim_{| P | \to 0}\sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} (\vec F_i\cdot\vec\tau_i)\,\Delta s_i. $$ At each representative point $|\vec F_i|=F$ and $\vec F_i\cdot\vec\tau_i=F\cos\theta$, so $$\begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} (\vec F_i\cdot\vec\tau_i)\,\Delta s_i &= F\cos\theta \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)}\Delta s_i \\[5pt] &= F \cos \theta \cdot L \end{aligned}$$ Hence $$\begin{aligned} \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r &= \lim_{| P | \to 0} \Bigl( F \cos \theta \cdot L\Bigr)\\[5pt] &= F \cos \theta \cdot L \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

articles.title: 仕事とエネルギー
articles.latexEn:
Definition of kinetic energy

When a particle of mass $m$ has speed $v$, $\displaystyle \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ is called the kinetic energy of the particle.

Proposition 1: In 1D when the force is aligned with the motion, with start $x_0$ and end $x_1$, the work is $$ W=\int_{x(t_0)}^{x(t_1)} F_x(x)\,dx $$

Proof
By definition of work, $$\begin{aligned} W &= \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r\\[4pt] &= \lim_{| P | \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} (\vec F_i\cdot\vec\tau_i)\,\Delta s_i \\[4pt] &\;\Bigl(= \lim_{| P | \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} |\vec F_i| \,\Delta s_i\Bigr)\\[4pt] \end{aligned}$$ As the mesh shrinks this becomes a Riemann sum and agrees with $$ W=\int_{x1}^{x0} F_x(x)\,dx $$ .　Q.E.D

Theorem 1: The work $W$ equals the integral $$\begin{aligned} W = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec F(t)\cdot \vec v(t)\,dt. \end{aligned}$$
Proof

By definition of work, $$\begin{aligned} W = \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \lim_{| P | \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} (\vec F_i\cdot\vec\tau_i)\,\Delta s_i \end{aligned}$$ Introduce a parameter $t$ along the curve.
For each interval $[t_{i-1},t_i]$, the mean-value theorem for integrals gives a point $\eta_i\in[t_{i-1},t_i]$ such that $$ \Delta s_i=\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}|\vec v(t)|\,dt=|\vec v(\eta_i)|(t_i-t_{i-1}). $$ Taking this $\eta_i$ as the representative point of each subinterval, $$ \vec F_i\cdot\vec\tau_i\,\Delta s_i =\vec F(\vec r(\eta_i))\cdot\vec v(\eta_i)\,(t_i-t_{i-1}). $$ Letting $|P|\to0$, the Riemann sum yields $$\begin{aligned} W&=\vec F(\vec r(\eta_i))\cdot\vec v(\eta_i)\,(t_i-t_{i-1}) \\[5pt] &= \int_{t_0}^{t_1}\vec F(\vec r(t))\cdot\vec v(t)\,dt. \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Theorem 2: Relation between work and kinetic energy

The change in kinetic energy of a particle of mass $m$ from time $t_0$ to $t_1$ equals the total work done on the particle by all forces acting on it from $t_0$ to $t_1$.

Proof
Let the resultant force be $\vec{F}(t)\Bigl(= \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \vec{F}_i(t) \Bigr) $.
From the equation of motion, $m \vec{a}(t) = \vec{F}(t)$.
Taking the inner product with $\vec{v}(t)$ and integrating from $t_0$ to $t_1$, $$ \int_{t_0}^{t_1} m \vec{a}(t) \cdot \vec{v}(t)\, dt = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{F}(t) \cdot \vec{v}(t)\, dt $$
Right-hand side

By Theorem 1, this is precisely the work $W$ done by the resultant from $t_0$ to $t_1$.

Left-hand side

From the product rule, $\displaystyle \frac{1}{2} \bigl(v(t)^2\bigr)' = \vec{a}(t) \cdot \vec{v}(t)$, so the left-hand side becomes $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ &\int_{t_0}^{t_1} \Bigl(\frac{1}{2} m v(t)^2\Bigr)'\, dt\\[6pt] &=\Bigl[\frac{1}{2} m v(t)^2\Bigr]_{t_0}^{t_1} \\[6pt] &=\frac{1}{2} m v(t_1)^2 - \frac{1}{2} m v(t_0)^2\\[6pt] \end{aligned}$$

which is the change in kinetic energy between $t_1$ and $t_0$.
Hence the work done by the resultant from $t_0$ to $t_1$ equals that change in kinetic energy. 　Q.E.D
Proposition: A force perpendicular to the velocity does no work
Proof
Let $\vec{f}(t)$ be a force perpendicular to the velocity. Then at every time $t$, $\vec{f}(t) \cdot \vec{v}(t) = 0$. Hence the work $W$ from $t_0$ to $t_1$ is, by Theorem 1, $$ W = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \vec{f}(t) \cdot \vec{v}(t)\, dt = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} 0\, dt = 0 $$ . Therefore a force perpendicular to the velocity does no work. Q.E.D.

articles.title: 保存力
articles.latexEn:
Definition of a conservative force

Taking some point as the origin, when a particle moves from $\overrightarrow a$ to $\overrightarrow b$ under a force $\overrightarrow F$, if the work done by $\overrightarrow F$ depends only on the endpoints $\overrightarrow a ,\overrightarrow b$ and not on the path, the force is called conservative.

Proposition: Uniform gravity is a conservative force

Proof
It suffices to show that the work done by uniform gravity on a particle of mass $m$ is path-independent. Since $\overrightarrow{F}=m\overrightarrow g$ everywhere, for any path $\overrightarrow r(t)$ with $\overrightarrow r(t_0) = \overrightarrow a, \ \overrightarrow r(t_1) = \overrightarrow b$, $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ &\displaystyle \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \overrightarrow{F}(t) \cdot \overrightarrow{v}(t) dt\\[6pt] &= \displaystyle \int_{t_0}^{t_1} m\overrightarrow g \cdot \frac {d\overrightarrow r}{dt} dt\\[6pt] &= \displaystyle \int_{t_0}^{t_1} mg\frac {dy}{dt} dt \\[6pt] &= \displaystyle mg \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \frac {dy}{dt} dt \\[6pt] &= \displaystyle mg \bigl[ y(t) \bigr]_{t_0}^{t_1} \\[6pt] &= \displaystyle mg \bigl( y(t_1) - y(t_0)\bigr)\\[6pt] &= \displaystyle mg \bigl( b_y - a_y\bigr) \end{aligned}$$ . The work depends only on the $y$-coordinates of $\overrightarrow a$ and $\overrightarrow b$, hence only on the endpoints. Q.E.D

Proposition: A force proportional to the position vector is conservative

Proof
It suffices to show that the work of $-k\overrightarrow{r}(t)$ is path-independent. For any path with $\overrightarrow r(t_0) = \overrightarrow a,\ \overrightarrow r(t_1) = \overrightarrow b$, $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ &\displaystyle \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \overrightarrow{F}(t) \cdot \overrightarrow{v}(t) dt\\[6pt] &= \displaystyle \int_{t_0}^{t_1} -k \overrightarrow{r}(t) \cdot \overrightarrow{v}(t) dt \\[6pt] &= \Bigr[-\frac {1}{2} k |\overrightarrow r (t)|^2 \Bigr]_{t_0}^{t_1} \\[6pt] &= -\frac {1}{2} k \Bigl( |\overrightarrow b|^2 - |\overrightarrow a|^2 \Bigr) \end{aligned}$$ . The work depends only on the endpoint position vectors $\overrightarrow a, \overrightarrow b$. Q.E.D

Lemma
For a vector function $\overrightarrow r(t)$ with $r(t)=|\overrightarrow r(t)|$, $$ \bigl(r^{-1}\bigr)'=-\,\frac{\overrightarrow r \cdot \overrightarrow v}{r^3}. $$

Proof
From $r(t) = \sqrt{\overrightarrow r(t)\cdot\overrightarrow r(t)}$, $r'(t)=\displaystyle \frac{\overrightarrow r(t)\cdot\overrightarrow v(t)}{r(t)}$. Hence $$ \Bigl(\frac 1 {r(t)}\Bigr)'=-\frac{1}{r(t)^2} r(t)'=-\frac{\overrightarrow r(t)\cdot\overrightarrow v(t)}{r(t)^3}. $$ Q.E.D.

Proposition: Universal gravitation is a conservative force

Proof
For a particle of mass $m$ and a central mass $M$, $$ \overrightarrow{F}(\overrightarrow{r})=-G\frac{Mm}{r^3}\,\overrightarrow{r}, $$ . The work along a path from $\overrightarrow r(t_0)=\overrightarrow a$ to $\overrightarrow r(t_1)=\overrightarrow b$ is $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ &\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\overrightarrow{F}(\overrightarrow r)\cdot{\overrightarrow v}\,dt\\[6pt] &=-GMm\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\frac{\overrightarrow r\cdot{\overrightarrow v}}{r^3}\,dt \\[6pt] &=-{GMm}\Bigl[\frac{1}{|\overrightarrow{r}(t)|}\Bigr]_{t_0}^{t_1}\\[6pt] &=-GMm\Bigl(\frac{1}{|\overrightarrow {r}(t_1)|}-\frac{1}{|\overrightarrow {r}(t_0)|}\Bigr) \\[6pt] &=-GMm\Bigl(\frac{1}{|\overrightarrow b|}-\frac{1}{|\overrightarrow a|}\Bigr) \end{aligned}$$ which depends only on the endpoints, so universal gravitation is conservative. Q.E.D

Proposition: Kinetic friction is not a conservative force

Proof
When a body slides on a contact surface with velocity $\overrightarrow v$, kinetic friction is $$ \overrightarrow{F}_{\rm fr}=-\,\mu_{k}N\,\frac{\overrightarrow v}{|\overrightarrow v|}, $$ where $\mu_{k}$ is the coefficient of kinetic friction and $N$ the normal force. Work along any path from $\overrightarrow a$ to $\overrightarrow b$ is $$\begin{aligned} W_{\rm fr}&=-\mu_{k}N\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\frac{\overrightarrow v}{|\overrightarrow v|}\cdot\overrightarrow v\,dt\\[6pt] &=-\mu_{k}N\int_{t_0}^{t_1}|\overrightarrow v|\,dt \end{aligned}$$ . Here $\displaystyle \int_{t_0}^{t_1}|\overrightarrow v|\,dt$ is the path length from $\overrightarrow a$ to $\overrightarrow b$, which is not uniquely determined by the endpoints alone. Hence kinetic friction is not conservative. Q.E.D

articles.title: 地上の重力下のエネルギー保存
articles.latexEn:
Proposition (energy conservation under surface gravity): When the equation of motion $mx''(t)= mg$ holds, $$\begin{aligned} E = \frac{1}{2}mv(t)^2 -mgx(t) \end{aligned}$$ is constant in time.

Proof
It suffices to show that the time derivative vanishes. Multiplying both sides by $x'(t)$ gives $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ \ \ &mx'(t)x''(t) = mgx'(t) \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}mx'(t)^2\Bigr]' = \bigl[m g x(t)\bigr]' \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}mx'(t)^2 - mgx(t)\Bigr]' = 0 \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D.

articles.title: 単振動のエネルギー保存
articles.titleEn: Energy conservation in simple harmonic motion
articles.latexEn:
Proposition (energy conservation in simple harmonic motion): When the equation of motion $mx''(t)= -kx(t)$ holds, $$\begin{aligned} E = \frac{1}{2}mv(t)^2 + \frac {1}{2}kx(t)^2 \end{aligned}$$ is constant in time.

Proof
It suffices to show that the time derivative vanishes. Multiplying both sides by $x'(t)$ gives $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ \ \ & mx'(t)x''(t) = -kx'(t)x(t) \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}mx'(t)^2\Bigr]' = -\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}k x(t)^2\Bigr]' \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}mx'(t)^2 + \frac {1}{2}k x(t)^2\Bigr]' = 0 \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D.

articles.title: 地上の重力と弾性力の下でのエネルギー保存
articles.titleEn: Energy conservation under surface gravity and elastic force
articles.latexEn:
Proposition (energy conservation for a system with both a spring and gravity): When the equation of motion $m x''(t) = -kx(t) + mg$ holds, $$\begin{aligned} E = \frac{1}{2}m v(t)^2 + \frac{1}{2}k x(t)^2 - mgx(t) \end{aligned}$$ is constant in time.

Proof
It suffices to show that the time derivative vanishes. Multiplying both sides by $x'(t)$ gives $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ \ \ &m x'(t)x''(t) = -k x(t) x'(t) + mg x'(t) \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}m \bigl(x'(t)\bigr)^2\Bigr]' = \Bigl[-\frac{1}{2}k \bigl(x(t)\bigr)^2 + mg x(t)\Bigr]' \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ &\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}m \bigl(x'(t)\bigr)^2 + \frac{1}{2}k \bigl(x(t)\bigr)^2 - mg x(t)\Bigr]' = 0 \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D.

Remark (choice of coordinates)

In this proposition the positive direction is taken vertically downward, so energy conservation takes the form $$ E = \frac{1}{2} m v(t)^2 + \frac{1}{2} k x(t)^2 - mgx(t) $$ .
If the positive direction is taken vertically upward, the equation of motion becomes $m x''(t) = -kx(t) - mg$, and the gravitational potential term becomes $+mgx(t)$. The conserved quantity is then $$ E = \frac{1}{2} m v(t)^2 + \frac{1}{2} k x(t)^2 + mgx(t) $$ . The sign difference comes only from the choice of coordinates and amounts to a constant shift of the reference energy.

articles.title: 万有引力エネルギー保存
articles.latexEn:
Assumptions and notation
•The prime “ ' ” and $\displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}$ are used interchangeably for readability; both mean time differentiation.
•Let $\vec e_x, \vec e_y, \vec e_z$ be unit vectors in the $x,y,z$ directions.
•Position: $\vec r(t) = x(t)\vec e_x+y(t)\vec e_y+z(t)\vec e_z$
•Velocity: $\vec v(t) = \displaystyle\frac{d\vec r}{dt}(t) = v_x(t)\vec e_x+v_y(t)\vec e_y+v_z(t)\vec e_z$
•Acceleration: $\vec a(t) = \displaystyle\frac{d\vec v}{dt}(t) = a_x(t)\vec e_x+a_y(t)\vec e_y+a_z(t)\vec e_z$
•Position magnitude: $r(t) = \lVert \vec r(t)\rVert = \sqrt{x(t)^2+y(t)^2+z(t)^2}$
•Speed: $v(t) = \lVert \vec v(t)\rVert = \sqrt{v_x(t)^2+v_y(t)^2+v_z(t)^2}$
•Acceleration magnitude: $a(t) = \lVert \vec a(t)\rVert = \sqrt{a_x(t)^2+a_y(t)^2+a_z(t)^2}$
.
•The equation of motion is $\ \displaystyle m\vec{a}(t):=-\frac{GMm}{r^3(t)}\vec{r}(t)$.
Lemma 1. $\displaystyle r(t)\frac{dr}{dt}(t)=x(t)v_x(t)+y(t)v_y(t)+z(t)v_z(t)$ holds.
Proof
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{dr}{dt}(t)&=\frac{x(t)v_x(t)+y(t)v_y(t)+z(t)v_z(t)} {\sqrt{x(t)^2+y(t)^2+z(t)^2}}\\ \\ \Leftrightarrow \frac{dr}{dt}(t)&=\frac{x(t)v_x(t)+y(t)v_y(t)+z(t)v_z(t)}{r(t)} \end{aligned}$$ Multiplying both sides by $r(t)$ yields the claim.　⬜︎
Proposition 1 (energy conservation) In motion under the gravitational potential, $${\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}mv^2(t)-\frac{GMm}{r(t)}}$$ is a constant fixed by the initial conditions and independent of time.
Proof
Show that the time derivative of $\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}mv^2(t)-\frac{GMm}{r(t)}$ is $0$. Starting from the equation of motion, take the inner product of both sides with the velocity. $$\begin{aligned} &\ \ \ m\vec{a}(t)=-\frac{GMm}{r^3(t)}\vec{r}(t)\\ &\Rightarrow m\vec{a}(t)\cdot \vec{v}(t) =-\frac{GMm}{r^3(t)}\vec{r}(t)\cdot \vec{v}(t)\\ \end{aligned}$$
Left-hand side

$$\begin{aligned} \ &m\vec{a}(t)\cdot \vec{v}(t)\\ &=m\Bigr(a_x(t)v_x(t)+a_y(t)v_y(t)+a_z(t)v_z(t)\Bigr)\\ &=\frac{1}{2}m\Biggr(\Bigr(v_x(t)^2\Bigr)'+\Bigr(v_y(t)^2\Bigr)'+\Bigr(v_z(t)^2\Bigr)'\Biggr)\\ &=\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr(\frac{1}{2}mv^2(t)\Bigr) \end{aligned}$$
Right-hand side

$$\begin{aligned} &\ \ \ -\frac{GMm}{r^3(t)}\vec{r}(t)\cdot \vec{v}(t)\\ &= -\frac{GMm}{r^3(t)}\Bigr(x(t)v_x(t)+y(t)v_y(t)+z(t)v_z(t)\Bigr)\\ &=-\frac{GMm}{r^3(t)}r(t)\frac{dr}{dt}(t)\\ &=-\frac{GMm}{r^2(t)}\frac{dr}{dt}(t)\\ &=\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr(\frac{GMm}{r(t)}\Bigr)\\ \end{aligned}$$ Hence $$\begin{aligned} & \ \ \ m\vec{a}(t)=-\frac{GMm}{r^3(t)}\vec{r}(t)\\ & \Rightarrow m\vec{a}(t)\cdot \vec{v}(t)=-\frac{GMm}{r^3(t)}\vec{r}(t)\cdot \vec{v}(t)\\ & \Leftrightarrow \frac{d}{dt}\Bigr(\frac{1}{2}mv^2(t)\Bigr)=\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr(\frac{GMm}{r(t)}\Bigr)\\ & \Leftrightarrow \frac{d}{dt}\Bigr(\frac{1}{2}mv^2(t)-\frac{GMm}{r(t)}\Bigr)=0\\ \end{aligned}$$ 　⬜︎
