articles.title: 質点の角運動量ベクトルと力のモーメント
articles.titleEn: Angular momentum vector and torque of a particle
articles.latexEn:
Definition (angular momentum of a particle about the origin)

Define the angular momentum $\vec L$ of a particle about the origin using the cross product $\times$ by $$\overrightarrow{L} = \overrightarrow{r}(t) \times \overrightarrow{p}(t)$$ .

Definition (moment of force / torque)

When a force $\overrightarrow{F}(t)$ acts on a particle at position $\overrightarrow{r}(t)$, $\overrightarrow{r}(t) \times \overrightarrow{F}(t)$ is the moment of the force about the origin.

Proposition 1: When a torque $\overrightarrow{M} = \displaystyle \overrightarrow{r}(t) \times \overrightarrow{F}(t)$ acts on a particle, with angular momentum $\overrightarrow{L}(t)$ about the origin, $\overrightarrow{L}(t)' = \overrightarrow{M}(t)$ holds.

Proof
Differentiate the definition $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{L}(t)=\overrightarrow{r}(t)\times\overrightarrow{p}(t)$. $$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{L}(t)' &= \bigl(\overrightarrow{r}(t)\times\overrightarrow{p}(t)\bigr)'\\[6pt] &= \overrightarrow{r}(t)'\times\overrightarrow{p}(t) + \overrightarrow{r}(t)\times\overrightarrow{p}(t)' \end{aligned}$$ For the first term on the right, $\overrightarrow{p}=m\overrightarrow{r}'$ is parallel to $\overrightarrow {r}(t)' $, so by properties of the cross product $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{r}(t)' \times \overrightarrow{p}(t) = \vec 0$ . Hence $$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{L}(t)' &= \overrightarrow{r}(t)'\times\overrightarrow{p}(t) + \overrightarrow{r}(t)\times\overrightarrow{p}(t)'\\[6pt] &= \overrightarrow{r}(t)\times\overrightarrow{p}(t)' \end{aligned}$$ Using Newton's second law $\overrightarrow{p}(t)'=\overrightarrow{F}(t)$, $$ {\overrightarrow{L}}(t)'=\overrightarrow{r}(t)\times\overrightarrow{F}(t)=\overrightarrow{M}(t) $$ Q.E.D

Definition (central force)
A force whose magnitude is a function of the distance from the origin and whose direction lies along the line from the origin to the body; that is, a force of the form $$\overrightarrow{F}= F(|\overrightarrow{r}|) \frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{|\overrightarrow{r}|}$$
Example (central force)
Universal gravitation $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{F} = \frac{GMm}{r^2}\frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{r}$ is a central force.
Definition (centripetal force)

The force toward the center of the circle that acts on a body in uniform circular motion is called the centripetal force.

Proposition 2: Taking the origin as the center of a central force, the angular momentum of a particle about the origin is conserved under a central force.

Proof
By definition of a central force, the torque is $$ \overrightarrow{M}(t) = \overrightarrow{r}(t) \times F(|\overrightarrow{r}|) \frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{|\overrightarrow{r}|} $$ . Since $\overrightarrow{r}(t)$ and $F(|\overrightarrow{r}|) \frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{|\overrightarrow{r}|}$ are parallel, $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{r}(t) \times F(|\overrightarrow{r}|) \frac{\overrightarrow{r}}{|\overrightarrow{r}|}=\vec 0$
. Hence $\overrightarrow{M}(t) = \vec 0\ $. By Proposition 1, $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{L}(t)'=\overrightarrow{M}(t)=\vec{0}$
. Therefore the angular momentum $\overrightarrow{L}(t)$ about the origin is conserved.

Q.E.D

articles.title: 単振り子の周期
articles.latexEn:
Proposition (period of a simple pendulum): When the swing angle $\theta(t)$ is sufficiently small, the period $T$ of a pendulum of string length $L$ can be approximated by $$\begin{aligned} T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \quad [\text{s}] \end{aligned}$$
Proof
From the figure, take the particle position as $$\begin{aligned} x(t) = L\sin\theta(t), \quad y(t) = L\cos\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ . Differentiating with respect to time as functions of $\theta(t)$: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} v_x(t) = \displaystyle\frac{dx}{dt} = L\cos\theta(t) \displaystyle\frac{d\theta}{dt} \\[6pt] v_y(t) = \displaystyle\frac{dy}{dt} = -L\sin\theta(t) \displaystyle\frac{d\theta}{dt} \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Differentiating again for the acceleration: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} a_x(t) = L \left( \displaystyle\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} \cos\theta(t) - \left( \displaystyle\frac{d\theta}{dt} \right)^2 \sin\theta(t) \right) \\[6pt] a_y(t) = -L \left( \displaystyle\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} \sin\theta(t) + \left( \displaystyle\frac{d\theta}{dt} \right)^2 \cos\theta(t) \right) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ The force components on the body are: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} F_x = -T \sin \theta(t) \\[6pt] F_y = mg - T \cos \theta(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Using Newton's equation $ma = F$, $$\begin{aligned} mL\left( \displaystyle\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} \cos\theta(t) - \left( \displaystyle\frac{d\theta}{dt} \right)^2 \sin\theta(t) \right) &= -T \sin\theta(t) \quad \cdots (1) \\[6pt] -mL\left( \displaystyle\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} \sin\theta(t) + \left( \displaystyle\frac{d\theta}{dt} \right)^2 \cos\theta(t) \right) &= mg - T \cos\theta(t) \quad \cdots (2) \end{aligned}$$ Multiplying (1) by $\cos\theta(t)$ and (2) by $\sin\theta(t)$ and subtracting eliminates the tension $T$: $$\begin{aligned} & \ \ \ \ \ mL \displaystyle\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} (\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = -mg\sin\theta(t) \\[6pt] & \Leftrightarrow mL \displaystyle\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -mg\sin\theta(t) \\[6pt] & \Leftrightarrow \displaystyle\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -\frac{g}{L} \sin\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ Assuming $\theta(t)$ is small enough that $\displaystyle \sin\theta(t) \fallingdotseq \theta(t)$, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -\frac{g}{L} \theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ . This is the SHM differential equation; the angular frequency $\omega$ and period $T$ are $$\begin{aligned} \omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}} \quad [\text{rad/s}],\ \ T = \displaystyle\frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \quad [\text{s}] \end{aligned}$$

articles.title: 単振り子の周期と楕円積分
articles.titleEn: Period of a simple pendulum and elliptic integrals

articles.title: 円錐振り子の周期
articles.latexEn:
Proposition: Under the setup of Fig. 1 (conical pendulum; the bob moves in uniform horizontal circular motion), the period $T$ of the bob is $$ \displaystyle T = 2\pi \sqrt {\frac{L \cos \theta }{g}}\ [\mathrm{s}] $$

Proof
Vertical forces on the body balance. Letting the string tension be ${T \ [\mathrm{N}]} $, $$\displaystyle mg = T \cos \theta\ \Leftrightarrow \ T = \frac{mg}{\cos \theta} \ \cdots (1) $$ If the body moves in uniform circular motion with radius ${r = L \sin \theta \ [\mathrm{m}]} $, the radial equation of motion gives $$ \displaystyle m\frac{v^2}{r} = T\sin \theta  \\ \ \\\Leftrightarrow m\frac{v^2}{L \sin \theta } = T\sin \theta \ \cdots (2) $$ Substituting ${(1)} $ into ${(2)} $, $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ &\displaystyle m\frac{v^2}{L \sin \theta } = mg\frac{ \sin \theta }{\cos \theta}  \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ \ &\frac{v^2}{L \sin \theta } = g \tan \theta\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ \ &v^2 = g L \sin \theta \tan \theta \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ \ &v = \sqrt{g L \sin \theta \tan \theta} \ [\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}] \ \cdots (3) \end{aligned}$$ The period of the conical pendulum is $\displaystyle T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} \ [\mathrm{s}]$, so from ${(3)} $, $$\begin{aligned} T &= \frac{2\pi r}{v} \\[6pt] &= \frac{2\pi L \sin \theta }{\sqrt{g L \sin \theta \tan \theta}} \\[6pt] &= 2\pi \sqrt {\frac{L \sin \theta }{g \tan \theta}} \\[6pt] &= 2\pi \sqrt {\frac{L \cos \theta }{g}} \ [\mathrm{s}] \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

articles.title: 等速円運動の運動方程式
articles.titleEn: Equation of motion for uniform circular motion
articles.latexEn:
Definition of symbols

$\cdot \ \displaystyle F_r\cdots$ radial (centripetal) component of $\vec F$
$\cdot \ \displaystyle F_\theta \cdots$ angular component of $\vec F$
$\cdot \ \displaystyle \theta(t)=\omega t \cdots$ angle of the particle from the $x$-axis (angular velocity $\omega$ constant)
$\cdot \ \vec r(t) \cdots$ position vector
$\cdot \ \vec v(t) \cdots$ velocity vector
$\cdot \ \vec a(t) \cdots$ acceleration vector
$\cdot \ v(t)=|\vec v(t)|\cdots$ speed

Definition (radial and angular unit vectors)
Define the radial and angular unit vectors for circular motion by $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec e_r(t) = \cos(\omega t)\vec e_x + \sin(\omega t)\vec e_y\\[6pt] \vec e_{\theta}(t) = -\sin(\omega t)\vec e_x + \cos(\omega t)\vec e_y \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$
Proposition 1: The time derivatives of the radial and angular unit vectors are $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec {e_r}'(t) = \omega \vec {e_{\theta}}(t)\\[6pt] \vec {e_\theta}'(t) = -\omega \vec e_r(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

Proof
From $\displaystyle \vec e_r(t)=\cos(\omega t)\,\vec e_x + \sin(\omega t)\,\vec e_y$, $$\begin{aligned} \vec e_r'(t) &= -\sin(\omega t)\,\omega\,\vec e_x + \cos(\omega t)\,\omega\,\vec e_y \\ &= \omega\bigl(-\sin(\omega t)\vec e_x + \cos(\omega t)\vec e_y\bigr)\\ &= \omega\,\vec e_{\theta}(t) \end{aligned}$$ Similarly for $e_{\theta}(t) = -\sin(\omega t)\,\vec e_x + \cos(\omega t)\,\vec e_y$, $$\begin{aligned} \vec e_{\theta}'(t) &= -\cos(\omega t)\,\omega\,\vec e_x - \sin(\omega t)\,\omega\,\vec e_y \\ &= -\omega\bigl(\cos(\omega t)\vec e_x + \sin(\omega t)\vec e_y\bigr)\\ &= -\omega\,\vec e_r(t). \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 2: The velocity of a particle in uniform circular motion is $$\begin{aligned} \vec v(t) = R \omega \vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$

Proof
With $\vec r(t) = R \vec e_r(t)$ and Proposition 1 ($R$ constant), $$\begin{aligned} \vec v(t) &= \vec r'(t)\\[6pt] &= \Bigl(R \vec e_r(t)\Bigr)'\\[6pt] &= R \vec e_r'(t)\\[6pt] &= R \omega \vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 3: The speed $v$ in uniform circular motion is $R |\omega|$.

Proof
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle v(t) &= |\vec v (t)|\\[6pt] &= |R \omega \vec e_\theta(t)|\\[6pt] &= |R|\,|\omega|\,|\vec e_\theta(t)|\\[6pt] &= R　|\omega| |\vec e_\theta(t)| \end{aligned}$$ Since $e_\theta(t)$ is a unit vector, $\displaystyle v(t) = R|\omega|$.　Q.E.D

Proposition 4: The acceleration in uniform circular motion is $$\begin{aligned} \vec a(t) = - R \omega^2 \vec e_r(t) \end{aligned}$$

Proof
Differentiate $\vec v(t) = R \omega \vec e_\theta(t)$ using Proposition 1: $$\begin{aligned} \vec a(t) &= \vec v'(t) \\[6pt] &= \Bigl(R \omega \vec e_\theta(t)\Bigr)'\\[6pt] &= R \omega \vec e_\theta'(t)\\[6pt] &= R \omega (-\omega \vec e_r(t))\\[6pt] &= - R \omega^2 \vec e_r(t) \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 5: With the circle center as the origin, the equation of motion for uniform circular motion is $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \displaystyle -m \frac {v^2}{R} = F_r\\[6pt] F_\theta = 0 \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

Proof
From $m \vec a(t) = \vec F(t)$ and Proposition 4, $$\begin{aligned} m \vec a(t) &= m(- R \omega^2 \vec e_r(t))\\[6pt] &= -m R \omega^2 \vec e_r(t) \end{aligned}$$ . Decomposing the force as $\vec F(t) = F_r \vec e_r(t) + F_\theta \vec e_\theta(t)$, $$\begin{aligned} -m R \omega^2 \vec e_r(t) &= F_r \vec e_r(t) + F_\theta \vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ . With $v=R |\omega|$ from Proposition 3, comparing components yields $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \displaystyle -m R \omega^2 = -m \frac{v^2}{R} = F_r\\[6pt] F_\theta = 0 \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

articles.title: 非等速円運動の運動方程式
articles.titleEn: Equation of motion for non-uniform circular motion
articles.latexEn:
Definition of symbols

$\cdot \ \displaystyle F_r\cdots$ radial (centripetal) component of $\vec F$
$\cdot \ \displaystyle F_\theta \cdots$ angular component of $\vec F$
$\cdot \ \displaystyle \theta \cdots$ angle of the particle from the $x$-axis
$\cdot \ \vec r(t) \cdots$ position vector
$\cdot \ \vec v(t) \cdots$ velocity vector
$\cdot \ \vec a(t) \cdots$ acceleration vector
$\cdot \ v(t)=|\vec v(t)|\cdots$ speed

Definition (radial and angular unit vectors)

Define the radial and angular unit vectors for circular motion by $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec e_r(t) = \cos\theta(t)\vec e_x + \sin\theta(t)\vec e_y\\[6pt] \vec e_{\theta}(t) = -\sin\theta(t)\vec e_x + \cos\theta(t)\vec e_y \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

Proposition 1: The time derivatives of the radial and angular unit vectors are $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec {e_r}'(t) = \theta'(t) \vec {e_{\theta}}(t)\\[6pt] \vec {e_\theta}'(t) = -\theta'(t) \vec {e_r}(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

Proof
From $\displaystyle \vec e_r(t)=\cos\theta(t)\,\vec e_x + \sin\theta(t)\,\vec e_y$, by the chain rule $$\begin{aligned} \vec e_r'(t) &= -\sin\theta(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_x + \cos\theta(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_y \\ &= \theta'(t)\bigl(-\sin\theta(t)\vec e_x + \cos\theta(t)\vec e_y\bigr)\\ &= \theta'(t)\,\vec e_{\theta}(t) \end{aligned}$$ Similarly for $e_{\theta}(t) = -\sin\theta(t)\,\vec e_x + \cos\theta(t)\,\vec e_y$, $$\begin{aligned} \vec e_{\theta}'(t) &= -\cos\theta(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_x - \sin\theta(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_y \\ &= -\theta'(t)\bigl(\cos\theta(t)\vec e_x + \sin\theta(t)\vec e_y\bigr)\\ &= -\theta'(t)\,\vec e_r(t). \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 2: The velocity of a particle in (not necessarily uniform) circular motion is $$\begin{aligned} \vec v(t) = \vec r'(t) = R \theta'(t) \vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$

Proof
With $\vec r(t) = R \vec e_r(t) = R \Bigl( \cos\theta(t)\vec e_x + \sin\theta(t)\vec e_y \Bigr)$ and Proposition 1 ($R$ constant), $$\begin{aligned} \vec v(t) &= \vec r'(t)\\[6pt] &= \Bigl(R \vec e_r(t)\Bigr)'\\[6pt] &= R \vec e_r'(t)\\[6pt] &= R \theta'(t) \vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 3: The speed in (not necessarily uniform) circular motion is $$\begin{aligned} v(t) = R |\theta'(t)| \end{aligned}$$

Proof
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle v(t) &= |\vec v (t)|\\[6pt] &=|R \theta'(t) \vec e_\theta(t)|\\[6pt] &=|R| |\theta'(t)| |\vec e_\theta(t)|\\[6pt] &=R |\theta'(t)| |\vec e_\theta(t)|\\[6pt] \end{aligned}$$
Since $e_\theta(t)$ is a unit vector, $\displaystyle v(t) = R |\theta'(t)|$.　Q.E.D

Proposition 4: The acceleration in (not necessarily uniform) circular motion is $$\begin{aligned} \vec a(t) = R \theta''(t) \vec e_\theta(t) - R (\theta'(t))^2 \vec e_r(t) \end{aligned}$$

Proof
Differentiate $\vec v(t) = R \theta'(t) \vec e_\theta(t)$ using the product rule and Proposition 1: $$\begin{aligned} \vec a(t) &= \vec v'(t) \\[6pt] &= \Bigl(R \theta'(t) \vec e_\theta(t)\Bigr)'\\[6pt] &= R \theta''(t) \vec e_\theta(t) + R \theta'(t) \vec e_\theta'(t)\\[6pt] &= R \theta''(t) \vec e_\theta(t) - R (\theta'(t))^2 \vec e_r(t) \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 5: With the circle center as the origin, the equation of motion for (not necessarily uniform) circular motion is

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \displaystyle -m \frac {v(t)^2}{R} = F_r\\[6pt] m R \theta''(t) = F_\theta \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

Proof
From $m \vec a(t) = \vec F(t)$ and Proposition 4, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle &m \vec a(t) = \vec F(t)\\[6pt] \displaystyle \Leftrightarrow &- m R (\theta'(t))^2 \vec e_r(t) + m R \theta''(t) \vec e_\theta(t) \\[6pt] \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ &= F_r \vec e_r(t) + F_\theta \vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ . Comparing components and using Proposition 3, $v(t)= R|\theta'(t)|$, $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \displaystyle - m R (\theta'(t))^2 = -m \frac{v(t)^2}{R} = F_r\\[6pt] \displaystyle m R \theta''(t) = F_\theta \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

articles.title: 極座標運動方程式(2次元）
articles.titleEn: Equations of motion in polar coordinates (2D)
articles.latexEn:
Definition of symbols

$\cdot \ \displaystyle F_r\cdots$ radial (centripetal) component of $\vec F$
$\cdot \ \displaystyle F_\theta \cdots$ angular (tangential) component of $\vec F$
$\cdot \ \displaystyle \theta(t) \cdots$ angle of the particle from the $x$-axis
$\cdot \ \vec r(t) \cdots$ position vector
$\cdot \ \vec v(t) \cdots$ velocity vector
$\cdot \ \vec a(t) \cdots$ acceleration vector
$\cdot \ v(t)=|\vec v(t)|\cdots$ speed

Definition (radial and angular unit vectors)
Define the radial and angular unit vectors by $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec e_r(t) = \cos\theta(t)\vec e_x + \sin\theta(t)\vec e_y\\[6pt] \vec e_{\theta}(t) = -\sin\theta(t)\vec e_x + \cos\theta(t)\vec e_y \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$
Proposition 1: The time derivatives of the radial and angular unit vectors are $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec {e_r}'(t) = \theta'(t) \vec {e_{\theta}}(t)\\[6pt] \vec {e_\theta}'(t) = -\theta'(t) \vec {e_r}(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

Proof
From $\displaystyle \vec e_r(t)=\cos\theta(t)\,\vec e_x + \sin\theta(t)\,\vec e_y$, by the chain rule $$\begin{aligned} \vec e_r'(t) &= -\sin\theta(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_x + \cos\theta(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_y \\ &= \theta'(t)\bigl(-\sin\theta(t)\vec e_x + \cos\theta(t)\vec e_y\bigr)\\ &= \theta'(t)\,\vec e_{\theta}(t) \end{aligned}$$ Similarly for $e_{\theta}(t) = -\sin\theta(t)\,\vec e_x + \cos\theta(t)\,\vec e_y$, $$\begin{aligned} \vec e_{\theta}'(t) &= -\cos\theta(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_x - \sin\theta(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_y \\ &= -\theta'(t)\bigl(\cos\theta(t)\vec e_x + \sin\theta(t)\vec e_y\bigr)\\ &= -\theta'(t)\,\vec e_r(t). \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 2: For a general radial function $r(t)$, the velocity is $$\begin{aligned} \vec v(t) = r'(t)\,\vec e_r(t) + r(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$

Proof
With $\vec r(t) = r(t)\,\vec e_r(t)$, the product rule and Proposition 1 give $$\begin{aligned} \vec v(t) &= \vec r'(t)\\[6pt] &= \bigl(r(t)\,\vec e_r(t)\bigr)'\\[6pt] &= r'(t)\,\vec e_r(t) + r(t)\,\vec e_r'(t)\\[6pt] &= r'(t)\,\vec e_r(t) + r(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 3: For general $r(t)$, the speed is $$\begin{aligned} v(t) = \sqrt{\bigl(r'(t)\bigr)^2 + \bigl(r(t)\,\theta'(t)\bigr)^2} \end{aligned}$$

Proof
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle v(t) &= |\vec v (t)|\\[5pt] &= \sqrt{\bigl(r'(t)\bigr)^2 + \bigl(r(t)\,\theta'(t)\bigr)^2} \end{aligned}$$ (using that $\vec e_r$ and $\vec e_\theta$ are orthonormal). Q.E.D

Proposition 4: For general $r(t)$, the acceleration is $$\begin{aligned} \vec a(t) &= \Bigl(r''(t)- r(t)\,(\theta'(t))^2\Bigr)\,\vec e_r(t) \\[7pt] &+ \Bigl(r(t)\,\theta''(t) + 2 r'(t)\,\theta'(t)\Bigr)\,\vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$

Proof
Differentiate $\vec v(t) = r'(t)\,\vec e_r(t) + r(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_\theta(t)$ using the product rule and Proposition 1: $$\begin{aligned} \vec a(t) &= \vec v'(t) \\[6pt] &= \bigl(r''(t)\,\vec e_r(t) + r'(t)\,\vec e_r'(t)\bigr) + \bigl(r'(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_\theta(t) + r(t)\,\theta''(t)\,\vec e_\theta(t) + r(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_\theta'(t)\bigr)\\[6pt] &= r''(t)\,\vec e_r(t) + r'(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_\theta(t) + r'(t)\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_\theta(t) + r(t)\,\theta''(t)\,\vec e_\theta(t) - r(t)\,(\theta'(t))^2\,\vec e_r(t)\\[6pt] &= \bigl(r''(t)- r(t)\,(\theta'(t))^2\bigr)\,\vec e_r(t) + \bigl(r(t)\,\theta''(t) + 2 r'(t)\,\theta'(t)\bigr)\,\vec e_\theta(t). \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D

Proposition 5: For general $r(t)$, with the origin at the center, the equation of motion is
$$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \displaystyle m\bigl(r''(t)- r(t)\,(\theta'(t))^2\bigr) = F_r\\[6pt] \displaystyle m\bigl(r(t)\,\theta''(t) + 2 r'(t)\,\theta'(t)\bigr) = F_\theta \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

Proof
From $m \vec a(t) = \vec F(t)$ and Proposition 4, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle &m \vec a(t) = \vec F(t)\\[6pt] \displaystyle \Leftrightarrow &m\bigl(r''(t)- r(t)\,(\theta'(t))^2\bigr)\,\vec e_r(t) + m\bigl(r(t)\,\theta''(t) + 2 r'(t)\,\theta'(t)\bigr)\,\vec e_\theta(t) \\[6pt] &= F_r \vec e_r(t) + F_\theta \vec e_\theta(t) \end{aligned}$$ . Comparing components yields the claim. Q.E.D

Remark 1: the case $r(t)=R$ (constant)
Substituting $r(t)=R$ into Proposition 5 gives $r'=r''=0$, so $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec v(t) &= R\,\theta'(t)\,\vec e_{\theta}(t), \\ \vec a(t) &= -R\,\bigl(\theta'(t)\bigr)^2\,\vec e_r(t) + R\,\theta''(t)\,\vec e_{\theta}(t), \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ reducing to the equation of motion for non-uniform circular motion.
Remark 2: $r(t)=R$ (constant) and $\theta(t)=\omega t$ ($\omega$ constant)
Then $\theta'(t)=\omega$, $\theta''(t)=0$, so $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec v(t) &= R\,\omega\,\vec e_{\theta}(t), \\ \vec a(t) &= -R\,\bigl(\omega\bigr)^2\,\vec e_r(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ reducing to uniform circular motion.

articles.title: 慣性系に対し加速運動する座標系から見た時の慣性力
articles.titleEn: Inertial force in a frame accelerating relative to an inertial frame
articles.latexEn:
Suppose the origin of a non-inertial frame moves as $\vec{R}(t)$ relative to the origin of an inertial frame. If the position vector of a body as seen from the non-inertial frame is $\vec{\tilde{r}}(t)$, then the following equation of motion holds. $$ m\vec{\tilde{r}}''(t) = \vec{F}(t) - m\vec{R}''(t) $$
Proof
The relation between the position vectors in the two frames is $$ \vec{r}(t) = \vec{R}(t) + \vec{\tilde{r}}(t) $$ Differentiating twice with respect to time: $$\begin{aligned} \vec{r}''(t) = \vec{R}''(t) + \vec{\tilde{r}}''(t)\ \ \cdots{(1)} \end{aligned}$$ In an inertial frame the law of motion holds, $$\begin{aligned} m\vec{r}''(t) = \vec{F}(t)\ \ \cdots{(2)} \end{aligned}$$ From (1) and (2): $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\vec{F}(t)}{m} &= \vec{R}''(t) + \vec{\tilde{r}}''(t) \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \vec{F}(t) &= m\vec{R}''(t) + m\vec{\tilde{r}}''(t) \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow m\vec{\tilde{r}}''(t) &= \vec{F}(t) - m\vec{R}''(t) \ \ \ \ \text{Q.E.D} \end{aligned}$$

articles.title: 慣性系に対し一定の角速度で回転する座標系から見た時の慣性力(遠心力,コリオリ力)
articles.titleEn: Inertial forces in a frame rotating at constant angular velocity relative to an inertial frame (centrifugal and Coriolis forces)
articles.latexEn:
Proposition: In a frame rotating at constant angular velocity $\omega$, let the coordinates of a particle of mass $m$ be $(\tilde{x}(t), \tilde{y}(t))$ and the force components $(\tilde{F}_x(t), \tilde{F}_y(t))$. Then the equation of motion in this frame is $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} m\tilde{x}''(t) = \tilde{F}_x(t) + 2m\omega \tilde{y}'(t) + m\omega^2 \tilde{x}(t) \\[6pt] m\tilde{y}''(t) = \tilde{F}_y(t) - 2m\omega \tilde{x}'(t) + m\omega^2 \tilde{y}(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$

Proof
Let the inertial-frame basis vectors be $\vec{e}_x, \vec{e}_y, \vec{e}_z$. The rotating basis with angle $\theta(t) = \omega t$ is $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) = \cos(\omega t)\vec{e}_x + \sin(\omega t)\vec{e}_y \\[6pt] \vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t) = -\sin(\omega t)\vec{e}_x + \cos(\omega t)\vec{e}_y \\[6pt] \vec{\tilde{e}}_z = \vec{e}_z \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Its time derivatives are $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \vec{\tilde{e}}_x'(t) = -\omega \sin(\omega t)\vec{e}_x + \omega \cos(\omega t)\vec{e}_y = \omega \vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t) \\[6pt] \vec{\tilde{e}}_y'(t) = -\omega \cos(\omega t)\vec{e}_x - \omega \sin(\omega t)\vec{e}_y = -\omega \vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) \\[6pt] \vec{e}_z' = 0 \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ The position $\vec{r}(t)$ in both frames is $$\begin{aligned} \vec{r}(t) = x(t)\vec{e}_x + y(t)\vec{e}_y = \tilde{x}(t)\vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) + \tilde{y}(t)\vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t) \end{aligned}$$ Differentiating once gives the velocity $$\begin{aligned} \vec{r}'(t) = (\tilde{x}'(t) - \omega \tilde{y}(t))\vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) + (\omega \tilde{x}(t) + \tilde{y}'(t))\vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t) \end{aligned}$$ Differentiating again for the acceleration: $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ \vec{r}''(t) &= (\tilde{x}''(t) - 2\omega \tilde{y}'(t) - \omega^2 \tilde{x}(t))\vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) \\[3pt] &+ (\tilde{y}''(t) + 2\omega \tilde{x}'(t) - \omega^2 \tilde{y}(t))\vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t)\\[8pt] \Leftrightarrow m\vec{r}''(t) &= m(\tilde{x}''(t) - 2\omega \tilde{y}'(t) - \omega^2 \tilde{x}(t))\vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) \\[3pt] &+ m(\tilde{y}''(t) + 2\omega \tilde{x}'(t) - \omega^2 \tilde{y}(t))\vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t) \ \ \cdots(1) \\[8pt] \end{aligned}$$ From Newton's law in the inertial frame, $$\begin{aligned} m\vec{r}''(t) = \vec{F}(t) \end{aligned}$$ Decomposing $\vec {F}(t)$ in the rotating basis, $\displaystyle \vec {F}(t) = \tilde{F}_x(t)\vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) + \tilde{F}_y(t)\vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t)$, so $$\begin{aligned} m\vec{r}''(t) = \displaystyle \vec {F}(t) = \tilde{F}_x(t)\vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) + \tilde{F}_y(t)\vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t)\ \ \cdots(2) \end{aligned}$$ From (1) and (2), $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ &m(\tilde{x}''(t) - 2\omega \tilde{y}'(t) - \omega^2 \tilde{x}(t))\vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) \\[5pt] + \ &m(\tilde{y}''(t) + 2\omega \tilde{x}'(t) - \omega^2 \tilde{y}(t))\vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t) \\[5pt] &\ \ = \tilde{F}_x(t)\vec{\tilde{e}}_x(t) + \tilde{F}_y(t)\vec{\tilde{e}}_y(t) \end{aligned}$$ Comparing components: $$\begin{aligned} &\begin{cases} m\tilde{x}''(t) - 2m\omega \tilde{y}'(t) - m\omega^2 \tilde{x}(t) = \tilde{F}_x(t)\\[6pt] m\tilde{y}''(t) + 2m\omega \tilde{x}'(t) - m\omega^2 \tilde{y}(t) = \tilde{F}_y(t) \end{cases} \\[8pt] \Leftrightarrow & \begin{cases} m\tilde{x}''(t) = \tilde{F}_x(t) + 2m\omega \tilde{y}'(t) + m\omega^2 \tilde{x}(t) \\[6pt] m\tilde{y}''(t) = \tilde{F}_y(t) - 2m\omega \tilde{x}'(t) + m\omega^2 \tilde{y}(t) \end{cases}\\[6pt] \ \ \ \ &\text{Q.E.D}\end{aligned}$$

Definition: Coriolis force
The second terms on the right, $2m\omega \tilde{y}'(t)$ and $-2m\omega \tilde{x}'(t)$, are called the Coriolis force.
Definition: centrifugal force
The third terms on the right, $m\omega^2 \tilde{x}(t)$ and $m\omega^2 \tilde{y}(t)$, are called the centrifugal force.

articles.title: 2質点系における諸命題
articles.latexEn:
Definition: A problem involving only two particles is called the two-body problem.

Definition: For masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, $\mu= \displaystyle\frac {m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ is the reduced mass of particles 1 and 2.

Definition: With position vectors $\overrightarrow{r_1}(t),\overrightarrow{r_2}(t)$, the relative position of particle 2 as seen from particle 1 is $\overrightarrow{R}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t) = \overrightarrow{r_2}(t) - \overrightarrow{r_1}(t)$.

Definition: The equation describing the time evolution of that relative position is the relative equation of motion of particle 2 with respect to particle 1 (see below).

Proposition 1: In the two-body problem the center of mass of the two particles moves in uniform straight-line motion.

Proof
The only forces between the bodies are internal. Writing the force on particle 1 as $\overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)$, the equations of motion are $$ \begin{cases} m_1\,\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t) &= -\overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)\\[6pt] m_2\,\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t) &= \overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t) \end{cases} $$ . Adding them cancels the internal forces: $$ m_1\,\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t)+m_2\,\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t)=\vec 0. $$ By definition $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{R_G}(t)=\frac{m_1\overrightarrow{r}_1(t)+m_2\overrightarrow{r}_2(t)}{m_1+m_2} $, so $$\begin{aligned} &\ \ \ \ \ \ \ m_1\,\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t)+m_2\,\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t)=\vec 0 \\[6pt] &\Leftrightarrow (m_1+m_2) \frac{m_1\,\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t)+m_2\,\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t)}{m_1+m_2}=\vec 0 \\[6pt] &\Leftrightarrow (m_1+m_2)\,\overrightarrow{R_G}''(t)=\vec 0 \\[6pt] &\Leftrightarrow \overrightarrow{R_G}''(t)=\vec 0, \end{aligned}$$ i.e. the center-of-mass acceleration vanishes. Integrating, the center-of-mass velocity is constant, $$ \overrightarrow{R_G}'(t)=\overrightarrow{V}=\text{constant} $$ and integrating again $$ \overrightarrow{R_G}(t)=\overrightarrow{V}t+\overrightarrow{R_G}(0) $$. Hence the center of mass moves uniformly in a straight line. Q.E.D

Proposition 2: Let the masses be $m_1$,$m_2$ and the force from 1 on 2 be $\overrightarrow{F}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t)$. With reduced mass $\mu$, the relative equation of motion of 2 with respect to 1 is $$ \displaystyle \mu \overrightarrow{R}_{2 \leftarrow 1}''(t) = \overrightarrow{F}(t)\ \ \ ;\ \ \ \overrightarrow{R}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t):= \overrightarrow{r}_2(t)-\overrightarrow{r}_1(t)$$

Proof
$$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \ \begin{cases} m_1\,\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t) &= -\overrightarrow{F}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t)\ \ \cdots (1)\\[6pt] m_2\,\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t) &= \overrightarrow{F}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t)\ \ \cdots (2) \end{cases}\\[6pt] \end{aligned}$$ From $(2) \times m_1 - (1)\times m_2$, $$\begin{aligned} m_1m_2\bigl(\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t)-\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t)\bigr) &= (m_1+m_2)\,\overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)\\[6pt] \end{aligned}$$ With $\displaystyle \ \mu = \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$ and $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{R}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t) = \overrightarrow{r}_2(t)-\overrightarrow{r}_1(t)$, $$ \mu\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2 \leftarrow 1}''(t) = \overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)$$ 　　Q.E.D

Proposition 3: Given the center-of-mass position $\overrightarrow{R_G}(t)$ and the relative position $\overrightarrow{R}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t)$, the individual positions are $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \overrightarrow{r_1}(t) = \displaystyle \overrightarrow{R_G}(t) - \frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2} \overrightarrow{R}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t)\\[6pt] \overrightarrow{r_2}(t) = \displaystyle \overrightarrow{R_G}(t) + \frac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2} \overrightarrow{R}_{2 \leftarrow 1}(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ .

Proof
$$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \overrightarrow{R_G}(t)=\displaystyle \frac{m_1\overrightarrow{r}_1(t)+m_2\overrightarrow{r}_2(t)}{m_1+m_2}\\[6pt] \overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)=\overrightarrow{r}_2(t)-\overrightarrow{r}_1(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ . From the relative-position equation $\overrightarrow{r}_2(t)=\overrightarrow{r}_1(t)+\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)$; substitute into the center-of-mass equation: $$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{R_G}(t)&=\frac{m_1\overrightarrow{r}_1(t)+m_2\bigl(\overrightarrow{r}_1(t)+\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)\bigr)}{m_1+m_2}\\[6pt] &=\overrightarrow{r}_1(t)+\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t) \end{aligned}$$ Rearranging, $$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{r}_1(t)=\overrightarrow{R_G}(t)-\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t) \end{aligned}$$ . Likewise, substituting into $\overrightarrow{r}_2=\overrightarrow{r}_1+\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}$, $$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{r}_2(t)&=\overrightarrow{R_G}(t)-\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)+\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t) \\[6pt] &=\overrightarrow{R_G}(t)+\frac{m_1}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t) \end{aligned}$$ . Q.E.D

Proposition 4: The two-body equations of motion $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} m_1\,\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t) = -\overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t),\\[6pt] m_2\,\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t) = \ \overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t), \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ are equivalent to the pair of center-of-mass and relative equations $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} (m_1+m_2)\,\overrightarrow{R_G}''(t)=\vec{0}\\[6pt] \mu\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}''(t)=\overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ (each set implies the other).

Proof
Propositions 1 and 2 derive the CM and relative equations from the two equations of motion; it remains to show the converse.
From Proposition 3, $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \overrightarrow{r}_1(t) = \overrightarrow{R_G}(t) - \frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)\\[6pt] \overrightarrow{r}_2(t) = \overrightarrow{R_G}(t) + \frac{m_1}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ . Differentiating twice, $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \overrightarrow{r}_1''(t) = \overrightarrow{R_G}''(t) - \frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}''(t)\\[6pt] \overrightarrow{r}_2''(t) = \overrightarrow{R_G}''(t) + \frac{m_1}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}''(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ . Multiplying by $m_1, m_2$, $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} m_1\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t) = m_1\overrightarrow{R_G}''(t) - \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}''(t),\\[6pt] m_2\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t) = m_2\overrightarrow{R_G}''(t) + \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}''(t). \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Using $\overrightarrow{R_G}''(t)=\overrightarrow{0}$, $\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}=\mu$, and $\mu\,\overrightarrow{R}_{2\leftarrow1}''(t)=\overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t)$, $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} m_1\overrightarrow{r}_1''(t) = -\overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t),\\[6pt] m_2\overrightarrow{r}_2''(t) = \ \overrightarrow{F}_{2\leftarrow1}(t), \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ recovering the original equations.　 Q.E.D

articles.title: 衝突における運動量保存
articles.latexEn:
Notation and symbols
  • Force on particle 2 from particle 1 during the collision: $\overrightarrow{F_{2 \leftarrow 1} }(t)$
  • Force on particle 1 from particle 2 during the collision: $\overrightarrow{F_{1 \leftarrow 2} }(t)$.
  • External force on particle 1 during the collision: $\overrightarrow{f_1}(t)$
  • External force on particle 2 during the collision: $\overrightarrow{f_2}(t)$.
  • Start time of the collision: $t_0$
  • End time of the collision: $t_1$
Proposition: In a collision of two bodies, if the collision duration may be regarded as sufficiently short, then momentum is conserved before and after the collision.

Proof
The interaction forces are between the two bodies, so the action–reaction law applies. $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} m_1 \overrightarrow{a_1}(t) = \overrightarrow{F_{1 \leftarrow 2} }(t) + \overrightarrow{f_1}(t) \\[6pt] m_2 \overrightarrow{a_2}(t) = -\overrightarrow{F_{1 \leftarrow 2} }(t) + \overrightarrow{f_2}(t) \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Adding the two equations, $m_1 \overrightarrow{a_1}(t) + m_2 \overrightarrow{a_2}(t) = \overrightarrow{f_1}(t) + \overrightarrow{f_2}(t) $. Integrating from $t_0$ to $t_1$, $$\begin{aligned} &\ \ \ \ \ \int_{t_0}^{t_1} m_1 \overrightarrow{a_1}(t) + m_2 \overrightarrow{a_2}(t) dt = \int_{t_0}^{t_1}\ \overrightarrow{f_1}(t) + \overrightarrow{f_2}(t)dt \\[8pt] & \Leftrightarrow \Bigr[ m_1 \overrightarrow{v_1}(t) + m_2 \overrightarrow{v_2}(t) \Bigr]_{t_0}^{t_1} = \int_{t_0}^{t_1}\ \overrightarrow{f_1}(t) + \overrightarrow{f_2}(t)dt \\[9pt] & \Leftrightarrow \Bigr( m_1 \overrightarrow{v_1}(t_1) + m_2 \overrightarrow{v_2}(t_1) \Bigr) - \Bigr( m_1 \overrightarrow{v_1}(t_0) + m_2 \overrightarrow{v_2}(t_0) \Bigr)\\[5pt] & \ \ \ \ \ = \int_{t_0}^{t_1}\ \overrightarrow{f_1}(t) + \overrightarrow{f_2}(t)dt \\[9pt] &\Leftrightarrow \Bigr( m_1 \overrightarrow{v_1}(t_1) + m_2 \overrightarrow{v_2}(t_1) \Bigr) \\[5pt] & \ \ \ \ \ = \Bigr( m_1 \overrightarrow{v_1}(t_0) + m_2 \overrightarrow{v_2}(t_0) \Bigr) + \int_{t_0}^{t_1}\ \overrightarrow{f_1}(t) + \overrightarrow{f_2}(t)dt \end{aligned}$$ Since the collision duration is very short, taking the limit $t_1 - t_0 \rightarrow 0$ gives $\displaystyle \int_{t_0}^{t_1}\ \overrightarrow{f_1}(t) + \overrightarrow{f_2}(t)dt \rightarrow 0$, hence $\displaystyle m_1 \overrightarrow{v_1}(t_1) + m_2 \overrightarrow{v_2}(t_1) = m_1 \overrightarrow{v_1}(t_0) + m_2 \overrightarrow{v_2}(t_0) \ \ \ $ Q.E.D

articles.title: 2質点系のエネルギーについての命題
articles.titleEn: Propositions on energy of a two-particle system
articles.latexEn:
Notation and symbols
  • $a:=b\ $: define $a$ by $b$
  • Total mass of the two particles: $ \displaystyle M := m_1 + m_2$
  • Center-of-mass velocity: $ \displaystyle \overrightarrow{V}_{\mathrm{cm}} := \frac{m_1\overrightarrow{v}_1 + m_2\overrightarrow{v}_2}{M}$
  • Relative velocity: $ \displaystyle \overrightarrow{v}_{\mathrm{rel}} := \overrightarrow{v}_1 - \overrightarrow{v}_2$
  • Center-of-mass speed: $ \displaystyle {V}_{\mathrm{cm}} := |\overrightarrow{V}_{\mathrm{cm}}|$
  • Relative speed: $ v_{\mathrm{rel}} :=|\overrightarrow{v}_{\mathrm{rel}} |$
  • Reduced mass: $ \displaystyle \mu := \frac{m_1 m_2}{M} = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1+m_2}$
Definition (center-of-mass kinetic energy)

For two particles of masses $m_1,m_2$, with center-of-mass velocity $\overrightarrow{V}_{\mathrm{cm}}$ and total mass $M$, define the center-of-mass kinetic energy by $\displaystyle K_{\mathrm{cm}} := \frac{1}{2} M V_{\mathrm{cm}}^2$.

Definition (relative kinetic energy)

For two particles of masses $m_1,m_2$, with relative velocity $\overrightarrow{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ and reduced mass $\mu$, define the relative kinetic energy by $\displaystyle K_{\mathrm{rel}} := \frac{1}{2} \mu v_{\mathrm{rel}}^2$.

Proposition: The total kinetic energy of a two-body system decomposes into the sum of center-of-mass and relative kinetic energies:
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2 = \frac{1}{2} M V_{\mathrm{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} \mu v_{\mathrm{rel}}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Proof
$$\begin{aligned} &\ \ \ \ \frac12\,M\,{V}_{\mathrm{cm}}^2 + \frac12\,\mu\,{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}^2 \\[6pt] &=\frac12\,M\,|\overrightarrow{V}_{\mathrm{cm}}|^2 + \frac12\,\mu\,|\overrightarrow{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}|^2 \\[6pt] &= \frac12\,(m_1 + m_2)\, \Bigl|\frac{m_1\overrightarrow{v}_1 + m_2\overrightarrow{v}_2}{m_1 + m_2}\Bigr|^2 + \frac12\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\, |\overrightarrow{v}_1 - \overrightarrow{v}_2|^2\\[6pt] &= \frac12\,\frac{\bigl|\,m_1\overrightarrow{v}_1 + m_2\overrightarrow{v}_2\,\bigr|^2}{m_1 + m_2} + \frac12\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\, \bigl(|\overrightarrow{v}_1|^2 - 2\,\overrightarrow{v}_1\!\cdot\!\overrightarrow{v}_2 + |\overrightarrow{v}_2|^2\bigr)\\[6pt] &= \frac12\frac{m_1^2|\overrightarrow{v}_1|^2 + 2m_1m_2\,\overrightarrow{v}_1\!\cdot\!\overrightarrow{v}_2 + m_2^2|\overrightarrow{v}_2|^2 + m_1m_2|\overrightarrow{v}_1|^2 - 2m_1m_2\,\overrightarrow{v}_1\!\cdot\!\overrightarrow{v}_2+ m_1m_2|\overrightarrow{v}_2|^2}{m_1 + m_2}\\[6pt] &= \frac12\frac{m_1(m_1 + m_2)|\overrightarrow{v}_1|^2 + m_2(m_1 + m_2)|\overrightarrow{v}_2|^2}{m_1 + m_2}\\[6pt] &= \frac12\,m_1\,|\overrightarrow{v}_1|^2+ \frac12\,m_2\,|\overrightarrow{v}_2|^2\\[6pt] &= \frac12\,m_1\,{v}_1^2+ \frac12\,m_2\,{v}_2^2 \end{aligned}$$ 　　Q.E.D

articles.title: 質点系の力学の諸命題
articles.titleEn: Propositions in the mechanics of systems of particles
articles.latexEn:
Definition (system of particles)

A collection of two or more particles is called a system of particles.

Definition (position vector of the center of mass)

Define the center-of-mass position $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{R_G}$ by $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \overrightarrow{R_G} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \overrightarrow{r_i} \end{aligned}$$

Definition (center-of-mass velocity and acceleration)
Define the center-of-mass velocity $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{V_G}$ and acceleration $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{A_G}$ by $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \displaystyle \overrightarrow{V_G} &= \overrightarrow{R_G}' = \displaystyle \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \overrightarrow{r_i}' \\[6pt] \displaystyle \overrightarrow{A_G} &= \overrightarrow{R_G}'' = \displaystyle \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \overrightarrow{r_i}'' \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$
Definition (center-of-mass momentum)

Define the center-of-mass momentum $\displaystyle \overrightarrow{P_G}$ by $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \overrightarrow{P_G} = M \overrightarrow{V_G} = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \overrightarrow{r_i}' \end{aligned}$$

Proposition: Total mass × center-of-mass acceleration equals the total external force.

Proof
Let $\overrightarrow{F_{i\leftarrow j}}$ be the force on $i$ from $j$, and $\overrightarrow{f_i}$ the external force. Then $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle m_i \overrightarrow{r_i}'' = \overrightarrow{f_i} + \sum_{j\neq i} \overrightarrow{F_{i \leftarrow j}} \end{aligned}$$ . Summing over all particles, action–reaction cancels the interaction terms, yielding $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \overrightarrow{r_i}'' &= \sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{f_i} \\[6pt] M \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n m_i \overrightarrow{r_i}''}{M} &= \sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{f_i} \\[6pt] \end{aligned}$$ . By definition of center-of-mass acceleration, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle M \overrightarrow{R_G}'' = \sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{f_i} \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D.

Proposition: If no external force acts, the center of mass moves in uniform straight-line motion.

Proof
By assumption $\overrightarrow{f_i}=0$, so $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle M \overrightarrow{R_G}'' &= \overrightarrow{0} \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \overrightarrow{R_G}'' &= \overrightarrow{0} \end{aligned}$$ . Therefore $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \overrightarrow{R_G}' = \text{a time-independent vector} \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D.

Definition (angular momentum of a system of particles)

Define the angular momentum $\overrightarrow L (t)$ of the system about an arbitrary point as the sum of the particles' angular momenta: $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \overrightarrow{L}(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{L_i}(t) \end{aligned}$$

Proposition: The time derivative of the system's angular momentum about an arbitrary point equals the total external torque.

Proof
For each particle $i$, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \overrightarrow{L_i}(t)' &= \overrightarrow{r_i} \times \overrightarrow{F_i} \end{aligned}$$ . Summing, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n \Bigl(\overrightarrow{L_i}(t)'\Bigr) & = \sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{r_i}\times\overrightarrow{F_i} \\[6pt] \displaystyle \Leftrightarrow \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{L_i}(t)\Bigr)' & = \sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{r_i}\times\overrightarrow{F_i}\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \overrightarrow{L}(t)' & = \sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{r_i}\times\overrightarrow{F_i} \end{aligned}$$ . Thus the time derivative of $\overrightarrow{L}(t)$ equals the total external torque. Q.E.D.

articles.title: ケプラー第二法則
articles.latexEn:
Setup and notation
A particle of mass $m$ moves in the gravitational field of a central mass $M$.
Write 3D vectors as columns: $$\begin{aligned} \vec{r}(t)&=\begin{pmatrix}x(t)\\[6pt] y(t)\\[6pt] z(t)\end{pmatrix}\\[6pt] \vec{v}(t)&=\vec{r}'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x'(t)\\[6pt] y'(t)\\[6pt] z'(t)\end{pmatrix}\\[6pt] r(t)&=\sqrt{x(t)^2+y(t)^2+z(t)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Definition of the cross product

For vectors $ \displaystyle \vec a=\begin{pmatrix}a_x\\[6pt] a_y\\[6pt] a_z\end{pmatrix},\quad \displaystyle \vec b=\begin{pmatrix}b_x\\[6pt] b_y\\[6pt] b_z\end{pmatrix} $, define the product $\times$ (producing a vector from two vectors) by $$ \vec a\times\vec b= \begin{pmatrix} a_yb_z-a_zb_y\\[6pt] a_zb_x-a_xb_z\\[6pt] a_xb_y-a_yb_x \end{pmatrix} $$
Definition of the angular momentum vector

The following vector is the angular momentum: $$\begin{aligned} \vec L &= m\bigl(\vec r(t)\times \vec v(t)\bigr)\\[6pt] &= \begin{pmatrix} m\bigl(z(t)v_y(t)-y(t)v_z(t)\bigr)\\[6pt] m\bigl(x(t)v_z(t)-z(t)v_x(t)\bigr)\\[6pt] m\bigl(y(t)v_x(t)-x(t)v_y(t)\bigr) \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} $$
Lemma 1 (conservation of angular momentum) The angular momentum vector is constant in time.
Proof
Show that the derivative of the $x$-component $m\bigl(z(t)v_y(t)-y(t)v_z(t)\bigr)$ vanishes (other components are similar). From the equation of motion, $$ m\vec a(t):=-\frac{G M m}{r^3(t)}\vec r(t) $$ in components $$ \begin{cases} \displaystyle m a_x(t):=-\frac{GMm}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}x(t)\quad\cdots(1)\\[6pt] \displaystyle m a_y(t):=-\frac{GMm}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}y(t)\quad\cdots(2)\\[6pt] \displaystyle m a_z(t):=-\frac{GMm}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}z(t)\quad\cdots(3) \end{cases} $$ Multiply (1) by $y(t)$ and (2) by $x(t)$ and subtract: $$ m\bigl(y(t)a_x(t)-x(t)a_y(t)\bigr)=0\quad \cdots(4) $$ One has the identity $$\begin{aligned} &y(t)a_x(t)-x(t)a_y(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(y(t)v_x(t)-x(t)v_y(t)\bigr) \end{aligned}$$ , so (4) becomes $$\begin{aligned} m\bigl(y(t)a_x(t)-x(t)a_y(t)\bigr)&=0\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(m \bigl(y(t)v_x(t)-x(t)v_y(t)\bigl)\Bigl)&=0 \end{aligned}$$ Hence the $x$-component of angular momentum is constant.
The other two components follow similarly, proving that the angular momentum vector is constant in time. This is the conservation of angular momentum. ⬜︎
Lemma 2. Magnitude of a cross product If ${\theta}$ is the angle between ${\vec a, \vec b}$, then $${|\vec a \times \vec b| = \Biggr| \left(\begin{smallmatrix} \displaystyle a_yb_z- a_zb_y \\ \ \\ \displaystyle a_zb_x- a_xb_z \\ \ \\ \displaystyle a_xb_y - a_yb_x \end{smallmatrix} \right)\Biggr| = |\vec a| |\vec b| \sin \theta }$$
Proof
Compute both sides. $$\begin{aligned} &\Biggr| \left(\begin{smallmatrix} \displaystyle a_yb_z- a_zb_y \\ \ \\ \displaystyle a_zb_x- a_xb_z \\ \ \\ \displaystyle a_xb_y - a_yb_x \end{smallmatrix} \right)\Biggr| \\ \ \\ &=\sqrt {(a_yb_z- a_zb_y)^2+(a_zb_x- a_xb_z )^2+(a_xb_y - a_yb_x )^2} \\ \ \\ &=\sqrt {a_y^2b_z^2+ a_z^2b_y^2-2a_yb_za_zb_y+a_z^2b_x^2+ a_x^2b_z^2 -2a_zb_x a_xb_z+a_x^2b_y^2 + a_y^2b_x^2-2a_xb_y a_yb_x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} &|\vec a| |\vec b| \sin \theta \\ \ \\ &=|\vec a| |\vec b| \sqrt{1-\cos^2 \theta} \\ \ \\ &=|\vec a||\vec b|\sqrt {1-\Biggr(\frac{\vec a \cdot \vec b}{|\vec a||\vec b|}\Biggr)^2}\\ \ \\ &=\sqrt {|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a \cdot \vec b)^2}\\ \ \\ &=\sqrt{(a_x^2+a_y^2+a_z^2)(b_x^2+b_y^2+b_z^2)-(a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z)^2} \\ \ \\ &=\sqrt{a_x^2b_y^2+a_x^2b_z^2+a_y^2b_x^2+a_y^2b_z^2+a_z^2b_x^2+a_z^2b_y^2-2a_xb_xa_yb_y-2a_xb_xa_zb_z-2a_yb_ya_zb_z} \\ \ \\ &=\sqrt{a_x^2b_y^2+a_x^2b_z^2+a_y^2b_x^2+a_y^2b_z^2+a_z^2b_x^2+a_z^2b_y^2-2a_xb_xa_yb_y-2a_xb_xa_zb_z-2a_yb_ya_zb_z} \end{aligned}$$ 　⬜︎
Theorem (Kepler's second law): If ${S(t)}$ is the area swept by the particle's trajectory about the origin, then ${\displaystyle \frac{dS}{dt}}$ is constant in time.
Proof
Write ${\theta_{\vec a, \vec b}}$ for the angle between ${\vec a}$ and ${\vec b}$. For sufficiently small $\Delta t$, approximate the change of area $\Delta S$ by the area $\Delta T$ of the green triangle, and accept that the areal velocity is $$ \lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta S}{\Delta t} = \lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} $$ .
Then $$\begin{aligned} &\lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta S}{\Delta t} = \lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} \\ \ \\ &= \lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{2}|\vec r(t)| \frac{ |\vec r(t+\Delta t)- \vec r(t)|}{\Delta t}\sin \theta_{\vec r(t), \vec r(t) - \vec r(t+\Delta t)}\\ \ \\ & = \frac{1}{2}|\vec r(t)||\vec v(t)|\sin \theta_{\vec r(t), \vec v(t)} \\ \ \\ &\underset{lemma.2}{=}\ \ \Biggr|\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\displaystyle y(t){v_x}(t) - x(t){v_y}(t) \\ \ \\ \displaystyle z(t){v_y}(t) - y(t){v_z}(t) \\ \ \\\displaystyle x(t){v_z}(t) - z(t){v_x}(t)\end{smallmatrix}\right)\Biggr|\\ \ \\ & \underset{lemma.1}{=}constant \ value \end{aligned}$$　⬜︎

Proposition 1 (orthogonality of a cross product) For two non-parallel vectors $\vec a=\begin{pmatrix}a_x\\[6pt]a_y\\[6pt]a_z\end{pmatrix} \neq \vec 0, \quad \vec b=\begin{pmatrix}b_x\\[6pt]b_y\\[6pt]b_z\end{pmatrix} \neq \vec 0$, $\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{pmatrix}a_yb_z-a_zb_y\\[6pt]a_zb_x-a_xb_z\\[6pt]a_xb_y-a_yb_x\end{pmatrix}$ is orthogonal to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$.

Proof

Compute the inner product and show it vanishes:

$$\begin{aligned} & \ \ (\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec a \\[6pt] &= (a_yb_z-a_zb_y)a_x + (a_zb_x-a_xb_z)a_y + (a_xb_y-a_yb_x)a_z\\[6pt] &= a_xa_yb_z - a_xa_zb_y + a_ya_zb_x - a_ya_xb_z + a_za_xb_y - a_za_yb_x. \end{aligned}$$ All terms cancel, so $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec a=0$. Similarly $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b=0$. Hence $\vec a\times\vec b$ is orthogonal to $\vec a,\vec b$. 　⬜︎
Proposition 2: If $\vec r (t) \neq \vec 0$ and $\vec v (t) \neq \vec 0$ are not parallel, the angular momentum is orthogonal to both position and velocity.
Proof
Immediate from Proposition 1.　⬜︎
Proposition 3 (vanishing cross product and parallelism): For $\vec a ,\vec b \neq \vec 0$, $\vec a\times\vec b = \vec 0 \Leftrightarrow \vec a \parallel \vec b$
Proof
$\Rightarrow$

By Lemma 2, $ |\vec a\times\vec b|= |a||b| \sin \theta$
By assumption $|a||b| \sin \theta = 0$, so $\sin\theta=0$, hence $\theta=0$ or $\pi$ (parallel or anti-parallel).
$\Leftarrow$

By Lemma 2, $ |\vec a\times\vec b|= |a||b| \sin \theta$
By assumption $\theta = 0$ or $\pi$, so $\sin \theta = 0$ and $ |\vec a\times\vec b|= 0$, hence $\vec a\times\vec b = \vec 0$.
Proposition 4: Choosing the origin and axes so that $z(0)=0,\ v_z(0)=0$ at the initial time, and assuming $\vec L(0)\neq\vec0$, one has $z(t)=0,\ v_z(t)=0$ for all $t$.

Proof

By angular-momentum conservation (Lemma 1) and the assumption, in components

$$ \begin{pmatrix} z(t)v_y(t) - y(t)v_z(t)\\[6pt] x(t)v_z(t) - z(t)v_x(t)\\[6pt] y(t)v_x(t) - x(t)v_y(t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0\\[6pt] 0\\[6pt] y(0)v_x(0)-x(0)v_y(0) \end{pmatrix}. $$

Hence

$$ \begin{cases} z(t)v_y(t) = y(t)v_z(t) &\quad\cdots(1)\\[6pt] x(t)v_z(t) = z(t)v_x(t) &\quad\cdots(2)\\[6pt] y(t)v_x(t) = x(t)v_y(t) + y(0)v_x(0)-x(0)v_y(0) &\quad\cdots(3) \end{cases} $$

Multiply (3) by $v_z(t)$ and use (1),(2):

$$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ &y(t)v_x(t) = x(t)v_y(t) + y(0)v_x(0)-x(0)v_y(0) &\quad\cdots(3)\\[6pt] \underset{\times v_z(t)}{\Leftrightarrow}\ &y(t)v_x(t)v_z(t) = x(t)v_y(t)v_z(t) + \Bigl(y(0)v_x(0)-x(0)v_y(0)\Bigr)v_z(t)\\[6pt] \underset{(1),(2)\text{ subst.}}{\Leftrightarrow}\ &v_x(t)z(t)v_y(t) = v_y(t)z(t)v_x(t) + \Bigl(y(0)v_x(0)-x(0)v_y(0)\Bigr)v_z(t)\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow\ &v_z(t)\Bigl(y(0)v_x(0)-x(0)v_y(0)\Bigr) = 0 \end{aligned}$$

Nonzero initial angular momentum means the parenthesis is nonzero, so $v_z(t)=0$.
Substituting into (1),(2), $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} z(t)v_y(t)=0\\[6pt] z(t)v_x(t)=0 \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Since $\vec v(t)\neq\vec 0$, at least one of $v_x(t),v_y(t)$ is nonzero, hence $z(t)=0$. Q.E.D.

Theorem: Motion under a gravitational potential takes place in a plane.
Proof
By Proposition 4, with suitably chosen axes one has $z(t)=0,\ v_z(t)=0$ for all $t$, so there is no motion in the $z$ direction; the motion is planar. Q.E.D

articles.title: ケプラー第三法則
articles.latexEn:
Definition of symbols
  • $G$ : gravitational constant
  • $M$ : mass of the central star (e.g. the Sun)
  • $m$ : mass of the planet (cancels in the equation of motion, but introduced for convenience)
  • $a$ : perihelion distance (closest approach to the center)
  • $b$ : aphelion distance (farthest distance from the center)
  • $l$ : semi-major axis of the elliptical orbit
  • $m$ : semi-minor axis of the elliptical orbit
  • $S$ : area of the ellipse
  • $v_a$ : speed of the planet at perihelion (distance $a$)
  • $v_b$ : speed of the planet at aphelion (distance $b$)
  • $V_s$ : areal velocity (area swept per unit time)
  • $T$ : orbital period (time to complete one revolution)
Lemma 1: By Kepler's first law, a planet orbits in an ellipse with the central star at a focus. In terms of perihelion distance $a$ and aphelion distance $b$, the area $S$ of the ellipse is $$ S = \pi\frac{a+b}{2}\sqrt{ab} $$
Proof
Let the semi-major and semi-minor axes be $l$ and $m$. The area is $\pi l m$.
From the figure, $l = \displaystyle \frac {a+b}{2}$
By the Pythagorean theorem, $l ^2 = (l - a) ^2 + m ^2$, so $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ l ^2 &= (l - a) ^2 + m ^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \Bigl(\frac{a+b}{2}\Bigr)^2 &= \Bigl(\frac{a+b}{2} - a\Bigr)^2 + m ^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \Bigl(\frac{a+b}{2}\Bigr)^2 &= \Bigl(\frac{a-b}{2}\Bigr)^2 + m ^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \frac{a^2+2ab+b^2}{4} &= \frac{a^2-2ab+b^2}{4} + m ^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow ab &= m ^2 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow m &= \sqrt{ab} \end{aligned}$$ Hence $$ S = \pi l m = \pi\frac{a+b}{2}\sqrt{ab} $$
　⬜︎
Lemma 2: In terms of perihelion $a$ and aphelion $b$, the areal velocity $V_s$ is $$ \displaystyle V_s = \sqrt{GM\frac{ab}{2(a+b)}}$$
Proof
Let $v_a$ and $v_b$ be the speeds at perihelion and aphelion. Energy conservation and Kepler's second law give $$ \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{1}{2}mv_a^2 - \frac{GMm}{a} = \frac{1}{2}mv_b^2 - \frac{GMm}{b} \\ \displaystyle \frac{1}{2}av_a = \frac{1}{2}bv_b \end{cases} $$ Expressing $v_a, v_b$ in terms of $a, b$, $$ \frac{1}{2}m\frac{b^2}{a^2}v_b^2 - \frac{GMm}{a} = \frac{1}{2}mv_b^2 - \frac{GMm}{b} $$ $$ \Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2}m\Bigl(\frac{b^2}{a^2}-1\Bigr)v_b^2 = \frac{GMm}{a}- \frac{GMm}{b} $$ $$ \Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2}m\Bigl(\frac{b^2-a^2}{a^2}\Bigr)v_b^2 = \frac{GMm(b-a)}{ab} $$ $$ \Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2}m(a+b)v_b^2 = GMm\frac{a}{b} $$ $$ \Leftrightarrow v_b^2 = 2GM\frac{a}{b(a+b)} $$ $$ \Leftrightarrow v_b = \sqrt{2GM\frac{a}{b(a+b)}}\ \ (\ \because v_b > 0\ ) $$ Similarly $$ v_a = \pm\sqrt{2GM\frac{b}{a(a+b)}}\ \ (\ \because v_a > 0\ ) $$ The areal velocity is $\displaystyle \frac 1 2 v_a a \sin 90^{\circ}$ (or $\displaystyle \frac 1 2 v_b b \sin 90^{\circ}$), so $$ V_s = \frac 1 2 v_a a = \frac 1 2 v_b b = \sqrt{GM\frac{ab}{2(a+b)}} $$　⬜︎
Theorem (Kepler's third law): For gravitational constant $G$, semi-major axis $l$, period $T$, and central mass $M$, $$\frac{T^2}{l^3}=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}$$
Proof
The period is the elliptical area $S$ divided by the areal velocity $V_s$. Substituting Lemmas 1 and 2, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle T &=\frac{S}{V_s}\\[6pt] \displaystyle &= \frac{\pi\frac{a+b}{2}\sqrt{ab}}{\sqrt{GM\frac{ab}{2(a+b)}}}\\[6pt] \displaystyle &= \frac{\pi (a+b)}{\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{(a+b)}}}\\[6pt] \displaystyle &= \frac{\pi (a+b)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{2GM}} \end{aligned}$$ Hence $$\begin{aligned} \ \ \ \ \frac{T^2}{(a+b)^3} &= \frac{\pi^2}{2GM}\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \frac{T^2}{\Bigl(\frac{a+b}{2}\Bigr)^3} &= \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \frac{T^2}{l^3} &= \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} \end{aligned}$$ Q.E.D.

articles.title: レンツベクトルの定義と保存について
articles.titleEn: Definition and conservation of the Runge–Lenz vector
articles.latexEn:
Setup and notation
A particle of mass $m$ moves in the gravitational field of a central mass $M$.
Kepler's second law implies the motion is confined to a fixed plane; take that plane as the $(x,y)$ plane and write 3D vectors as columns: $$\begin{aligned} \vec{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x(t)\\[6pt] y(t)\\[6pt] 0\end{pmatrix}\\[6pt] \vec{v}(t)=\vec{r}'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x'(t)\\[6pt] y'(t)\\[6pt] 0\end{pmatrix} \\[6pt] r(t)=\sqrt{x(t)^2+y(t)^2} \end{aligned}$$ The angular momentum vector is $$ \vec L:=\begin{pmatrix}0\\[6pt] 0\\[6pt] m\bigl(xy'-yx'\bigr) \end{pmatrix} $$ .
By the law of universal gravitation, with the central star at the origin, the equation of motion is $$ m\vec{r}''(t)=-\frac{GMm}{r(t)^3}\,\vec{r}(t) $$ In $xy$ components, $\displaystyle x''=-\frac{GM}{r^3}x,\quad y''=-\frac{GM}{r^3}y$ .
Definition: Runge–Lenz vector, eccentricity vector, eccentricity
Although introduced by fiat, $$\displaystyle \vec{A}:=\begin{pmatrix}mL\,y' - \frac{GM\,m^2 x}{r}\\[6pt] \displaystyle -mL\,x' - \frac{GM\,m^2 y}{r}\\[6pt] 0\end{pmatrix} $$ is a known conserved quantity, called the Runge–Lenz vector. The dimensionless vector $$\vec{e}:=\frac{\vec{A}}{GM\,m^2} $$ is the eccentricity vector, and its magnitude $ \displaystyle e:=\lvert\vec{e}\rvert $ is the eccentricity.
Theorem: The Runge–Lenz vector and the eccentricity vector are constant in time.
Proof
Since they differ only by a constant factor, it suffices to show that the eccentricity vector is time-independent. The components of $\vec{e}$ are $$\begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \displaystyle e_x=\frac{A_x}{GMm^2}=\frac{L\,y'}{GMm}-\frac{x}{r}\\[6pt] \displaystyle e_y=\frac{A_y}{GMm^2}=-\frac{L\,x'}{GMm}-\frac{y}{r} \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ Compute $e_x'$ ($L$ is constant by Kepler's second law): $$ e_x'=\frac{Ly''}{GMm}-\Bigl(\frac{x}{r}\Bigr)' $$ First term on the right:
$\displaystyle \frac{Ly''}{GMm}$ with $y''=-\frac{GM}{r^3}y$ from the equation of motion gives $$ \displaystyle \frac{Ly''}{GMm}=-\frac{Ly}{m r^3} $$ Second term: $$\begin{aligned} &\quad \Bigl(\frac{x}{r}\Bigr)'\\[6pt] &=\frac{x'}{r}-\frac{x}{r^2}r'\\[6pt] &=\frac{x'}{r}-\frac{x}{r^2}\Bigr(\frac{xx'+yy'}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\Bigl)\\[6pt] &=\frac{x'}{r}-x\frac{x x'+y y'}{r^3}\\[6pt] &=\frac{x'(x^2+y^2)}{r^3}-x\frac{x x'+y y'}{r^3}\\[6pt] &=\frac{x'y^2-xy y'}{r^3}\\[6pt] &=y\frac{x'y-xy'}{r^3}\\[6pt] &=-y\frac{L}{r^3} \end{aligned}$$ Hence $$\begin{aligned} e_x' &= \frac{Ly''}{GMm}-\Bigl(\frac{x}{r}\Bigr)' \\[6pt] &=-\frac{Ly}{mr^3} -\Bigl(-y\frac{L}{r^3}\Bigr) = 0 \end{aligned}$$ A similar calculation gives $e_y'=0$, and $e_z\equiv0$, so every component has vanishing time derivative and $\vec{e}'=\mathbf0$. 　⬜︎

articles.title: ケプラー第一法則
articles.latexEn:
Setup and notation
A particle of mass $m$ moves in the gravitational field of a central mass $M$.
Kepler's second law implies the motion is confined to a fixed plane; take that plane as the $(x,y)$ plane and write 3D vectors as columns: $$\begin{aligned} \vec{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x(t)\\[6pt] y(t)\\[6pt] 0\end{pmatrix}\\[6pt] \vec{v}(t)=\vec{r}'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x'(t)\\[6pt] y'(t)\\[6pt] 0\end{pmatrix} \\[6pt] r(t)=\sqrt{x(t)^2+y(t)^2} \end{aligned}$$ By the law of universal gravitation, with the central star at the origin, $$ m\vec{r}''(t)=-\frac{GMm}{r(t)^3}\,\vec{r}(t) $$ In $xy$ components, $\displaystyle x''=-\frac{GM}{r^3}x,\quad y''=-\frac{GM}{r^3}y$ .
For a particle obeying this equation, the following three quantities are constant in time, as proved in this article and this article.
Angular momentum vector

$$ \vec L:=\begin{pmatrix}0\\[6pt] 0\\[6pt] m\bigl(xy'-yx'\bigr) \end{pmatrix} $$
Runge–Lenz vector

$$\displaystyle \vec{A}:=\begin{pmatrix}mL\,y' - \frac{GM\,m^2 x}{r}\\[6pt] \displaystyle -mL\,x' - \frac{GM\,m^2 y}{r}\\[6pt] 0\end{pmatrix} $$
Eccentricity vector (Runge–Lenz vector divided by ${GM\,m^2}$ to make it dimensionless)

$$\vec{e}:=\frac{\vec{A}}{GM\,m^2}$$
Proposition 1 (orbit equation)
In polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ the orbit is $\displaystyle r(\theta)=\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}\bigl(1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha)\bigr)}$
Proof
Computing $\vec{e}\cdot\vec{r}=e_x x+e_y y$ in components, $$\begin{aligned} \vec{e}\cdot\vec{r}&=\frac{L}{GMm}(x y'-y x')-\frac{x^2+y^2}{r}\\[6pt] &=\frac{L^{2}}{GM m^2}-r\quad\cdots(1) \end{aligned}$$ Writing $\vec{e}=e(\cos \alpha, \sin \alpha)$ with angle from the $x$-axis, $$ \vec{e}\cdot\vec{r}=e\,r\cos(\theta-\alpha)\quad\cdots(2) $$ From (1) and (2), $$\begin{aligned} &e\,r\cos(\theta-\alpha)=\frac{L^{2}}{GM m^2}-r\\[6pt] &r\bigl(1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha)\bigr)=\frac{L^{2}}{GM m^2}\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow\quad & r=\frac{L^{2}}{GM m^2\bigl(1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha)\bigr)} \end{aligned}$$ as claimed. 　⬜︎
Proposition 2 (eccentricity and total energy)
Eccentricity $e$ and energy $E$ are related by $\displaystyle e^{2}=1+\frac{2E L^{2}}{G^{2}M^{2}m^{3}} $.
Proof
Direct computation: $$\begin{aligned} e^2 &= e_x^2 + e_y^2 \\[6pt] &= \left(\frac{L\, y'}{GM m} - \frac{x}{r}\right)^2 + \left(-\frac{L\, x'}{GM m} - \frac{y}{r}\right)^2 \\[6pt] &= \frac{L^2(x'^2 + y'^2)}{G^2 M^2 m^2} + \frac{x^2 + y^2}{r^2} -\frac{2L( xy'- x' y )}{GM mr} \end{aligned}$$ From total energy, $\displaystyle E = \frac12 m v^2 - \frac{GM m}{r} \Leftrightarrow v^2 = \frac{2E}{m} + \frac{2 GM}{r}$
and $\displaystyle xy'- x' y = \frac L m $. Substituting, $$\begin{aligned} e^2 &= \frac{L^2}{G^2 M^2 m^2} \Bigl( \frac{2E}{m} + \frac{2 GM}{r} \Bigr) + 1- \frac{2L^2}{GM m^2r}\\[6pt] &= \frac{2EL^2}{G^2 M^2 m^3} + \frac{2L^2}{GM m^2r} + 1 - \frac{2L^2}{GM m^2r}\\[6pt] &= 1 + \frac{2EL^2}{G^2 M^2 m^3} \end{aligned}$$ 　⬜︎
Proposition 3 (classification by eccentricity $e$)
From the polar equation $$ r(\theta)=\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^2(1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha))} ; \quad L\neq0 $$ orbits are classified by $e$ as follows.
(1) $0 \le e < 1$ (ellipse: bound orbit)

•This case is Kepler's first law. The denominator is always positive, so $r(\theta)$ is bounded (has a max and min).
•Pericenter and apocenter are $$ \begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \displaystyle r_{\min}=\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}(1+e)}\quad\\[6pt] \displaystyle r_{\max}=\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}(1-e)} \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ The semi-major axis is $$ a=\frac{1}{2}\,(r_{\min}+r_{\max})=\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}(1-e^{2})} $$ .
•Pericenter and apocenter are also $a(1-e)$ and $a(1+e)$.
•$\theta=\alpha$ is the pericenter direction giving $r_{\min}=\displaystyle\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}(1+e)}$, and $\theta=\alpha+\pi$ the apocenter giving $r_{\max}=\displaystyle\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}(1-e)}$.
•Special case: $e=0$ is a circular orbit.
(2) $e=1$ (parabola: critical orbit)

The polar equation is $$ r(\theta)=\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}(1+\cos(\theta-\alpha))} $$ . As $1+\cos(\theta-\alpha)=0$, i.e. $\theta=\alpha+\pi$, one has $r\to\infty$. Thus a parabola has a single escape direction $\theta=\alpha+\pi$.
(3) $e>1$ (hyperbola: unbound orbit)

•Pericenter occurs at $\cos(\theta-\alpha)=1$ ($\theta=\alpha$), with $$ r_{\min}=\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}(1+e)}>0 $$ •Asymptotic directions where the denominator vanishes satisfy $$ 1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha)=0 \iff \cos(\theta-\alpha)=-\frac{1}{e} $$ ; there are two such angles, the two asymptotes of the hyperbola, along which $r\to\infty$.
Proposition 4 (semi-major axis and energy)
For an elliptical orbit, $\displaystyle E=-\frac{GM\,m}{2a}\quad(<0)$ ; energy is determined by the semi-major axis alone.
Proof
From Proposition 2, $$ e^2=1+\frac{2EL^2}{G^2M^2m^3} $$ solving for $E$, $$ E=\frac{G^2M^2m^3}{2L^2}(e^2-1) =-\frac{G^2M^2m^3}{2L^2}(1-e^2) $$ Substitute the semi-major axis $$\begin{aligned} a= \frac {r_{min} +r_{max}}{2} &= \frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}(1-e^{2})}\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ 1-e^{2}&=\frac{L^{2}}{GM\,m^{2}a} \end{aligned}$$ to obtain $$ E=-\frac{GM\,m}{2a} $$ 　⬜︎
Proposition 5 (focus at the origin and directrix)
The curve $\displaystyle r(\theta)=\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2(1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha))}; \quad L\neq 0 $ is a conic with focus at the origin, directrix $\displaystyle \mathcal D:\ x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha=\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2e}$, and eccentricity $e$.
Proof
Show that the conic definition with focus $F$, line $\mathcal D$, and eccentricity $e>0$ yields the orbit of Proposition 1. Take $F$ at the origin and (by fiat) $\displaystyle \mathcal D: x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha=\frac{L^2}{GM m^2e}$. The distance from $P=(x,y)$ to $\mathcal D$ is $$ d(P,\mathcal D)=\Bigl|x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha-\frac{L^2}{GM m^2e}\Bigr| $$ . By definition of eccentricity $\overline{PF}=ed(P,\mathcal D)$, so $\displaystyle r=e\Bigl|x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha-\frac{L^2}{GM m^2e}\Bigr|$ . In polar coordinates $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta$, $$ \cos(\theta-\alpha)=\frac{x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha}{r} $$ so $$\begin{aligned} r=e\Bigl|x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha-\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2e}\Bigr| \\[6pt] r=e\Bigl|r \cos(\theta-\alpha)-\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2e}\Bigr| \cdots(1) \end{aligned}$$ By the lemma below the expression inside the absolute value is negative. Rearranging (1) carefully, $$ r\bigl(1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha)\bigr)=\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2} $$ which matches Proposition 1. ⬜︎
[Lemma]$\quad \displaystyle r\cos(\theta-\alpha)-\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2e}$ is negative.
Proof
$$ r(\theta)=\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha)} $$ . Multiplying by $1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha)$, $$\begin{aligned} r\bigl(1+e\cos(\theta-\alpha)\bigr)=\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2}\\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow \ r\cos(\theta-\alpha)-\frac{L^2}{GM\,m^2e}=-\frac{r}{e}<0 \end{aligned}$$ 　⬜︎

articles.title: 電荷,電流の定義
articles.titleEn: Definitions of electric charge and current
articles.latexEn:
Definition (electric charge)

The unit is the coulomb ($\mathrm{C}$), also written $\mathrm{A \ s}$.
${1\ \mathrm{C}}$ is the charge of about $6.2415\times10^{18}$ electrons.

Definition (electric current)

The unit is the ampere (${\mathrm{A}}$), also written $\mathrm{C\ s^{-1}}$.
The current ${I}$ is defined as the time derivative of the flowing charge ${Q}$: ${\displaystyle I=\frac{dQ}{dt}}$.

$1\ \mathrm{A} = 1\ \mathrm{C\ s^{-1}}$ corresponds to about $ 6.2415\times10^{18}$ electrons flowing per second.

articles.title: クーロン力とローレンツ力
articles.latexEn:
Law (force on a charged particle)

When a charged particle moves with velocity $\vec{v}$ in an electric field $\vec{E}$ and a magnetic field $\vec{B}$, the force it receives from the electromagnetic field is given by

$$ \vec{F} = q \bigl( \vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B} \bigr) $$
Explanation
  • $q \vec{E}$ is the force due to the electric field and is called the Coulomb force.
  • $q \vec{v} \times \vec{B}$ is the force due to the magnetic field and is called the Lorentz force. (Sometimes the electric force is also included under the name Lorentz force.)
    (The symbol “$\times$” denotes the vector cross product; its direction is fixed by the right-handed screw rule.)
Remarks
  • The magnetic force is always orthogonal to $\vec{v}$, so it does no work (it does not change the speed).
  • How the force appears depends on the observer.
    What one observer sees as a “Coulomb force on a charge at rest” may appear to another as a “Lorentz force on a moving charge”.
  • Likewise, the electric and magnetic fields look different in different inertial frames.
    For example, a pure magnetic field for one observer may appear as both electric and magnetic fields to another. In relativity, the electric and magnetic fields are unified as the electromagnetic field tensor.

articles.title: 電場の定義
articles.latexEn:
Definition (magnitude of the electric field)
•When no magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is present, the magnitude of the electric field $\vec{E}$ is defined from the force $\vec{F}$ on a point charge $q$ as follows. $$ \vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q} $$ ※ This definition assumes that the charge $q$ is known.
Definition (direction of the electric field)
•The direction of the electric field is the same as the direction of the force on a positive charge.
•For a negative charge, the force is opposite to the electric field.

articles.title: 磁束密度の定義
articles.latexEn:
Definition (magnitude of magnetic flux density)
•When a current $I_0$ flows in a wire of length $\ell$, the magnitude $|\vec B|$ of the magnetic flux density is defined from the force $\vec{F}$ on the wire as follows. $$ \vec{B} = \frac{\vec{F}}{I_0 \ell} $$
Definition (direction of magnetic flux density)
•The direction of the magnetic flux density is always perpendicular to both the current and the force, and is fixed by the right-hand rule.

articles.title: 定義および命題
articles.latexEn:
Definition of flux of a uniform vector field through a plane The flux of a uniform vector field $ \vec F $ through a plane $S$ of area $A$ is defined by
$$ \Phi = |\vec F | A \cos\theta = ( \vec F \cdot \vec n )A $$ ※ Here $\theta$ is the angle between the unit normal $ \vec n $ to the plane and the field $\vec F$.
Definition of flux in general (surface integral)
In general, the flux of a vector field $\vec F$ that may vary in direction and magnitude through a surface $S$ is defined by $$\begin{aligned} \iint_S \vec F\cdot d\vec S & : = \lim_{| P | \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} (\vec F_i\cdot\vec n_i)\,\Delta S_i\\[4pt] &\;\Bigl(= \lim_{| P | \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} |\vec F_i|\cos\theta_i\,\Delta S_i\Bigr) \end{aligned}$$
Definition of symbols
  • $P$ : a partition of the surface $S$
  • $N(P)$ : number of partition regions
  • $R_i$ : the $i$-th partition region
  • $\operatorname{diam}(R_i) : $ diameter of $R_i$ (largest distance between points in $R_i$)
  • $|P| : $ $ \displaystyle \max_i \operatorname{diam}(R_i)$, the largest diameter among partition regions.
  • $\vec F_i$ : the vector field at a representative point of the $i$-th region
  • $\vec n_i$ : the unit normal at a representative point of the $i$-th region
  • $\theta_i$ : angle between $ \vec F_i $ and $ \vec n_i $
  • $\vec F_i\cdot\vec n_i\,\Delta S_i,\ |\vec F_i|\cos\theta_i\,\Delta S_i$: approximate flux of $\vec F$ through region $R_i$
Proposition: If $|\vec F|$ is a constant $F$ on a surface $\Sigma $ and the angle with the unit normal is a constant $ \theta $ on the surface, then with area $A$ of $S$, the flux is $$ \iint_S \vec F\cdot d\vec S = F\cos\theta\cdot A $$

Proof
By definition $$ \iint_S \vec F\cdot d\vec S = \lim_{| P | \to 0}\sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} (\vec F_i\cdot\vec n_i)\,\Delta S_i $$ At each representative point $|\vec F_i|=F$ and $ \vec F_i\cdot\vec n_i=F\cos\theta$, so $$ \sum_{i=1}^{N(P)} (\vec F_i\cdot\vec n_i)\,\Delta S_i = F\cos\theta\sum_{i=1}^{N(P)}\Delta S_i $$ Here $\sum_{i=1}^{N(P)}\Delta S_i$ is the sum of the areas of all partition regions, hence equals $ A $. Therefore $$ \iint_S \vec F\cdot d\vec S = \lim_{| P | \to 0}\Bigl(F\cos\theta\cdot A \Bigr)= F\cos\theta\cdot A $$　Q.E.D

articles.title: 電場のガウスの法則
articles.titleEn: Gauss\'s law for the electric field
articles.latexEn:
Law (Gauss's law for charge and the electric field): For any closed surface $S$, the following holds. This is called Gauss's law for the electric field. $$ \oint_{S} \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0} \displaystyle \sum_{\text{inside }S} Q $$ ※$\varepsilon_0 = \fallingdotseq 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$ : permittivity of free space (a constant)
Explanation

•Left-hand side: the net electric flux through the closed surface (outward positive)
•Right-hand side: the total charge enclosed by the surface
•Gauss's law for the electric field states that positive charge is a source of electric field lines and negative charge is a sink.
•The net electric flux is proportional to the total enclosed charge, with proportionality constant equal to the reciprocal of the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$.
※ The law also holds in matter; in material media one often rewrites it using $\vec D$ after separating free charges from bound charges in dielectrics.

articles.title: 磁場のガウスの法則
articles.titleEn: Gauss\'s law for the magnetic field
articles.latexEn:
Law (Gauss's law for the magnetic field): For any closed surface $S$, the following holds. This is called Gauss's law for the magnetic field. $$ \oint_{S} \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{S} = 0 $$
Explanation

•Right-hand side: the net magnetic flux through the closed surface (outward positive)
•Because isolated magnetic charges do not exist, magnetic field lines neither begin nor end. Hence $\vec{B}$ always forms closed loops, and the magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero
※ Gauss's law for the magnetic field also holds in matter; it is often rewritten using $\vec D$ and $\vec H$ after separating free and bound contributions of currents and charges.

articles.title: ファラデーの電磁誘導の法則
articles.latexEn:
Definition (magnetic flux)

Define the magnetic flux (the surface integral of magnetic flux density) by $$ \Phi_B := \iint_S \vec B\cdot d\vec S $$ .

Definition (induced electromotive force)

$$ V := \oint_{\partial S} \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} $$ represents the circulation work done by the electric field produced by electromagnetic induction on a unit charge. This is called the induced EMF.

Definition (induced current)

When the induced EMF causes a current to flow in a circuit, that current is called an induced current.

Law of electromagnetic induction (integral form)

“A time change of magnetic flux produces circulation work on a unit charge (an induced EMF).”
This is the law of electromagnetic induction, written as $$ \oint_{\partial S} \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} = -\frac{d}{dt}\iint_{S} \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{S}. $$ ※ The normal $\vec{n}$ of the surface $S$ and the orientation of $\partial S$ are linked by the right-hand rule.
※ The law also holds in matter and is commonly used in this form.

Proposition (Lenz's law)

From the law of electromagnetic induction and the Ampère–Maxwell law, the meaning of the minus sign ($-$) is that the induced current flows in the direction such that the magnetic field it produces opposes the original change of flux.

Remark: when a conductor moves

When a conductor moves, an additional EMF due to the Lorentz force appears in the circuit.
That is, when the surface $S(t)$ or boundary $\partial S(t)$ evolves in time, letting $\vec v$ be the velocity of each point on the boundary and including the motional term gives $$ \oint_{\partial S(t)} (\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B)\cdot d\vec r = -\frac{d}{dt}\iint_{S(t)}\vec B\cdot d\vec S $$ ※ The EMF from the motional term $\vec v\times\vec B$ also obeys Lenz's law and drives a current that opposes the flux change.

articles.title: アンペール・マクスウェルの法則
articles.latexEn:
Definition (displacement current)

The time derivative of the product of the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$ and the electric flux $\displaystyle \iint_S \vec E\cdot d\vec S$, namely $ \displaystyle \frac{d}{dt} \Biggl(\varepsilon_0 \iint_S \vec E\cdot d\vec S \Biggr)$, is called the displacement current.

Ampère–Maxwell law (integral form)

“Current and displacement current produce the circulation of the magnetic field.” This is the Ampère–Maxwell law, written as $$ \oint_{\partial S} \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{r} = \mu_0 \Biggr( \sum_{\text{through }S} I + \varepsilon_0 \frac{d}{dt}\iint_S \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} \Biggl) $$ ※ The normal $\vec{n}$ of the surface $S$ and the orientation of $\partial S$ are linked by the right-hand rule.
※ The law also holds in matter; for fields in materials one often rewrites it using $\vec D$ and $\vec H$ after separating free charges/currents from bound ones.

Theorem: Ampère's law When the electric field does not change with time, one obtains Ampère's law: $$ \oint_{\partial S} \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{r} = \mu_0 \sum_{\text{through }S} I $$

Proof
By assumption the displacement-current term $\Biggr( \displaystyle \varepsilon_0 \frac{d}{dt}\iint_S \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} \Biggl)$ vanishes, so Ampère's law follows immediately from the Ampère–Maxwell law.

Definition (speed of light in vacuum, $c$)

The speed of light in vacuum is determined by the vacuum permittivity and permeability: $$ \displaystyle c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}}\fallingdotseq 2.99792458\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s} $$ ※ Using $c$, the Ampère–Maxwell law can be written $\displaystyle \oint_{\partial S} \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{r} = \mu_0 \sum_{\text{through }S} I + \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{d}{dt}\iint_S \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S}$.

articles.title: 無限に長い直線電流の作る磁場(真空中)
articles.titleEn: Magnetic field of an infinitely long straight current (in vacuum)
articles.latexEn:
Assumptions and notation
  • Space is vacuum
  • An infinitely long straight current $I[\mathrm{A}]$ flows concentrated at $r=0$ along the $z$-axis (the system is rotationally symmetric about $z$ and translationally symmetric in $z$)
  • There is no displacement current
  • Unit vector in the $z$ direction: $\hat{\mathbf z}$
  • Radial unit vector: $\hat{\mathbf r}$
  • Azimuthal unit vector: $\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$
  • The magnetic field produced is $ \overrightarrow H=H_r(r,\phi,z)\,\hat{\mathbf r}+H_\phi(r,\phi,z)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}+H_z(r,\phi,z)\,\hat{\mathbf z} $
Theorem: Under the above assumptions, $\overrightarrow H = \displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r} \, \hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$
We prove this using Propositions 1–6.

Proposition 1: The field components depend only on $r$: $\displaystyle \overrightarrow H=H_r(r)\,\hat{\mathbf r}+H_\phi(r)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}+H_z(r)\,\hat{\mathbf z} $
Proof
In general write $\displaystyle \overrightarrow H=H_r(r,\phi,z)\,\hat{\mathbf r}+H_\phi(r,\phi,z)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}+H_z(r,\phi,z)\,\hat{\mathbf z} $ . Rotational symmetry about $z$ and translational symmetry in $z$ imply independence of $\phi$ and $z$, so each component is a function of $r$ alone: $\displaystyle \overrightarrow H=H_r(r)\,\hat{\mathbf r}+H_\phi(r)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}+H_z(r)\,\hat{\mathbf z} $. $\square$
Proposition 2: For a closed cylindrical surface of radius $r$ and height $L$, $\displaystyle \oint_A \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow A = 2\pi r L \times H_r(r)$
Proof
Compute the flux through the top, bottom, and side.
[1] Bottom: only the $z$ component contributes. The outward flux is $\displaystyle \int_{A_{under}} \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow A = - \displaystyle \int_{S} H_z(r) dS $
[2] Top: outward flux $\displaystyle \int_{A_{over}} \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow A = \displaystyle \int_{S} H_z(r) dS$
[3] Side: only the $r$ component contributes: $\displaystyle \int_{A_{side}} \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow A = \displaystyle \int_{S} H_r(r) dS = 2\pi r L \times H_r(r)$
Summing, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \oint_A \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow A &= - \displaystyle \int_{S} H_z(r) dS + \displaystyle \int_{S} H_z(r) dS + 2\pi r L \times H_r(r) \\ &= 2\pi r L \times H_r(r) \end{aligned}$$ $\square$
Proposition 3: For any $r$, $H_r(r)=0$
Proof
Gauss's law for the magnetic field: $\displaystyle \oint_A \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow A = 0$.
By Proposition 2, $\displaystyle 2\pi r L \times H_r(r) = 0 \Leftrightarrow H_r(r) = 0 $ $\square$
Proposition 4: The $z$ component $H_z(r)$ is independent of position
Proof
For a rectangular loop in the $rz$-plane with vertical sides at $r=r_1$ and $r=r_2$, $\displaystyle \oint_C \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow l = \displaystyle H_z(r_1)L - H_z(r_2)L$ . The loop encloses no current, so Ampère's law gives $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \oint_C \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow{l} &= 0 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow H_z(r_1) - H_z(r_2) &= 0 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow H_z(r_1) &= H_z(r_2) \end{aligned}$$ . Since $r_1,r_2$ are arbitrary, $H_z(r)$ is constant. $\square$
Proposition 5: The azimuthal component is $ \displaystyle H_\phi(r) = \frac{I} {2\pi r} $
Proof
On a concentric circle of radius $r$, $\displaystyle \oint_C \overrightarrow H \cdot d\overrightarrow l = H_\phi(r) \times 2\pi r $ . Ampère's law gives $$ \displaystyle H_\phi(r) \times 2\pi r = I \Leftrightarrow H_\phi(r) = \displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r}\ \ \square $$
Proposition 6: The field can be written $\overrightarrow H = \displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r} \, \hat{\boldsymbol\phi} + H_{z0} \, \hat{\mathbf z}$ (with $H_{z0}$ a position-independent constant)
Proof
Proposition 3: $H_r=0$; Proposition 4: $H_z=H_{z0}$; Proposition 5: $H_{\phi}=\displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r}$.
Combining with Proposition 1, $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \overrightarrow H &= H_r(r)\,\hat{\mathbf r}+H_\phi(r)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}+H_z(r)\,\hat{\mathbf z} \\[6pt] &= \displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r} \, \hat{\boldsymbol\phi} + H_{z0} \, \hat{\mathbf z} \end{aligned}$$ $\square $
Theorem: $\overrightarrow H = \displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r} \, \hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$
Proof
By Proposition 6 it remains to show $H_{z0} = 0$.
Imposing that the field vanish at infinity, $$\begin{aligned} & \lim_{r\to\infty}|\overrightarrow H| = 0 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow & \lim_{r\to\infty} \sqrt{\overrightarrow H \cdot \overrightarrow H} = 0 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow &\lim_{r\to\infty} \sqrt{\Bigl(\displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r} \, \hat{\boldsymbol\phi} + H_{z0} \, \hat{\mathbf z} \Bigr) \cdot \Bigl(\displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r} \, \hat{\boldsymbol\phi} + H_{z0} \, \hat{\mathbf z} \Bigr)} = 0 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow &\lim_{r\to\infty} \sqrt{\Bigl(\displaystyle \frac{I}{2\pi r} \Bigr)^2 + H_{z0}^2} = 0 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow & \sqrt{ H_{z0}^2} = 0 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow &|H_{z0}| = 0 \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow &H_{z0} = 0 \\[6pt] \end{aligned}$$ $\square$
