articles.title: 分極, 電気感受率, 誘電率, 比誘電率
articles.titleEn: Polarization, electric susceptibility, permittivity, and relative permittivity
articles.latexEn:
Definition (vacuum permittivity: $\varepsilon_0$)

The vacuum permittivity is an electromagnetic constant; in SI units its approximate value is $$ \displaystyle \varepsilon_0 \fallingdotseq 8.854\,187\,817\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m} $$ .

Definition (electric dipole)

When two point charges $+q$ and $-q$ of equal magnitude and opposite sign are separated by a displacement vector $\vec d$, the pair is an electric dipole. By convention $\vec d$ points from the negative to the positive charge, and the electric dipole moment $\vec p$ is $$ \vec p = q \vec d $$ (unit: $C\cdot m$).

Definition (polarization)

When an external electric field is applied, electron clouds in molecules or atoms of a dielectric shift slightly relative to the nuclei, so the centers of positive and negative charge separate. This phenomenon is polarization. (As a result, an electric dipole is induced in each molecule or atom.)

Definition (polarization vector)

When an electric field is applied to a dielectric, its constituent molecules polarize and electric dipoles appear. The electric dipole moment per unit volume is called the polarization vector.

Definition (electric susceptibility: $\chi_e\ $)

When the polarization vector responds linearly to the applied field, it can be written $$ \displaystyle \vec P = \chi_e\,\varepsilon_0\,\vec E $$ where $\chi_e$ is the electric susceptibility, measuring the strength of the dipole response in the medium.

Definition (electric displacement)
Define the electric displacement $\vec D$ from the electric field and the polarization $\vec P$ by $$ \vec D = \varepsilon_0 \vec E + \vec P $$
Proposition (electric displacement in vacuum): In vacuum the relation between $\vec D$ and $\vec E$ is $$ \vec D = \varepsilon_0 \vec E $$
Proof
In vacuum there is no polarization, so $\vec P = \vec 0\ $, and the result follows at once. Q.E.D

Definition (permittivity: $\varepsilon$)

Combining $\vec D=\varepsilon_0\vec E+\vec P$ with $\vec P = \chi_e \varepsilon_0 \vec E$, in a linear isotropic medium one obtains $$\begin{aligned} \vec D &= \varepsilon_0\vec E+\vec P\\[6pt] &=\varepsilon_0\vec E + \chi_e\,\varepsilon_0\,\vec E\\[6pt] &= \varepsilon \vec E \quad ;\ \varepsilon=\varepsilon_0(1+\chi_e) \end{aligned}$$ . This $\varepsilon$ is the permittivity of the medium. The unit is farad per meter ($\mathrm{F/m}$).

Definition (relative permittivity: $\varepsilon_r$)

$$ \displaystyle \varepsilon_r \equiv \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0} = 1+\chi_e $$ is the relative permittivity. In vacuum $\varepsilon_r=1$.

Proposition (electric field $\vec E$ in a linear medium): In a linear medium, using the definitions above, the electric displacement can be written in terms of $\vec E$ as $$ \displaystyle \vec D = \varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0 \vec E $$

Proof
In a linear medium $\vec D = \varepsilon \vec E\ $, and by definition $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0\ $, so $\displaystyle \vec D = \varepsilon \vec E = \varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0 \vec E\ $.　Q.E.D

articles.title: 磁化, 磁化率, 透磁率, 比透磁率
articles.titleEn: Magnetization, magnetic susceptibility, permeability, and relative permeability
articles.latexEn:
Definition (vacuum permeability: $\mu_0$)

The vacuum permeability is the reference magnetic constant; a conventional value is $$ \displaystyle \mu_0 \fallingdotseq 4\pi\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H/m} $$ (treated as a standard SI constant). In vacuum $\vec B=\mu_0\vec H$ holds.

Definition (magnetic dipole)

A magnetic dipole produced by a current loop or a localized circulating current is called a magnetic dipole.

Properties
  • A single magnetic dipole experiences a torque in an external field $\vec B$: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\tau}=\vec m\times\vec B$.
Definition (magnetization vector: $M$)

When a magnetic field is applied to matter, the circulating currents of constituent molecules align and behave as magnetic dipoles. The magnetic dipole moment per unit volume is the magnetization vector, denoted $\vec M$.

Definition (magnetic field: $\vec H $)
Define the magnetic field $\vec H$ from the magnetic flux density $\vec B$ and the magnetization $\vec M$ by $$ \vec H = \frac {\vec B - \vec M}{\mu_0} $$
Proposition (relation in vacuum): In vacuum the relation between $\vec B$ and $\vec H$ is $$ \vec B = \mu_0 \vec H $$
Proof

In vacuum there is no magnetization, so $\vec {M}= \vec 0\ $. Hence $$\begin{aligned} &\vec H = \frac {\vec B}{\mu_0} \\[6pt] \Leftrightarrow & \vec B = \mu_0 \vec H \end{aligned}$$ 　Q.E.D

Definition (magnetic susceptibility: $\chi_m$)

When the magnetization responds linearly to an applied field, it can be written $$ \vec M = \chi_m\,\mu_0\,\vec H $$ where $\chi_m$ is the magnetic susceptibility, measuring the magnetic response of electrons and atoms in the medium.

Theorem (relation in a linear isotropic medium)
In a linear isotropic medium, $\vec B=\mu_0( 1 + \chi_m\,)\vec H$ in terms of magnetization $ \vec {M}$ and $\vec H$.

Proof
Combining $\vec B = \mu_0 \vec H + \vec {M} $ with $\displaystyle \vec {M} = \chi_m\,\mu_0\,\vec H$ gives $$\begin{aligned} \vec B &= \mu_0 \vec H+\vec {M} \\[6pt] &= \mu_0( 1 + \chi_m\,) \vec H \\[6pt] \end{aligned}$$ .

Definition (permeability: $\mu$)
The coefficient of $\vec H$ above, $\mu_0(1+\chi_m)$, is the permeability of the linear isotropic medium, written simply $\mu$. The unit is henry per meter ($\mathrm{H/m}$).

Definition (relative permeability: $\mu_r$)

$$ \displaystyle \mu_r \equiv \frac{\mu}{\mu_0} = 1+\chi_m $$ is defined as the relative permeability. In vacuum $\mu_r=1$.

Proposition (magnetic field $\vec H$ in a linear medium): In a linear medium, using the definitions of permeability and relative permeability, $\vec B$ can be written in terms of $\vec H$ as $$ \displaystyle \vec B = \mu_r \mu_0 \vec H $$

Proof
In a linear medium $\vec B = \mu \vec H\ $, and by definition $\mu = \mu_r \mu_0\ $, so $\displaystyle \vec B = \mu \vec H = \mu_r \mu_0 \vec H\ $.　Q.E.D

Definition (right-hand rule)
When the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of $\vec{n}$, the curling direction of the fingers gives the positive orientation of the boundary.
